Physical modelling gave a 50 times energy improvement, 4.05 against 201 picojoules per operation in the reported comparison. TinyLlama-1.1B fits one 520 square millimetre die at 52 dollars; Llama-2-7B needs eight chiplets. Hardwiring raises extraction costs from a 2,000 dollar software dump to over 50,000 dollars of equipment.
arxiv-2511-22989:
Oshima and colleagues built MultiBanana, a benchmark for a newer image-generation skill: taking the look of subjects from several reference images at once and faithfully re-rendering them in a new scene. Existing tests mostly used one or a few references, so they could not show where models break as references multiply or become harder to combine.

The benchmark's 3,769 tasks vary five difficulty axes, including how many references are given. The axes include clashes between photo and anime styles, big scale gaps between reference and target, rare concepts such as a red banana, and instructions in several languages. Evaluating leading open and closed models, the team found two failure modes as references increase: models either ignore the editing instructions or collapse while trying to follow them. Cross-domain, rare-concept, and multilingual tasks stayed hard for every model tested in the study.
arxiv-2511-23089:
Švrčková and colleagues present a full study of δ Circini, a hierarchical triple of massive O- and B-type stars in which a close eclipsing binary, orbiting every 3.9 days, is circled by a third star. They combined TESS light curves, new and archival echelle spectra, and VLTI interferometry to pin down both orbits and all three stars at once.

The outer period is refined to 1603.24 days, measured to within a fifth of a day, both orbits lie in the same plane so no Kozai-Lidov tilting acts, and the system totals 53.04 solar masses at a distance of 809.9 parsecs, near the center of the young ASCC 79 population. Stellar models date the stars to roughly 4 to 5 million years and predict the inner pair will merge in about 1.7 million years, forming a roughly 36-solar-mass star that ends as a black hole.
arxiv-2511-23189:
Briganti and colleagues compute how blue straggler stars made by collisions would ring if they pulsate, offering a seismic test of how these youthful stars in globular clusters formed. Blue stragglers look younger than their cluster mates because collisions, mergers, or mass transfer rebuilt them. And the team modeled a grid of collision products at low metallicity, one percent of the Sun's metal content.

Against ordinary single-star models of the same mass, the collision products follow similar lives but keep a peculiar internal chemical layering. The layering leaves fingerprints in their high-order gravity modes, the slow internal oscillations that probe a star's deep interior. The altered layering adds a slope change in the composition profile and an extra peak in the buoyancy frequency. This produces periodic modulations in the period spacing pattern, a signature future observations with missions like PLATO could use to identify collision-born stars.
arxiv-2511-23289:
Skolimowski and colleagues model gray tin, the α-Sn allotrope, and find it carries two kinds of topology at once. A Z2 invariant and a nonzero mirror Chern number, a rare pairing. Their tight-binding model, built from density-functional calculations with a bond angle to mimic in-plane strain. Maps how the topological phase of multilayer films depends on strain and on the number of layers.

The quantum spin Hall state, the phase with protected helical edge channels, appears only under compressive strain and only once the film exceeds five layers. Surprisingly, both the trivial and the topological phases host edge states inside the bulk energy gap, sitting on the slab's side surfaces, its top and bottom faces. Or its hinges, and the team traces them to one-dimensional winding numbers in a chiral-symmetric limit of the model, warning they could distort the edge transport experiments seek.
arxiv-2512-00089:
Forecasting wildfires weeks or months ahead is difficult, yet fire managers need that lead time. Ioannis Prapas and five co-authors present TeleViT in a 2025 study, a vision transformer built for subseasonal to seasonal wildfire forecasts. Short-term fire forecasts lean on local weather, but long-range ones cannot.

Long-range patterns depend on teleconnections, the links between climate patterns in distant parts of the Earth. TeleViT is designed to account for those global patterns when it predicts fire risk. Better seasonal outlooks could help agencies plan fuel treatments and place crews and equipment before fire season peaks. Fire agencies already use seasonal outlooks, so even modest gains in skill have practical value.
arxiv-2512-00289:
Physics-based vehicle models are simplified on purpose, so they never match a real car exactly. Nguyen Ly and co-authors develop a data-driven framework for learning and correcting vehicle dynamics in 2025. The dynamics are non-autonomous, driven by time-dependent control inputs.

Learning predictive models directly from temporal snapshot data is challenging when controls keep changing the system's behavior. The framework aims to correct model-form uncertainty rather than discard the physics model entirely. More faithful vehicle models support safer self-driving tests, better simulators, and control systems that trust their own predictions. Correction, rather than replacement, keeps the physical knowledge already inside standard models. Snapshot data is what test tracks and fleets actually record.
arxiv-2512-00389:
Adversarial training and AI alignment can both be framed as games between two neural networks. Deep Patel and Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis study solving such neural min-max games in 2025, focusing on architecture, initialization, and dynamics. The desirable outcomes are von Neumann-Nash equilibria of the game.

These games usually have non-convex, non-concave objectives, yet simple gradient methods often converge in practice. That puzzle suggests hidden geometric structure in the problems. Understanding when and why training converges would make robust optimization and alignment methods more dependable across applications. Zero-sum framing fits adversarial training, where one network attacks and the other defends. Von Neumann's name on the equilibrium ties the work to classic game theory.
arxiv-2512-00589:
Cygnus X-2 is a bright X-ray binary where matter spirals from a star onto a neutron star. Misaki Mizumoto and co-authors present XRISM observations of its accretion disk corona in 2025. The high-resolution spectrum precisely characterizes iron emission lines from the corona.

The corona appears to have at least two distinct regions. The observations also suggest a possible ultra-fast outflow leaving the system. XRISM's sharp spectroscopy lets astronomers separate these components, refining the picture of how accreting neutron stars heat and expel the gas falling onto them. Z-sources are the brightest class of neutron star binaries, and Cyg X-2 is their prototype. Iron lines are the sharpest fingerprints in the X-ray band.
arxiv-2512-01089:
Peter Jansen, Samiah Hassan, and Pragnya Narasimha present CodeDistiller in a 2025 paper on scientific coding agents. Automated scientific discovery systems generate and run code-based experiments on their own. Their reach is limited by the code they can reliably produce from built-in knowledge alone.

Current systems either mutate a few hand-crafted examples or work purely from what the model already knows. CodeDistiller automatically generates code libraries for such agents, distilling dependable routines they can reuse. A good library would raise both the quality and reach of automated experiments, letting agents attempt studies that free-form code generation cannot sustain.
arxiv-2512-01189:
Chunzheng Zhu and six coauthors reconstruct speech gestures from brain signals in a 2025 paper. Decoding what the brain is doing has long challenged brain science. Most earlier work rebuilt images or language from brain activity, asking what a person saw or heard.

Their work instead reconstructs co-speech gestures, the hand and body movements that accompany speech a person perceives. The method, fMRI2GES, reads functional MRI signals and uses two matched decoding steps to turn them into gestures. Rebuilding perceived gestures extends brain decoding from words and pictures into body language, a new channel for brain-computer interfaces.
arxiv-2512-01389:
Haoyu Lei and co-authors build a fast decoder for error correction codes. Those codes guard digital messages from noise. New diffusion-based decoders are sharp but slow. They need many rounds of sampling to clean a message. That lag hurts low-delay uses.

Their model uses consistency flow to decode in one step. It keeps a transformer core for strength. One-step decoding cuts delay by a large margin. If accuracy holds, the method could serve in fast links like mobile and satellite systems where each delay counts. One-step decoding also cuts energy use per message, which counts for battery-powered links in phones, sensors, and small satellites.
arxiv-2512-01489:
Girardi and a large Euclid team give the first census of dusty, massive objects in the Perseus field. How stars formed long ago rests on far-off dusty galaxies. Those galaxies hide much of their light in dust. Euclid's sharp wide views can find them in bulk.

The team counts dusty and massive systems in early release data. They gauge their traits and how common they are. A firm census anchors claims about star birth at early times. It also shows what Euclid will add over its full survey of the sky.
arxiv-2512-01689:
A study extends the Klebanov theorem to a product group of reals and a two-element group. Klebanov's result links linear forms in independent random variables. It asks when distinct forms can share the same law. Such results sit in probability's core limit theory.

The extension moves the setting to variables on that product group. Linear forms are built the same way from shared inputs. Group structure changes what equality of laws forces. Results like this refine when sums of random parts must be Gaussian or near it. Group-valued variables arise in directional data and phase systems, so the extension speaks to applied probability as well as pure theory.
arxiv-2512-01889:
A robot or headset builds a map of its surroundings while tracking its own motion, a task called SLAM. A 2025 paper by Zaid Nasser and nine co-authors presents KM-ViPE, a real-time system that does this from a single ordinary camera, with no depth sensor and no advance calibration.

The system also labels what it sees in open vocabulary, meaning users can query objects by name rather than a fixed list. It works directly on raw video streams, even where the scene itself is moving. That makes it suited to head-worn, first-person applications and to learning from the huge supply of everyday internet video.
arxiv-2512-01989:
Physical AI aims at models that can perceive the real world and predict how it changes, a skill robots and vehicles depend on. Fengzhe Zhou and co-authors introduce PAI-Bench in 2025, a broad benchmark for measuring how well today's multimodal language models and video generators support that aim.

How far current models really grasp physical dynamics was poorly understood, because most benchmarks test words and pictures, not motion and cause. PAI-Bench evaluates models on their ability to perceive and forecast real-world behavior. The results give the field a shared yardstick for a capability that matters more as AI moves into physical settings.
arxiv-2512-02189:
NVIDIA's Blackwell generation of graphics processors adds fifth-generation tensor cores, a new tensor memory, and a dual-chip design aimed at machine learning and exascale computing. Aaron Jarmusch and Sunita Chandrasekaran microbenchmark the B200 architecture in 2025 to learn what these changes mean in practice.

Microbenchmarks poke one feature at a time, measuring exactly how fast each piece of hardware is rather than trusting headline numbers. The performance implications of the new architecture were poorly understood across diverse workloads. Careful measurements like these tell programmers how to write code that actually uses the silicon they paid for.
arxiv-2512-02289:
DocETL is an open-source system that runs language-model pipelines over messy, unstructured document collections, used in fields from journalism to law and medicine. Lindsey Wei and five co-authors extend it in 2025 with agentic rewrites that optimize these pipelines against several goals at once.

A year after release, the system had gathered thousands of users and GitHub stars across many domains. The new work lets an agent rewrite a data-processing pipeline and judge the rewrite on multiple objectives, like cost and accuracy together. Automated optimization of document pipelines could make large-scale text analysis cheaper and better at the same time.
arxiv-2512-02389:
Self-correction, noticing and fixing one's own mistakes, is something language models are usually taught by expensive reinforcement learning. David Wu and three co-authors test in 2025 a cheaper idea borrowed from driving and robotics: inject synthetic errors during supervised training and teach the model to recover.

Their title delivers the verdict: the trick fails to elicit genuine self-correction. Negative results of this clarity save a field from wandering down an attractive dead end. They also sharpen the question of what reinforcement learning provides that supervised exposure to mistakes does not, a question at the center of reasoning research.
arxiv-2512-02489:
Mithra D K takes on a hard health data problem: many measured traits, but few patients to learn from. Using NHANES survey data, the 2025 study tries to predict who has diabetes. Data shaped like this, with far more inputs than cases, can easily fool standard models.

The author first tests plain baselines, including logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. A hybrid model then pairs an XGBoost feature encoder with a small neural network head. Shrinking the input before the final step aims for steadier predictions, a useful pattern for clinics holding rich but small datasets. The same trick may help with heart, lung, or blood tests that share this shape of data.
arxiv-2512-02589:
Junyi Hou and four co-authors build an AI helper that lives inside the writing editor itself. Large language models already assist academic writing, but most tools sit outside the document. Cut off from structure and revision history, they cannot do deep, context aware work on a draft.

PaperDebugger is a plugin based multi agent system for editors such as Overleaf. Its agents review, edit, and polish text where the author actually writes. Help that sees the whole draft, and its past versions, could make AI feedback sharper and easier for scholars to accept or reject. Help that sits in the draft can flag a weak claim at the line where it first shows up.
arxiv-2512-02989:
Tommaso Tenna designs a relaxation scheme for flows moving through canal like networks. Hyperbolic conservation laws govern such flows, with physical conditions imposed where channels meet at a junction. Shallow water and blood flow equations both fit this network pattern.

The scheme approximates solutions without leaning on approximate Riemann solvers at each junction. A strategy drawn from earlier work handles the coupling cleanly. Robust network solvers help engineers model irrigation canals, flood channels, and blood vessel trees, where junction behavior decides the whole system's response. Joints are where net flows break ranks. A scheme that treats joints with care earns its keep on each run of a long canal or a heart tree.
arxiv-2512-03089:
A safe off switch for a rogue AI agent is the idea here. Kai Williams, Rohan Subramani, and Francis Rhys Ward set out the plan in this 2025 work. Top AI firms may fail to align or control very strong agents, they note.

Their plan uses a password to trigger a safe shutdown. The agent is built so that, given the password, it stops in a set way. A clear stop rule could block harm in the real world. The work adds a fresh tool to talks on how to keep strong AI under human control. Safety teams could treat the password plan as one layer in a wider control system for future agents.
arxiv-2512-03289:
Music software gives control, but it can break a creative flow. Aaron Elkins and co-authors present DAWZY, an AI helper for music making, in this 2025 work. Turning a wish like warm the vocals into many small edits is slow in normal workstations.

Most AI music tools generate a whole track at once, leaving little room for the human. DAWZY turns text, voice, or hummed requests into reversible actions inside REAPER software. Users can undo steps and keep shaping the piece. The tool aims to keep people in charge of their music. Reversible edits respect the artist, since each AI action can be tried, judged, and undone in the session.
arxiv-2512-03389:
Data streams never stop, but language models usually answer once. Shu Chen, Deepti Raghavan, and Uğur Çetintemel bridge that gap in this 2025 work. Monitoring streams needs steady, meaning-aware computing over text that keeps arriving.

They introduce Continuous Prompts, a framework that brings model reasoning into stream processing. It is presented as the first of its kind for long-running analytics. Persistent prompts could watch news, logs, or sensor text for patterns as they form. That would extend AI help to live operations, not just one-off questions. Persistent processing suits alerts and dashboards, where questions stay open for weeks.
arxiv-2512-03489:
Sharp inequalities govern how functions spread on finite groups. Gan Yao proves optimal bounds of that kind in this 2025 work. The setting is cyclic groups whose sizes are powers of two, sometimes times three.

Yao studies a Poisson-like semigroup tied to word length on the group. He proves it is hypercontractive between the stated function spaces. He also addresses log-Sobolev inequalities, which control entropy decay. Optimal constants matter in probability, analysis, and theoretical computer science, where these tools are used daily. Word length geometry drives the semigroup, linking combinatorics to analytic bounds.
arxiv-2512-03789:
Colour the vertices of a tree with three colours so neighbours always differ, then ask how many single-vertex changes separate the two most distant colourings. Shamil Asgarli, Sara Krehbiel, Simon MacLean, and Gjergji Zaimi study that distance in a 2025 combinatorics preprint. The colourings themselves become vertices of a new graph, with edges joining colourings that differ at exactly one vertex.

The diameter of that colouring graph measures the worst-case number of steps between two valid colourings. To compute it, the authors introduce balanced labellings of the tree and prove the diameter equals the largest L1 norm among them. That equivalence turns a hard graph problem into something tractable. With it, they find the maximum and minimum possible diameters across all trees on a given number of vertices. They also characterise exactly which trees achieve those extremes.
arxiv-2512-04089:
WebAssembly promises one program that runs anywhere, from a browser tab to a cloud server, inside a tight sandbox. Mario Colosi and colleagues test that promise for serverless workflows in a 2025 distributed computing preprint. They run the same workflow across browser, edge, and cloud deployments and measure where time and resources actually go.

The setup uses WebAssembly modules with a standard system interface: a web worker in the browser, and a lightweight streaming layer on edge and cloud machines. The team records total completion time, throughput, per-step delays, and how long cold and warm starts take, plus processor and memory use. Ahead-of-time compilation and keeping instances warm cut startup latency substantially. With small payloads, the browser stayed competitive thanks to fully in-memory exchanges. As payloads grew and work turned compute-heavy, edge and cloud nodes pulled distinctly ahead.
arxiv-2512-04289:
Lina Buitrago, Juan Sosa, and Oscar Melo tackle a gap in the study of data that come as shares of a whole, such as the mix of land uses in each county. For ordinary maps, a classic score tells whether near places look alike. No matching score existed for share data, so the team built one and named it Reyes's I in this 2025 arXiv paper.

The new score uses the special geometry that fits share data, and it stays the same if the shares are scaled, reordered, or coded in a new way. The authors work out what value to expect by chance and give exact and computer-run tests for judging a result. In trial runs on made-up maps, the score stayed steady and beat a plain first try, which makes it a sound tool for maps of shares.
arxiv-2512-04689:
Dan Hu, Shida Fan, Zhongsheng Yuan, and co-authors present X-ray views of SPT-CL J0217-5014, a massive galaxy cluster sitting where cosmic filaments cross. The cluster lies at redshift about one half, with a mass hundreds of trillions of times the Sun's. An earlier survey flagged it for record iron richness and a possibly disturbed shape. Their 2025 arXiv paper uses the Chandra observatory for a closer look at its hot gas.

The gas shows clear signs of disturbance. A brightness edge cuts the western side, while a tail-like streak reaches east. The best-fit metal level across the inner region lands well below the earlier record claim, near six tenths of the Sun's share. Central density, entropy, and cooling time mark the cluster as not a cool-core system. Such snapshots show clusters still assembling at cosmic intersections, stirring their gas as they grow.
arxiv-2512-04889:
Julia Pfitzer, Martin Uecker, Hermann Scharfetter, and co-authors present FENCE, a flexible shield that lets low-field MRI scanners work without a shielded room. Portable low-field scanners promise scans at the bedside and in small clinics. Electromagnetic interference from the building and the body floods their weak signals, though. Standard fixes cage the room, ground the patient with electrodes, or add costly cancellation hardware. Their 2025 arXiv paper tests a cheaper idea: block the interference where it couples in.

The team argues the interference couples mainly through capacitance from body to coil. First they segment the radio coil to cut that coupling. Then comes FENCE, a flexible printed-circuit shield worn inside, which blocks capacitive coupling while letting the magnetic MRI signal through. The approach preserves portability and patient comfort. Affordable shielding could carry MRI into rural clinics and intensive care units.
arxiv-2512-05089:
Eduardo Di Santi proposes a formal basis for how perception and representation work, in machines and in nature. His starting observation is that real processes do not produce arbitrary signals. The signals they can generate bunch into small, tidy regions of the space of possible signals. That bunching is why a learner can generalize from only a few examples. He formalizes that bunching with tools from functional analysis and topology.

In his framework, the valid signals of a process form a compact set with stable features, a measurable size, and a well-defined perceptual readout. He tests the idea on five real domains — railway switch machines, battery discharge, heart signals, sunlight, and tides — comparing real recordings with simulators where available. In each case the family's size and stability settle after surprisingly few samples, supporting the claim that compact signal families organize both physical processes and learned models.
arxiv-2512-05389:
Yuxuan Chen and seven co-authors present CLIO, a tour guide robot that gestures while it talks. Audio guides describe exhibits richly, but visitors struggle to find the detail being described. CLIO closes that gap with co-speech actions: it makes eye contact by tracking a visitor's face and blinking, and it aims attention with head movements and a laser pointer. A large language model coordinates the choreography with the narration script for each exhibit.

The team evaluated CLIO in a mock exhibition of historical photographs, collecting questionnaire feedback and eye-tracking data from visitors wearing mobile trackers. The engaging actions proved well designed, the robot demonstrably steered visitors' gaze to the right details, and engagement rose compared with an audio-only baseline. The study offers evidence that a robot's body — not just its script — is a working part of how museums can hold a visitor's attention.
arxiv-2512-05489:
Xiaoqing Liu, Yangshuai Wang, and Teng Zhao benchmark the optimizers used to fine-tune atomistic foundation models — the universal machine-learned potentials now reshaping computational materials science. Fine-tuning adapts a pretrained potential to a specific material, but the choice of optimization algorithm is usually habit, not evidence. The authors put seven first-order optimizers head to head across molecules, crystals, and liquids, scoring energy and forces, in and out of distribution, and traits like elastic moduli and phonon spectra.

Reading the results through preconditioning — each optimizer as a data-dependent reshaping of the gradient — they explain the winners. Two methods condition the curvature best and deliver the most accurate forces. Plain stochastic gradient descent lags and wobbles. A brief second-order polish afterwards further improves physical observables at no inference cost. The study gives practitioners both a ranking and a reason for it.
arxiv-2512-05689: Jörg Seiler's short paper in analysis introduces a new pseudodifferential calculus of Shubin type. Such calculi are toolkits for operators that mix differentiation with multiplication, and the Shubin family is tuned to problems on unbounded space. Seiler's version holds two kinds of operators side by side: those depending on a non-negative parameter, and those that do not. Within this one framework he constructs the resolvents of Shubin type operators and derives the expansion of their traces, giving later work one calculus for fixed and parameter dependent questions.
arxiv-2512-06389:
Manuel Rieger and nine co authors fight a failure mode of a prized defect in diamond. The defect, a silicon vacancy with a negative charge, can emit light in ways that suit quantum networks. Shine the right laser on it, though, and it can slip into a dark state that no longer glows.

The team shows the same laser, paired with steady electric fields, can flip the defect back fast. They lay metal fingers on the diamond surface to shape those fields. With the fields on, the glow under laser light rose at least threefold for most defects, and held steady for some. Defects near one electrode, dark without the field, lit up on command. Timed tests show the laser also frees charges that restore the glowing state within milliseconds. The fix gives builders firmer control of these quantum light sources.
arxiv-2512-06489:
Quentin Henry and Anna Heffernan compute how tides deform a neutron star locked in an oval orbit with a partner, a case raised by a real gravitational wave event. That event, the first with signs of an eccentric orbit, joined a neutron star to a black hole. Waveform models for such pairs must include how each body's tides respond as the pair swings close and apart, not just on round orbits.

Working in the post Newtonian frame, where gravity is treated as a series of corrections to Newton's laws, the authors include the main tidal shapes the star can take. They build a Kepler style parametrization of the steady motion, then give the separation and phase through the orbit in terms of frequency and eccentricity, carried to high order in that eccentricity. From the known radiation reaction they derive how the orbit's shape and size drift over time.
arxiv-2512-06789:
Dinh Van Duong and Tuan Anh Dao widen the conditions under which a damped wave equation is known to have solutions that last for all time. The equation models waves that lose energy as they travel, with a nonlinearity that depends on the wave's rate of change, raised to a power. Matsumura's pioneering work in the nineteen seventies set the first thresholds on that power for global solutions, by dimension.

The new result extends those thresholds: in one and two dimensions any power above one now works, and in three dimensions the bar drops to three halves. Their approach builds carefully weighted spaces for the solutions and leans on tools from harmonic analysis plus a fixed point argument. Knowing the exact range where solutions cannot blow up matters wherever damped waves model real media, from acoustics to materials.
arxiv-2512-07089:
Chase Jenquin and co-authors watch a hypersonic flow begin to misbehave where a shock wave meets the boundary layer on a cone with a step. At six times the speed of sound, such interactions can tremble in several ways, from flickering shear layers to whole shock systems swinging back and forth. The team films the flow with time-resolved Schlieren imaging, which makes density changes visible, in a quiet wind tunnel across a range of flow densities.

A statistical technique then pulls the dominant unsteady patterns out of the movies. Experiments are compared against detailed simulations, both symmetric and fully three-dimensional. Together they map a transition across the parameter space: gentle shear-layer breakdown gives way to shock oscillation and finally to large-amplitude pulsation.
arxiv-2512-07189:
Jiahao Zhang and co-authors add privacy to decentralized storage, the peer-to-peer filing systems pitched as infrastructure for a user-owned web. In such networks, fetching a file normally reveals which file you wanted, a leak that endangers sensitive uses. Their protocol, PIR-DSN, is described as the first in its class to support private information retrieval. Fetching data in a way that hides the request, for both single-server and multi-server setups.

A secure mapping turns sparse file identifiers into compact numerical indexes, keeping operations publicly verifiable while retrieval stays private. Replication across several storage miners makes the private fetching robust even when some participants turn hostile, in the Byzantine sense. The team implemented the protocol and raced it against three prominent industrial storage networks.
arxiv-2512-07289:
Peijia Lin and co-authors generate crystal structures with a diffusion model that respects every symmetry a crystal demands. Predicting a material's crystal structure from its composition is a conditional building task, and diffusion models have become the tool of choice. But a generated crystal must be unchanged, in the right sense, when its atoms are permuted, the whole pattern rotated, or the repeating cell shifted. Existing models had left one of those, lattice reshuffling, unhandled.

EquiCSP closes the gaps. It maintains permutation, rotation, and periodic translation rules throughout, and its noising procedure is designed to preserve the translation symmetry rigorously during both training and use. In experiments the model produced accurate crystals well beyond the reach of earlier systems, and it settled into training faster than they did. For materials discovery, where each candidate structure must survive contact with physics.
arxiv-2512-07489:
Mohammad Amini and eight co-authors wrote this 2025 physics paper on designer quantum materials. Stacked thin layers, called van der Waals heterostructures, let scientists build new materials to order. Monolayer ferroelectrics have lately joined the toolbox, adding electric control to the stack.

Electric fields can flip ferroelectric domains, which promises outside control of material traits. The team asks whether such stacks can couple electric and magnetic behavior together. Their test system pairs a double layer of tin telluride with iron phthalocyanine molecules. The molecules act as sensor spins sitting at the boundary. A scanning tunneling microscope reads their response with nanometre precision. The readings reveal a coupling route that is purely structural in origin. Because it rests on structure alone, it should hold in many materials. Electric and magnetic traits, they show, can be tied at the nanoscale by design.
arxiv-2512-07789:
Kyle Stoltz wrote this 2025 mathematics paper on generalized splines, a meeting point of two fields. Classical splines stitch function pieces together for smooth approximation. Generalized splines also carry the combinatorics of GKM theory from geometry.

The gluing conditions between pieces can be read as a scheme construction. That view yields a local-global principle for the whole theory. Behavior over local rings then controls global traits like projectivity and freeness. Stoltz builds a bridge between local ring homology and spline combinatorics. Two exact sequences regulate how local cohomology interacts with the spline module.  He then applies the machinery to a concrete freeness question. For graphs whose edge labels are principal ideals, freeness often follows. The ring needs to be Cohen-Macaulay of dimension two at each maximal point.  Two-variable polynomial rings fall out as a case.
arxiv-2512-08089:
Jebacyril Arockiaraj, Dhruv Parikh, and Viktor Prasanna, computer engineers, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about fast graph classification at the edge. Their accelerator, HyperX, runs hyperdimensional computing on an FPGA chip. Hyperdimensional computing encodes data as long, simple vectors, which suits small, low power devices, and recent work boosts its graph accuracy with Nystrom kernel approximations.

Moving that method to hardware raised four problems, from redundant landmark samples to memory limits and uneven sparse workloads. HyperX answers with smarter landmark selection, a streaming design for the projection matrix, a perfect hash lookup engine, and sparsity aware engines with balanced loads. Built on a standard FPGA board, it ran several times faster than optimized processor and graphics baselines while using far less energy. It also improved classification accuracy on standard graph benchmarks, a rare win on speed, power, and quality together.
arxiv-2512-08389:
N Goyal, F J Iguaz, S Aplin, and a large European team of detector scientists posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They present the first working prototype of a high purity germanium detector built under the LEAPS INNOV project. The device is a monolithic, multi element sensor tuned for high resolution spectroscopy of hard X rays, at very high count rates.

The study gives a full laboratory characterization, plus a test on a real beamline at the European Synchrotron in Grenoble, using single energy X rays. Their assessment covers energy sharpness and count rate handling, plus a practical model estimating defect depth inside the crystal. The prototype marks a step toward instruments that can keep up with brighter future X ray sources.
arxiv-2512-08489:
Agnieszka Janiuk, Gerardo Urrutia, Joseph Saji, and Piotr Plonka, astrophysicists, posted a conference paper on arXiv in December 2025. They simulate the most violent events in the universe: neutron star mergers and the collapse of massive stars. These events light up as gamma ray bursts and kilonovae, and many now arrive with gravitational wave detections, making them central to multimessenger astronomy.

Their tool is general relativistic magnetohydrodynamics, which follows matter, magnetic fields, and curved spacetime together. The paper presents recent results from the team simulations of merging and collapsing stars. It focuses on how the environment left around the newborn black hole or remnant shapes the gamma ray burst prompt emission, the first fierce flash telescopes see. Understanding that shaping helps observers read real bursts: why some are bright, some choked, and how debris leaves fingerprints on the light.
arxiv-2512-08689:
Connor Panish and Leo Villani survey matrix completion, the task of filling in missing entries of a table from the entries that are observed. Their review covers the core theory and presents implementations of several basic algorithms that are widely used for the task.

Both passive methods and adaptive methods are covered, where adaptive methods choose which entries to observe next. The authors also run controlled tests on synthetic data to show how a simple adaptive sampling scheme behaves in practice. Readers get a concise entry point that links theory, code, and experiment in one place.
arxiv-2512-08889:
Damiano Marsili and Georgia Gkioxari present a training framework that improves visual reasoning in artificial intelligence systems without any ground truth labels. Visual reasoning needs precise object grounding and an understanding of complex spatial relations. Language only reasoning methods need large labeled data sets, while program synthesis methods avoid training but often suffer from flawed logic and poor grounding.

Their framework uses artificial intelligence verifiers in two roles. A language model verifier refines reasoning through reinforcement learning. A vision language verifier strengthens grounding by mining hard negative examples automatically. Strong language models break spatial queries into simpler subtasks, while vision specialists are improved by the vision critic. Tests across diverse spatial tasks show the method beats open and proprietary models on reasoning. With the improved grounding model, it also beats recent text only visual reasoning methods. The key claim is that verification can replace annotation.
arxiv-2512-09189:
Sean R. Garner and five co-authors tackle a simulation problem in quantum error correction, the methods used to protect quantum computers from noise. The standard shortcut, called Pauli twirling, replaces real noise with a simpler version that computers can simulate. That shortcut can distort thermal relaxation, the natural process by which qubits lose energy and phase over time.

The team builds an exact model of thermal relaxation that still fits the fast stabilizer method used to simulate large codes. They show the combined energy-loss and dephasing channel splits into allowed operations under a stated condition, and they design a close approximation for harder cases, including finite temperature. Applying the model to large surface codes and bicycle codes on superconducting hardware, they find that performance depends on the code's state. Their results argue that future decoders must be built around the real shape of thermal noise.
arxiv-2512-09289:
Sukhrobbek Ilyosbekov presents MelanomaNet, a deep learning system that sorts skin lesions into diagnostic classes while explaining its answers. Automated lesion classification can be accurate, but clinics have been slow to adopt it because neural networks usually act as black boxes. A doctor cannot see why the model reached its verdict.

MelanomaNet pairs an EfficientNet V2 image model with four explanation tools. One highlights the image regions the model attended to. Another automatically measures the classic ABCDE warning signs that dermatologists check by hand. A third explains predictions through learned concepts, and a fourth estimates how uncertain each prediction is, splitting doubt into two kinds and flagging shaky cases for human review. On a large public dataset of dermoscopic images in nine classes, the system scored well while its explanations matched standard dermatology criteria.
arxiv-2512-09389:
Sabina Yeasmin and Atri Deshamukhya study warm inflation in a braneworld picture of the universe. Inflation is the burst of fast expansion in the universe's first moments. In warm inflation, the inflating field steadily sheds energy into radiation, so the universe stays warm instead of cooling to near emptiness. Braneworld scenarios add extra dimensions, with our universe as a surface inside a larger space.

The authors build a warm inflation model in that setting and study it under the slow-roll approximation, where the field rolls gently and expansion is steady. They consider both constant and varying dissipation, the rate at which the field loses energy, and examine both strong and weak dissipation regimes. They compute the standard observable fingerprints, the spectral index and the tensor-to-scalar ratio. Those predictions are then compared with data from the Planck satellite and the BICEP experiment to constrain the model's parameters.
arxiv-2512-09689:
Utsav Dewan and Sanjoy Pusti study when solutions of dispersive, wave-like equations whose components travel at different speeds, settle back to their initial state at almost every point as time shrinks. This convergence question, famous for the Schrödinger equation, is examined on Riemannian symmetric spaces of compact type, curved spaces with symmetry, of rank one and two.

They prove that modest Sobolev regularity of the initial data suffices for convergence on these spaces, with the required smoothness depending on the rank. Focusing on rotationally symmetric initial data in rank one, they sharpen the threshold for sufficiency. They show the phenomenon fails below a lower threshold for the Schrödinger equation. The results are transferred to the Boussinesq and beam equations through a transference principle that seems new for the circle. Their arguments combine harmonic analysis and the representation theory of compact Lie groups with number theory.
arxiv-2512-09889:
Justin Atsushi Otter leads a large team studying gas flowing out of the galaxy NGC 1266. Outflows driven by an active galactic nucleus can push on a galaxy's gas and help shut down star formation. NGC 1266 is a nearby case where star formation recently stopped outside the center. Earlier work traced its outflow in carbon monoxide, which shows diffuse gas. The team used the ALMA telescope array to look for denser, colder gas.

A rarer form of carbon monoxide showed no outflow, implying the outflowing gas is thin and spread out. Hydrogen cyanide appeared strongly in the outflow. The picture is clumpy: dense knots of gas ride inside a diffuse flow. The authors bound the outflow rate and estimate the galaxy will drain its gas over at least several hundred million years at current rates. So gentle feedback can empty a galaxy slowly after a fast quench.
arxiv-2512-10389:
Aleksandr Kovalenko and Andrey Leonidov study the Ising model through the lens of a game, where each unit picks between two choices and neighbours influence one another. Their paper focuses on a difference that games allow and classic physics setups often do not. Several players can change their minds at the same moment.

The authors let a chosen number of units flip at each step and work out the maths exactly, for any level of noise. They track how a shaky, metastable arrangement decays into a stable one, and how long that takes. The timing depends on the number of simultaneous flips in a surprising way, with a fastest point that they trace to a contest between random drift and a restoring pull.
arxiv-2512-10489:
J Askew and co-authors use the twinkling of a famous double pulsar to study the gas between the stars. The system PSR J0737-3039A/B gives some of the sharpest tests of strong-field gravity, and its radio pulses scintillate as they cross ionised plasma. The team read that interference pattern over eighteen months of MeerKAT telescope observations.

Their best model places a moderately stretched scattering screen a few hundred parsecs away, near the edge of the Gum Nebula, a suspected supernova remnant. They estimate how fast the nebula expands and judge it about a million years old. The pattern also pins down the double pulsar's orbital orientation and tilt. And gives a distance estimate matching the value from very long baseline interferometry, a check on both the method and the system.
arxiv-2512-10789:
F Taghiyev and A Aslanbayli let network administrators write firewall rules in plain words. Enterprise firewalls are configured in vendor-specific command languages, so a clear policy intent can be garbled in translation, and overly broad rules slip through. Their prototype turns plain-language access policies into finished configuration, with Palo Alto's PAN-OS as the first target.

A compact intermediate representation, bound to a strict schema, separates human intent from device syntax. Language models act only as assistive parsers that fill in typed representation objects, while compilation and enforcement stay deterministic, never left to the model. Three validation layers guard the output: a static linter for structural and vendor constraints, a safety gate that blocks dangerous any-to-any allows. And a Batfish-based simulation that checks the configuration against a synthetic device model. Tests ran on synthetic network contexts.
arxiv-2512-10989:
Michal Sanocki and Julija Zavadlav test how well machine learning models that predict forces between atoms carry over to new kinds of chemistry. Such potentials promise large simulations with near quantum accuracy, but they often fail on samples unlike their training data. The authors focus on models that include long range corrections.

Across diverse chemical spaces, long range schemes improved not only normal test scores but, more importantly, transfer to unseen regions. The team also introduces split strategies that deliberately place test cases in very different parts of chemical space. Worked out on metal organic frameworks, the framework helps diagnose systematic failures and points toward more robust, transferable potentials for other materials too.
arxiv-2512-11089:
Devansh Arpit introduces test prediction variance, a measure of how much a trained model's outputs shift when its parameters are nudged slightly. The idea gives one lens for studying robustness after training. Because it needs no labels, it can be computed from inputs alone, and its form separates the model's geometry from the source of the disturbance.

That single framework covers noise from training algorithms, mislabelled data, compression by quantisation, and pruning of weights. The resulting formulas recover the known preference for wide, flat minima and give a new spectral picture for label noise linked to harmless overfitting. Arpit proves training and test versions of the measure meet in very wide networks. Practical spin offs include a label free pruning rule that matches leading methods and a model selection signal that works from training data alone.
arxiv-2512-11189:
Anh-Kiet Duong and Petra Gomez-Krämer report a winning solution for finding when actions happen in video recorded from several viewpoints at once. The BinEgo-360 challenge at a major vision conference supplied panoramic, third person, and first person recordings labelled with fine grained action classes. Locating action boundaries across such mixed footage is difficult.

Their approach extends the Temporal Shift Module, an efficient video backbone, by adding a background class and classifying short fixed intervals. A multi task setup learns scene recognition alongside action localisation, so knowledge of the environment helps interpret the action. Several models were combined in a weighted ensemble for stability. The method placed first in both the opening and extended rounds of the competition, showing the value of pairing multi task learning with ensembling.
arxiv-2512-11489:
Lucas Fix, Gianna Götzmann, Malte Peter, and Jan-F. Pietschmann derive the effective behaviour of substances crossing a thin, changing membrane pierced by microscopic channels. Their model couples reaction, diffusion, and flow across two bulk regions joined by the membrane. Both channel width and membrane thickness shrink toward zero jointly, and the microscopic shape evolves in time in a prescribed way.

Non-linear flux settings line the channel walls, and diffusion inside the layer is scaled critically. Extending homogenisation methods for evolving microstructures to thin layers, the team uses two scale convergence and unfolding arguments to take the limit. The membrane collapses to a lower in extent interface. Crossing it imposes jump settings on the answer and total fluxes, computed from local cell problems in a reference channel. Such effective interface laws simplify model runs of filters and biological membranes.
arxiv-2512-11589:
Lukas Twist and Jie M Zhang ask how AI coding agents use software libraries when they do real work. Agents now write whole pull requests, the change proposals used on coding sites, yet little was known about their library habits. The study draws on 26,760 agent made pull requests from the AIDev data set.

Agents import a library in 29.5 percent of pull requests but add a brand new one in only 1.3 percent. When they do add one, 75.0 percent name an exact version, a far better habit than raw language models show. Agents also pick from a wide range of libraries, unlike the narrow tastes seen in past studies.
arxiv-2512-11689:
Manuela Chacon-Chamorro and co-authors compare how well people and AI agents protect a shared resource under stress. They call that skill cooperative resilience: sensing, resisting, and recovering from shocks to the common good. The test is a Tragedy of the Commons game from the Melting Pot suite.

A greedy bot drains the shared pool nonstop, and random shocks remove chunks of it. Human groups and language model agents each play with and without the right to talk. Human groups that could talk scored highest of all. Talk helped the AI agents too, but they still trailed humans. In a longer, harsher run, humans kept the pool alive across many shock patterns.
arxiv-2512-11989:
Grace M Forrey and co-authors introduce a new way to measure how deeply dust hides star birth inside galaxies. Using the NGDEEP survey with the Webb telescope, they study 14 star forming galaxies at cosmic noon, redshifts 1.0 to 2.5, when the universe formed stars at its peak rate.

For each galaxy they map the Balmer decrement pixel by pixel, turning it into dust and true star formation maps at about 1 kiloparsec detail. Sorting pixels by dust level gives the share of star birth behind each dust depth. Half of all star formation sits behind 3.41 magnitudes of dimming or more. The galaxy wide average tracks the least hidden tenth, so global values badly understate how buried typical star birth is.
arxiv-2512-12489:
Shuhui Qu and Cheolwoo Park present GoMS, a network for predicting molecule properties, in a 2025 paper. Graph neural networks read a molecule as atoms and bonds. A leading method, ESAN, treats a molecule as a bag of separate substructures, losing how those parts connect and overlap, though properties often emerge from exactly those links.

GoMS builds a second graph whose nodes are substructures and whose edges capture their relations and layout. That preserves topology that bag methods drop. Across public data sets, GoMS beat ESAN and other baselines, with the largest gains on big molecules over 100 atoms. Theory shows it can tell apart molecules with the same parts in different arrangements.
arxiv-2512-12589:
Andre Nies and Philipp Schlicht study automorphism groups of non-Archimedean Polish groups in a 2025 math paper. An automorphism is a symmetry of a group, a reshaping that preserves its operation. Non-Archimedean Polish groups are complete, separable groups with a basis of open subgroups, common in logic and infinite permutation group theory.

They show the automorphism group carries a unique Polish topology that makes its action on the group continuous, given a countable invariant basis of open subgroups. For classes with a Borel assignment of bases, a duality with countable groupoids gives another description of that topology. They also give a model theoretic proof that the outer automorphism group of an oligomorphic group is locally compact.
arxiv-2512-12689:
Mansour El Alami and four co-authors present FiD-QAE, a quantum autoencoder for credit card fraud detection, in a 2025 paper. Fraudulent transactions are rare, heavily outnumbered, and often look legitimate, so detectors must spot subtle anomalies. Classical and quantum methods each leave open questions on scale and shifting fraud patterns.

FiD-QAE encodes transactions into quantum states and compresses them through a variational quantum circuit. A SWAP test measures fidelity, the closeness between states, as the decision rule for flagging anomalies. Across imbalance levels it performed steadily, and it stayed robust under quantum noise models. Tests on IBM Quantum hardware matched simulations, showing it can run on real devices.
arxiv-2512-13589:
Ignacio Huerta and Pablo Monzón study two linked traits of time-varying control systems: observability and detectability. In plain terms, one asks whether outputs reveal the internal state, and the other whether unseen parts fade in a stable way. Recent work showed non-uniform observability ensures non-uniform exponential detectability.

The authors prove the reverse link, under added conditions that they state with care. Their proof rests on a close study of output feedback systems and on how observability survives such feedback. The result extends the classic match between the two traits beyond the uniform case. It gives new tools for the study of time-varying control systems.
arxiv-2512-13689:
Yuanwen Yue and co-authors design LitePT, a lighter backbone for 3D point cloud networks. Modern point cloud models mix convolution layers with attention blocks, but the best order was unclear. Their analysis gives a simple rule for how to stack the two block types.

Convolution suits early, high-resolution layers, where it extracts low-level geometry cheaply. Attention suits deep, low-resolution layers, where it captures high-level meaning with fewer parameters. LitePT follows that split and adds PointROPE, a parameter-free 3D positional encoding. The result has 3.6 times fewer parameters than Point Transformer V3, runs 2 times faster, and uses 2 times less memory. It still matched or beat that model across tasks and data sets.
arxiv-2512-13889:
Sergei N. Yurchenko and co-authors construct extensive line lists for 12 isotopologues of carbon dioxide. Isotopologues are versions of a molecule with different isotopes, and their spectral lines are needed to model planetary and exoplanet atmospheres. This is the 63rd paper in the ExoMol line list series.

The team used the TROVE variational program with an exact kinetic energy operator, the Ames-2 potential energy surface, and the Ames-2021-40K dipole surface. Measured energy levels from MARVEL, HITRAN, and CDSD replace calculated values where available. Machine learning estimators assign extra quantum numbers. The lists feed opacity calculations in four radiative transfer codes, for single isotopologues and for natural terrestrial abundance. All data are public at exomol.com.
arxiv-2512-13989:
Cindy Y. Zhang, Elif Ertekin, Peter Orbanz, and Ryan P. Adams build one neural architecture that can enforce invariance under any crystallographic space group. Symmetry-aware models predict material properties better, but exact invariance usually needs a bespoke design per group. With 230 space groups in three dimensions, that approach does not scale.

Their method builds symmetry-adapted Fourier bases by characterizing the constraints each group imposes on Fourier coefficients. Encoding those constraints in a network layer lets weights adapt automatically to an input group. Weight sharing across groups also transfers knowledge and eases data sparsity for rare groups. Tests show competitive material property prediction and zero-shot generalization to unseen groups, in a single model.
arxiv-2512-14389:
Sudhaker Upadhyay and three co-authors examine the Swampland program through holography. The program tries to separate low-energy theories that could come from quantum gravity from those that could not. Holography, especially the AdS/CFT correspondence, gives a working definition of quantum gravity in anti-de Sitter space.

Conditions from the boundary theory, including the shape of its spectrum, an averaged energy condition, and the modular bootstrap, are matched to limits inside the bulk. The authors argue these give geometric form to bounds on scalar field potentials and against long-lived de Sitter states. Holography, they suggest, may explain why the Swampland rules hold.
arxiv-2512-14489:
Alessia Micieli, Giovanni Maria Farinella, and Francesco Ragusa release SignIT, a video dataset for recognizing Italian Sign Language. It holds 644 videos totaling a little over three hours, sorted into 94 sign classes under five headings: animals, food, colors, emotions, and family. Alongside the footage, the team extracted two-dimensional keypoints for the hands, face, and body.

They also benchmark several leading recognition models on the data, testing what raw frames, motion over time, and keypoints each contribute. Even the best models struggled, which marks the dataset as a hard test. The data and annotations are public, giving LIS research a shared starting point.
arxiv-2512-14589: Marc Kegel and Paula Truöl prove a universality result in low-dimensional topology, in a short note. Dehn surgery builds three-dimensional spaces by cutting tubes out of ordinary space and gluing them back twisted, along a chosen link. Their theorem says every closed, oriented, connected three-manifold can be produced this way using a braid positive link, a link drawn from a braid whose crossings all go the same way.
arxiv-2512-14889:
Kaustav Mitra and three coauthors test a cosmic dispute using the motion of satellite galaxies. The dispute is the S8 tension, a mismatch between how clumpy the universe looks nearby and what the early universe predicts. Their tool, Basilisk, models how satellite galaxies orbit their hosts and how many there are.

The method first pins down how galaxies connect to their dark matter halos. It then demands that the same link reproduce the observed counts of galaxies by brightness, which constrains cosmology itself. Tests on mock data show it recovers the true values without bias. Applied to SDSS data, it finds S8 of 0.81 plus or minus 0.05, in full agreement with the Planck satellite results. Unlike many nearby probes, this one sees no tension at all.
arxiv-2512-14989:
Yiming Cui and five coauthors grade 40 multimodal language models on chemistry exam questions that mix text and pictures. The questions come from over two decades of U.S. National Chemistry Olympiad exams. They demand joint reasoning over words, molecular structures, and diagrams, a known weak spot for AI systems.

The roster includes GPT-5, o3, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and Qwen2.5-VL, among many open and closed models. Many models struggled to fuse the two channels, and in some cases deleting the image raised accuracy, a sign of poor vision language alignment. Chain of thought prompting steadily improved both accuracy and visual grounding, as shown by ablation and occlusion tests. The study gives the field a timely benchmark for scientific multimodal reasoning, and a clear list of what still fails.
arxiv-2512-15089:
Jinwu Hu and eight coauthors give language models a way to pick how hard to think, question by question. Current models lean on fast or slow modes, which waste effort on easy queries or skimp on hard ones. Their framework, CogER, takes its cue from human layered reasoning.

CogER first grades each query's complexity and routes it to a matching strategy. A reinforcement learning agent makes the routing choices, trained with rewards that balance answer quality against computing cost. For queries that need outside help, a tool assisted mode lets the model call external tools inside its chain of thought. In tests, CogER beat leading test time scaling methods, with at least 13 percent relative gains in exact match on in domain tasks and 8 percent on out of domain tasks. The work targets a better trade between accuracy and cost.
arxiv-2512-15189:
Zhao Zhu and two coauthors speed up decentralized optimization by letting machines remember. In decentralized learning, many nodes improve a shared model while talking only to neighbors. Past values and gradients hold rich information about the objective, and unlike second derivatives they are already computed or sent, so reuse costs nothing.

The authors build that memory into a proximal bundle framework and adapt it to decentralized gradient descent, giving the Decentralized Proximal Bundle Method. They extend it to asynchronous and stochastic settings as well. Theory shows both variants converge with fixed step sizes that do not depend on delays, unlike most asynchronous methods. Fixed steps are easier to pick and often converge faster. Tests on classification problems show faster convergence and stronger robustness in step size choice.
arxiv-2512-15389:
Fraser Aidan Kelvin Sanders extends contact geometry to infinite dimensions in a 2025 math paper. Contact and related structures help describe systems that change with time or lose energy as they move. Most of that theory was built for finite dimensional spaces, which limits its use for field like systems.

Sanders generalizes the theories of cosymplectic, contact, and cocontact manifolds to the infinite dimensional setting. The paper then works through model examples drawn from time dependent Hamiltonian systems and from dissipative ones, meaning systems that lose energy. The results give researchers a shared geometric language for such systems. Readers with a background in differential geometry will get the most from it.
arxiv-2512-15489:
Wei Du and co authors release Nemotron-Math, a large data set for teaching models to reason through math, in a 2025 paper. Good training data for math needs varied reasoning styles, long solution traces, and tool use, and older sets offer these only in part. The team builds on the multi mode output of the gpt-oss-120b model.

The set holds 7.5 million solution traces across high, medium, and low reasoning modes, each with and without Python tool use. Sources mix 85 thousand curated AoPS problems with 262 thousand StackExchange Math problems. Models trained on it beat the prior OpenMathReasoning set, and a bucketed training strategy speeds long context fine tuning by two to three times.
arxiv-2512-15589:
Anis Biswas and co authors review rare earth R2In intermetallic compounds in a 2025 paper, linking their magnetic ground states to magnetocaloric effects. These materials heat or cool when magnetized or demagnetized, which suits cryogenic cooling. Their behavior turns on subtle electronic effects, lattice distortions, and spin lattice coupling.

Most R2In compounds share a hexagonal structure at room temperature, while a few take an orthorhombic form. Light lanthanide members show first order magnetic transitions with giant low temperature magnetocaloric effects and little hysteresis. Heavy members show second order transitions with moderate effects. The review adds theory based descriptors that predict phase stability and cooling performance, guiding design of new compounds.
arxiv-2512-15789:
Amir Hossein Ghasemi presents a relational framework in which time emerges from links in a still quantum state in a 2025 paper, dated December 15. Instead of treating time as a background given, each subsystem carries an internal clock, and other parts evolve relative to those clock readings. The idea extends ideas from relational quantum mechanics.

The construction covers fast motion, gravity redshift, and cosmic expansion in one emergent time rule. It reproduces classic time dilation, predicts link based shifts from standard change for highly entangled systems, and assigns near zero internal time to non interacting or massless particles. The author suggests tests from multi clock quantum systems to precision measurement work.
arxiv-2512-16189:
Musarrat Zeba and ten co-authors tackle AI errors in medicine in a paper shared on arXiv in 2025, published in Expert Systems with Applications. Language models can invent false facts, called hallucinations, which is risky when summaries guide patient care. The team pairs a medical summary model with an independent fact-checking module.

The summarizer was fine-tuned on the MIMIC-III hospital data set using a light method called LoRA. The checker breaks summaries into single claims and tests each against electronic health records with numeric and logic checks. On 104 sampled summaries split into 3,786 claims, the checker reached a precision of 0.8904, recall of 0.8234, and an F1 score of 0.8556. Summary quality also scored well on standard text measures. The design aims to make clinical AI output safer to trust.
arxiv-2512-16989:
Ali Ahmad Khostovan and the AURORA team report mass-metallicity relations for galaxies at redshift near 2.3, built purely on direct temperature-based metal measures. Their sample holds 34 galaxies seen with JWST NIRSpec, with oxygen auroral lines caught for exact measures.

The sample spans metal shares from 7.68 to 8.65 in log oxygen terms, masses from a hundred million to twenty-five billion solar masses, and star formation from 1 to 100 solar masses a year. The main relation has a slope of 0.27 and a scatter of 0.10 dex. None of six simulations matched its growth from redshift zero to two. Yet the sample fits the local fundamental relation within 0.1 dex, a sign that steady enrichment rules were set by cosmic noon.
arxiv-2512-17189:
Xiao Liang and coauthors present Anatomical Region-Guided Contrastive Decoding, a plug-and-play fix for hallucinations in medical vision-language models. Such models often answer from learned text habits instead of the scan in front of them, a risky flaw in clinical use.

Their module uses an anatomical mask to steer a three-tier contrastive decoding process, reweighting at token, attention, and logit levels. That steering verifiably pulls focus onto the named region and damps false outputs. Across chest X-ray, CT, brain MRI, and ocular ultrasound data, the method improved regional understanding, cut hallucinations, and lifted diagnostic accuracy, with no retraining of the base model.
arxiv-2512-17289:
G M Refatul Islam and three co-authors work on software that can write essay-style questions and grade the answers. Objective questions, with one right answer, already have strong automated tools. Subjective questions, which ask students to explain ideas in their own words, are much harder to make and to score fairly by machine.

Their system takes a passage, such as a book chapter, and produces open questions from it. It then judges written answers, so students can check their own grasp after reading and teachers get help with marking. The team aims to improve current language models for this job, or build a new one that handles both making questions and scoring replies.
arxiv-2512-17389:
Guangneng Hu maps what language models do and do not grasp about shopping and watching habits. Such models are being plugged into recommendation engines, yet they learn from text about the world, while recommenders learn from clicks and buys. No broad test had charted where the models' mental picture of taste breaks down.

The new benchmark, LRWorld, holds over 38,000 samples and 23 million tokens drawn from public data sets. It grades three skills across 31 tasks: linking related items, modeling a person's taste, and knowing facts about items. Dozens of models did well on shallow item matching and on item facts. None captured the deep personal patterns that real recommenders use, and none scored well across the board.
arxiv-2512-17489:
Muhammad Atif Butt and three co-authors give image generators a lighting dial they normally lack. A designer may love a generated chair yet hate its cold blue cast, and today's text-to-image tools offer no clean way to change only the light. LumiCtrl learns the light falling on an object from a single photo and stores it as a reusable prompt.

Three steps keep the light separate from the object. First comes physics-based recoloring under standard lamps. An edge guide then stops the prompt from absorbing shape. A masked loss teaches the object zone while letting the backdrop adjust. In tests, its images matched target lighting better and looked more coherent than rivals. Human raters, too, picked its output by a wide margin.
arxiv-2512-17589:
Yunhao Deng and four co-authors speed up how one chip core can broadcast the same data to many others. AI chips constantly copy one result to many compute tiles, yet standard on-chip networks only speak one-to-one, so senders repeat the same message again and again. Bolting multicast onto the network itself means redesigning hardware and protocols.

Torrent instead spreads the job across small transfer engines that pass data along a chain of targets, like a bucket brigade. Every hop stays an ordinary one-to-one transfer, so nothing in the network changes. Two scheduling rules order the chain to fit the chip's layout. Chip tests showed up to 7.88 times faster delivery than repeated one-to-one sends, for just 1.2 percent extra area.
arxiv-2512-17689:
Pegah Golchian and Marvin N Wright warn that filling in missing data once can make a model's explanation look surer than it is. Real data sets are full of holes, and analysts plug them before asking explanation tools which features matter. Prior work showed the choice of plug can shift the explanation itself. The pair ask what it does to the error bars around that explanation.

They test single versus multiple filling across three popular tools: permutation importance, partial dependence plots, and Shapley values. Single filling understated the spread, so confidence intervals missed their promised coverage rate. Multiple filling, which averages over several plausible plugs, came close to the promised rate in most cases. Honest explanations, the lesson runs, must carry the hole-filling doubt with them.
arxiv-2512-18289:
Marco Stefanelli, Žiga Zaplotnik, and Gregor Skok teach a neural network to translate weather model states into radar echoes. Forecast systems blend live radar into their maps through a translator step, but radar brightness hangs on tiny droplet physics in a tangled way. Hand built translators are fussy and hard to tune.

Their network learned the translation from five years of Slovenian radar and model runs, taking in heat, moisture, winds, and pressure. In the storm that flooded Slovenia on August 4, 2023, folding in the full radar view cut the average echo error from 5.99 to 3.47 units and lined the rain bands up with the real ones. Sharper storm maps mean better warnings.
arxiv-2512-18389:
Alessandro Abate outlines an ongoing research line on proofs that mix neural networks with strict logic. The goal is to certify that complex systems with chance in them, from robots to reactive software, truly meet time based safety demands. Pure machine learning can guess, but a guess is not a proof.

His neural proofs pair firm proof rules with certificates built step by step. Samples from the system train a network, and logic queries then stretch that network into a claim that covers the whole model, not just the samples. The same frame can stamp out control policies that are correct by construction. Abate frames the note as a progress report on a young method.
arxiv-2512-18489:
Jensen Zhang, Jing Yang, and Keze Wang ask how large language models update their beliefs as new evidence streams in. Earlier work mostly tested static tasks, but agents and world models must revise their views step by step. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds a Bayesian filtering framework to probe this online reasoning.

Their test suite covers discrete cases like dice rolls and continuous ones like Gaussian processes, with true values that shift over time. They find that model updates resemble Bayesian reasoning but with a twist: each model acts like an exponential forgetting filter, discounting older evidence by a factor below one. The built-in priors are often off, yet the updating itself stays orderly. Prompting tricks that reset the priors fix much of the miscalibration at little cost.
arxiv-2512-18589:
Yifan Zhao and four co-authors design a chip that lets small edge devices compute on encrypted data. Homomorphic encryption allows cloud servers to process data without seeing it, but schemes like RNS-CKKS are slow and bulky on weak hardware. Hybrid schemes ease the edge burden with light symmetric ciphers like Rubato, then pay a conversion cost in the cloud. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, builds one accelerator for both modes.

DNA-HHE switches between RNS-CKKS and Rubato under flexible custom instructions, and it couples directly to the network interface to cut transfer delays. Compact tricks, a DSP-efficient modular reduction and a shared butterfly unit, keep the design small. On ASIC and FPGA tests it beats leading single-mode designs on speed and area, and trims end-to-end latency by 1.09 to 1.56 times.
arxiv-2512-18889:
Ashley Colley and three co-authors study plastic recycling where it actually happens: Finnish kitchens. Through short interviews, their first study maps how residents store, sort, and discard packaging. The frictions repeat: too little space, improvised storage, confusion about sorting rules, and bulky or dirty items. A second study zooms in on laundry detergent bottles, a major source of big containers. Their article, posted to arXiv in December 2025, then turns findings into designs.

Four student teams built interactive concepts pairing physical bins or bags with phone apps: modular storage, sensing with compaction, playful feedback, and reward schemes. Shoppers, the interviews show, choose detergent by price and cleaning power while feeling unsure about rinsing and recyclability. The authors argue the design space spans packaging, home infrastructure, and digital services together, with open questions about cost, privacy, and feasibility.
arxiv-2512-18989:
Youzhi Zhang studies games where a team of players works together against a single opponent. Older theory assumed every team member wants the same payoff. Zhang argues that real teams, like countries chasing joint goals, often want different things. Ignoring those differences can make a computed plan unstable.

Zhang names that loss the Price of Ignoring Heterogeneity, and shows it can grow without bound. He then defines a new solution, the Co-opetition Equilibrium, where teammates link their moves against the rival. Finding one is hard in a precise sense, yet for a broad class of zero-sum games the best team version can be found fast with linear programming.
arxiv-2512-19589:
Charles Shaw releases srvar-toolkit, an open-source Python package for forecasting the economy when interest rates sit at their floor. At the effective lower bound, the true policy stance hides in a shadow rate that can dip below zero. The package fits Bayesian vector autoregressions built around that idea, with stochastic volatility.

Conjugate priors with Minnesota-style shrinkage keep the estimates tame, and Gibbs sampling fills in the latent shadow rate. A mixture trick handles the volatility, and a search step selects variables. Only NumPy, SciPy, and Pandas are required, with plotting extras and a settings-driven command line. The MIT-licensed code follows a 2025 forecasting method.
arxiv-2512-19689:
Jiyu Chen, Jernej Mravlje, Denis Golež, and Philipp Werner ask whether a fancy optical probe can tell two kinds of order apart. In the material Ta2NiSe5, a phase transition might be driven by excitons, bound electron-hole pairs condensing on their own, or by the lattice distorting. Ordinary linear optics mixes single-particle and collective signals, blurring that distinction.

Two-dimensional coherent spectroscopy, a nonlinear technique, separates them in their calculations. In the excitonic regime, the signal is dominated by the condensate's amplitude and phase modes, with little single-particle contamination. As electron-phonon coupling grows, the amplitude contribution collapses once phonons take over, and the method can also catch the phase mode, a relative of the Leggett mode in superconductors. The analysis uses time-dependent Hartree-Fock theory on a realistic model.
arxiv-2512-19889:
Christian Ferko and Keiichiro Furuya compute fingerprints for two famed families of quantum states. The tool is entanglement cohomology. It attaches a graded ring to a pure state of many parts. The ring's features do not change under local unitaries. So they can tell unlike patterns of entanglement apart. The test cases are generalized GHZ and W states. Those are the two classic classes. The counts hold for any number of parties and any local size.

Exact formulas for the group dimensions settle conjectures from 2019. Extra structure adds two more families of invariants. One is the spectrum of a natural Laplacian on entanglement forms. The other is a set of intersection numbers from wedge products. Computer checks on set states probe whether the finer marks earn their keep.
arxiv-2512-20289:
Partha Sarathi Mondal, Tamas Vicsek, and Shradha Mishra simulate a mixture of two kinds of self-propelled particles. One species is polar, aligning its motion; the other is apolar, with head-tail symmetry. Unlike living liquid crystals, where the apolar part is passive, here both components drive themselves.

Solutions of the hydrodynamic equations reveal several complex states. At intermediate polar density and activity, the apolar species responds non-monotonically and the system breaks into dense, restless bands. Half-integer topological defects are created and destroyed continually in this regime. The authors confirm genuine spatiotemporal chaos using spectra of density fluctuations and the maximal Lyapunov exponent. Bacterial suspensions and synthetic microswimmers are suggested as experimental homes for these states.
arxiv-2512-20389:
Victoria E Galanopoulou and co-authors choose which antennas to switch on in a pinching antenna array. These reconfigurable radiating structures hang on a waveguide and serve ground users in turns. The received rate depends on how the complex channel gains of the active antennas add up, so phase alignment is everything.

Trying every subset is exponential work. Their Viterbi state selection method instead tracks a quantized phase of the accumulated gain as its trellis state. A survivor rule prunes dominated subsets stage by stage. Numerical tests show the method finds exactly the same subsets and rates as exhaustive search. The cost, however, drops from exponential to polynomial in the number of available antennas.
arxiv-2512-20489:
Arzu Aktaş and İhsan Yılmaz propose a blockchain whose security comes from quantum physics rather than hard mathematics. Classic blockchains worry that quantum computers and machine learning will crack their protections. Their protocol instead builds blocks from high-dimensional Bell states linked by time-entanglement.

Classic block data is encoded into qudit states delimited in time. Verification then rests on the causal ordering of quantum measurements instead of hash functions. Each block derives its own key pair from correlations measured in successive time steps, so tampering with data or timing destroys the correlations and exposes itself. High-dimensional coding packs more information per carrier and resists noise better. Recent experiments with time-slice entanglement suggest the needed resources are becoming available.
arxiv-2512-20589:
