The team's 2026 preprint develops adaptively robust methods for this model. Adaptive robustness is a strong demand. The algorithm must keep its guarantees even when future inputs react to its earlier outputs. That is much harder than handling a fixed stream. Guarantees like this matter for monitoring systems that adversaries, or simply responsive users, can probe and steer.
arxiv-2601-22089:
Ilaria Colazzo and Geoffrey Janssens link a puzzle law to a branch of algebra. The law is the pentagon law. It sets rules for how paired maps must agree, and it shows up in physics and in the theory of types. Its set-based forms use plain sets and swaps that can be run both ways.

The pair ask how these set forms tie to Hopf algebras. Such algebras act a bit like groups of traits, with rules to split and join them. They prove that the finite set forms match Hopf algebras with a good basis trait. They also stretch a known rank list to more fields. The work shows how a plain law on sets can breed rich new structure.
arxiv-2601-22189:
Han-Yu Lin, Li-Wei Chen, and Hung-Shin Lee clean up compressed video before the damage settles. Standard video codecs leave compression artifacts that degrade how footage looks. Heavy enhancement models can fix them, but they cost too much for routine use.

The team's 2026 preprint proposes SCENE, a lightweight preprocessing framework that is aware of meaning. It folds semantic embeddings from a vision-language model into an efficient convolutional network. The system spends its effort where viewers notice, protecting faces, text, and key objects while smoothing the rest. Smarter preprocessing could raise the quality of streaming and video calls without raising bitrates, a gain felt on every screen.
arxiv-2601-22389:
Bruce Stephenson and Robin Macomber find that many fields, each on its own, built the same tools to spot tipping points. A tipping point here is a phase shift, where ties stretch far and small nudges have huge effects. Their 2026 preprint surveys six to nine fields across nine decades.

Again and again, scholars derived near-identical measures of how ties scale near the edge. Few knew of the match across fields. Naming the shared core can save each field from rework. It may also yield one strong, shared test for early warning signs. The survey spans physics to social science.
arxiv-2601-22489:
Mohammad Rowshan sets the terms a quantum code must meet to serve as a fountain of magic states. Magic states fuel the hard gates that make quantum machines more than classical ones. His 2026 preprint works with qLDPC codes, which promise steady rates and long reach with light checks.

No known family of this kind yet meets all four marks at once: steady rate, long reach, light checks, and native three-way gates. Rowshan lays out the structural terms that would allow it. Clear terms guide the search for such a family. A find would cut the cost of quantum computing a great deal.
arxiv-2601-22689:
Stina Klein and a team test whether helper robots and fair task splits cut the stigma faced by workers with disabilities. Robots can ease physical strain at work. Their 2026 preprint notes that the social side is less clear: visible help could raise stigma, or lower it.

The team study how co-workers judge assisted staff under varied task assignments. Reasonable splits — fair shares for all — seem to shape that judgment. The results can guide firms that add robots to mixed teams. Inclusion, not just output, is the measure here. The work keeps dignity in the frame.
arxiv-2601-22889:
Yuxuan Lou and eight co-authors present DiffuSpeech, a speech model that thinks before it speaks. Most speech models answer at once, so an early error gets spoken and cannot be taken back. Their slogan is silent thought, spoken answer.

The model drafts internal text reasoning alongside the spoken reply, using a shared diffusion process. The silent draft can catch mistakes before they reach the listener's ear. Clearer, better-checked speech could improve voice assistants, tutors, and hands-free tools. The spoken reasoning stays internal, so listeners hear only the final answer while the model still gains the benefit of thinking first. That split mirrors how people rehearse an answer before speaking it aloud in a meeting.
arxiv-2601-23089:
Chandrashekhar B. Khare and Alexander Merkurjev classify which finite groups have a certain lifting property. The property concerns representations, structured descriptions of groups, taken modulo a prime. Lifting asks whether a description modulo a prime can be raised to one modulo the prime squared.

They settle the classification completely, for all finite groups and all primes. Such lifting questions sit inside number theory's study of symmetry and equations. A full classification tells researchers exactly where to expect obstructions, and where lifts always exist. Mod prime representations and their lifts to prime-squared precision are the objects the full classification organizes.
arxiv-2601-23189:
Markus Schmassmann and three co-authors improve computer models of sunspots. Existing models fail to match the observed magnetic field pattern in sunspots. The mismatch traces to an wrongly boosted sideways field at the model's upper boundary.

Using the MURaM radiative MHD code, they explore other boundary setups. The aim is to reproduce both the magnetic and dynamic behavior of real sunspots. Better sunspot models support forecasts of solar activity that affects Earth. The MURaM code includes radiative transfer, so the models track both magnetic structure and the energy the spots radiate. Matching the observed sideways field pattern is the specific failure the other boundaries are meant to repair.
arxiv-2602-02789:
Neal J. Evans and 4 co-authors ask whether the Milky Way's molecular gas distribution is odd, by finding other galaxies shaped the same way, in a 2026 paper. Complete molecular cloud catalogs now let astronomers analyze our galaxy with the same methods used for external ones. The Milky Way shows a big dip in how its molecular gas spreads with radius.

Several other galaxies share the pattern. All carry the same morphological classification: a clearly defined long bar feeding a grand-design spiral. That category is rare in the PHANGS survey sample, yet every galaxy with the classification shows some dip in its carbon monoxide emission profile. Bar lengths correlate with dip extents. The dip galaxies also share high stellar masses and star formation rates. Our galaxy's gas layout, the authors conclude, is a recognizable family trait, not a peculiarity.
arxiv-2602-02889:
Balázs Maga studies the shape of a mathematical space in his solo 2026 paper. The space consists of permutons, which are limit objects for large permutations, or arrangements. Distance between them is measured with the rectangular distance, a way of comparing their patterns over rectangles.

Maga determines the Chebyshev radius of the set, the smallest radius of a ball covering it. That radius is one quarter. He also characterizes every center of such a smallest ball. A permuton is a center exactly when it repeats with period one half in each coordinate. He further describes which permutons sit at the extreme distance of one quarter from a given center.
arxiv-2602-03189:
Keeping a giant stream processing platform alive through failures is documented by Yong Fang, with 5 co-authors, in a live-systems report from ByteDance. Apache Flink powers one of the world's largest live clusters there, handling real-time processing and analytics. Resiliency and stable results under strict service goals are essential, yet cluster scale, business diversity, and running overhead make both hard to guarantee each day.

Their answer, StreamShield, works along engine and cluster perspectives together. Techniques cover runtime tuning, fine-grained fault tolerance, a hybrid replication strategy, and high availability with external systems. A robust testing and deployment pipeline guards live releases. Tests on a live cluster showed the speed and effectiveness of the new techniques.
arxiv-2602-03489:
Malware families mutate to dodge detectors, and that drift quietly degrades machine learning models trained on older samples. Olha Jurečková and Martin Jureček propose an interpretable way to track the change in a 2026 paper. Instead of opaque scores, their method describes malware with a rule-based classifier whose rules a human can read.

The classifier writes rule sets for both original and evolved samples of the same family. A similarity function compares the sets to detect and quantify drift. The comparison names the exact features and values that changed, explaining how the family learned to bypass detection. Experiments show accurate drift detection plus practical insight for analysts defending against evolving malware.
arxiv-2602-03789:
Gabriel Damsholt and 2 co-authors study the schedules that steer generative sampling in flow and diffusion models. Their 2026 paper works in the stochastic interpolant framework, which unifies the two families. A schedule dictates how a Gaussian starting distribution morphs into the target, and the choice strongly affects sampling speed.

The authors prove how to convert a sample path between arbitrary schedules and diffusion coefficients. They extend the framework to point mass schedules, where the Gaussian start collapses to a single point. For Gaussian data they identify lazy schedule families whose drift vanishes entirely. Applied to a pretrained flow model, their schedule conversion generates images in fewer steps without any retraining.
arxiv-2602-03889:
Mixture models group data into hidden clusters, but their fitting algorithm can collapse. Ernest Fokoué addresses that failure in a 2026 paper on transcendental regularization. The method adds penalty functions that act as walls, stopping components from shrinking onto single points during maximum likelihood estimation.

The resulting algorithm, TAMD, comes with proofs of identifiability, consistency, and robustness. In practice it keeps fitting steady and stops collapse, yet scores improve only modestly. Fokoué reports that limit plainly, framing it as evidence about mixture models themselves in high dimensions. An open-source R package accompanies the work.
arxiv-2602-03989:
Two families of interstellar molecules may be chemically linked in space. Christopher N. Shingledecker and 5 co-authors test whether ethanol can turn into acetaldehyde in the gas phase. Their 2026 astrochemistry paper focuses on the star-forming region Sgr B2 (N), rich in complex organic molecules.

Quantum chemical calculations show fluorine and chlorine atoms strip hydrogen from ethanol with no energy barrier. The leftover radicals can then react with hydrogen atoms along routes ending at acetaldehyde. Added to a model of hot cores, these reactions run efficiently under real interstellar conditions. The pathway offers a top-down route between alcohols and aldehydes in space.
arxiv-2602-04089:
Learning by doing, inside the conversation, is what Xiaofeng Lin and 8 co-authors train language models to do. Many real tasks reveal information only through interaction, with delayed feedback and a tension between exploring and exploiting. Their 2026 framework, ORBIT, meta-trains models across many episodes using reinforcement learning.

After training, a mid-sized open model learned in context on entirely unseen environments. It matched a far larger frontier model's performance and beat standard fine-tuning. The gains came without any weight updates at test time. Reliable in-context online learning would let deployed agents improve from experience alone, between retrainings.
arxiv-2602-04189:
A solver that returns samples should be judged on the distribution, not just the average. Xiaoyu Qiu and 4 co-authors evaluate posterior fidelity of diffusion inverse solvers in a 2026 paper. Existing benchmarks grade reconstruction accuracy and ignore whether the spread of samples matches true uncertainty.

In controlled settings with known true posteriors, they systematically compared many solvers' sample distributions. For real problems, where truth is unavailable, they propose a score-based Kernel Stein Discrepancy metric needing no ground truth. It checks consistency between generated samples and the diffusion score itself. Honest uncertainty decides whether inverse solutions can be trusted in science and engineering.
arxiv-2602-04589:
Kai Li and 4 co-authors study a holographic model of fermions, particles probed here through a gravity-based dual description, in a 2026 paper. The background includes an ionic lattice, a repeating charge pattern, which can develop a charge density wave that breaks the pattern's symmetry.

The team examines how Fermi surfaces, the boundaries separating filled and empty electron states, form across momentum regions. The charge density wave strengthened the spectral signal and shifted the Fermi surface momentum. As doping or lattice strength increased, the surface expanded and the band gap widened. One setting even pushed the surface beyond its first zone. The trends match patterns reported in condensed matter experiments, linking the model to real materials.
arxiv-2602-04689:
Mahima Lakra and 4 co-authors test deep learning as a way to predict ocean phytoplankton in a 2026 paper. These tiny plants anchor marine food webs and drive global chemical cycles, yet standard ocean models simulate them poorly because data are sparse and processes are complex.

Several network designs were compared on satellite data and physical inputs. A UNet model best matched seasonal and year-to-year biomass patterns, though it understated slow, low-frequency shifts. An auto-regressive version, feeding its own outputs back in, improved forecasts for up to about five months. Skill faded at longer ranges. The authors suggest such models could aid ocean health monitoring and ecosystem care under climate change.
arxiv-2602-04789:
Video models that generate frame by frame are slowed by attention whose cost grows quadratically. Chengtao Lv and 5 co-authors propose Light Forcing in a 2026 work, the first sparse attention method designed specifically for autoregressive video generation rather than adapted from bidirectional models.

Two flaws hurt older sparse methods here: chunks are treated in isolation, and useful past context is wasted. A chunk-aware growth mechanism estimates each chunk's contribution and allocates sparsity accordingly, letting later chunks inherit earlier knowledge. Hierarchical sparse attention then captures historical and local context from coarse to fine. Experiments showed better quality and faster end-to-end generation than existing sparse methods, with further speedups when combined with other efficient techniques.
arxiv-2603-01489:
Aman Desai presents a small software tool in this 2026 work for particle physics studies. Event files in the Les Houches format hold records of particle crashes made by simulation programs. Many teams study those records with ROOT, a common analysis toolkit, but the two formats do not match directly.

The tool, LHEReader, turns a Les Houches file into a ROOT file so the study can proceed in ROOT. Desai tests the change on a few standard crash types, such as pairs of jets and Higgs-related events. One full case tracks a Higgs event from first generation through fast simulation, all handled in ROOT. The code is shared in public, so other groups can use the same bridge in their own work.
arxiv-2603-01789:
Andreas Happe and Jurgen Cito document how to rebuild a study that asked if AI can hack business networks. Their 2026 report is a replication package, not the original study itself. The source study tested language models on penetration tests of Microsoft Active Directory networks under an assumed-breach setup.

The report lists the artifacts used, walks through building the evaluation setup, and highlights the analysis scripts. Most setup effort goes into installing a third-party testbed that mimics a real company network. Log data from the original test runs ship with the prototype for teams that cannot build the full testbed. With those logs, the data analysis can still run as the report describes. Such packages let other groups verify security claims about AI attackers on shared ground.
arxiv-2603-01889:
Sebastiao Amaro, Joao Goncalves, and Miguel Matos speed up programs that use persistent memory without changing their safety rules. Their 2026 work studies a storage type that is fast, byte-addressable, and keeps data through crashes. To stay consistent after a crash, coders add flush and fence instructions by hand.

Those guards are hard to place well, so coders often add more ordering than needed and lose speed. The team tests which mixes of persistency instructions help across several real programs. One specific mix lifts performance while keeping the exact crash-consistency meaning of the code. Their tool, Bento, rewrites program binaries automatically to apply that mix, with no source edits. Gains reach a solid margin with minimal effort from the programmer, the tests show.
arxiv-2603-01989:
David Gentile, Joshua Huang, and James Murphy find stable states in time series by watching how data patterns shift. Their 2026 work uses the Wasserstein metric, a transport cost between two patterns, to spot change points. Stable states are long-lived modes that a system keeps coming back to, as in molecule simulations.

Their method tracks how fast that cost changes along a path with many measures at each step. Sharp shifts mark borders, which split the series into a few clear stretches. Each stretch is then grouped with like stretches, with the same cost used to judge how close two stretches are. No fixed form is assumed for the data at any step. Cost grows in a straight line with data size, which keeps large paths cheap to treat. Tests span fake paths, molecule runs, and sound traces from under the sea.
arxiv-2603-02289:
Kwangho Kim and Hajin Lee build a framework for cause and effect on shapes in this 2026 paper. Outcomes sometimes live in complex spaces, like networks or images, not plain numbers. Standard causal methods then miss how the shape itself changes. Their approach compares the topological structure of outcomes under treatment and control.

Shape is summarized by persistence diagrams, which record features across scales. Weighted silhouette functions turn those diagrams into curves that can be compared. The team gives an efficient estimator that stays robust if one part is mis-modeled. They prove it settles into a stable pattern as data grows, and build a formal test for no effect. Trials show the method measures shape-level treatment effects reliably across varied outcome types.
arxiv-2603-02389:
Radiative corrections in supergravity models of inflation are examined in this 2026 paper, with Keith Olive among the authors. Supergravity is the natural supersymmetric frame for early universe cosmology. Many no-scale models in it mimic the successful Starobinsky model at first pass. Quantum loop corrections, though, can distort that clean picture.

The authors derive conditions that keep the gravitino mass finite during inflation. They also require loop effects on the potential to stay finite or small. In the original no-scale model, corrections grow at large field values and can take over. Predictions for the cosmic microwave background then become unreliable. A class of Starobinsky-like models, including the Cecotti model, stays safe. There corrections remain tiny across the relevant range, preserving agreement with Planck data.
arxiv-2603-02489:
Gal Ben-Itzhak and Ender Ayanoglu tune smart radio surfaces to clean up wireless signals in this 2026 paper. These surfaces are passive arrays that reshape how signals travel. Wideband links suffer pulse distortion when signals bounce along many paths. A surface inside the channel could fix that distortion before reception.

Their classic method tunes surface settings from full channel knowledge. It cuts multipath effects while boosting signal strength at the receiver. No delay elements are needed, unlike classic adaptive filters. Learning-based control offers an alternative that skips channel estimation entirely. Three learning methods were tested across channel conditions and array sizes. One, SAC, converged fast and stably. It matched the classic method's quality with far less channel knowledge.
arxiv-2603-02589:
Krutika Tawri, Roger Temam, and Xinwu Yang analyze a wave equation shaken by random jumps. Their 2026 paper studies the damped KdV equation, a classic model of shallow water waves, on a ring-shaped domain. Random forcing arrives as sudden jumps rather than smooth noise, which makes long-run behavior harder to pin down.

First they prove that, for any positive damping, the equation has exactly one well-behaved solution path. Then they turn to the long term and ask whether the system settles into a steady statistical state. Using methods from Maslowski and Seidler, they show such a steady state exists when damping is strong enough. Jump noise can disturb averages, so the damping threshold is the key condition.
arxiv-2603-02689:
Joakim Blikstad, Yannic Maus, and Tijn de Vos speed up edge coloring for networks where nodes can only swap short messages. Edge coloring assigns colors to links so that no node touches two links of the same color. Their 2026 algorithm works in the CONGEST model and never uses randomness.

The method colors any graph with only slightly more colors than the busiest node degree demands, in few communication rounds. For mid-sized degrees it beats the classic two-times-degree color count in fast rounds for the first time. The trick came from an online coloring algorithm with very low locality, adapted and derandomized for distributed use. A side result also improves the round count for the classic color bound in all degree ranges.
arxiv-2603-02789:
Jiyuan Shen, Peiyue Yuan, Atin Ghosh, and colleagues ask whether document reading software still needs a separate OCR step. Their 2026 study benchmarks ready-made multimodal language models on pulling data from real business documents. The simpler image-only pipeline is attractive, but its true standing against OCR-assisted setups was unclear.

Across a large set of real-world documents, image-only input matched OCR-enhanced pipelines when the model was strong. The team also built an automated tool that sorts errors into a hierarchy, using language models to spot failure patterns. Careful design of the output schema, examples, and instructions lifted scores further. Their guidance helps teams decide when OCR can be skipped and where effort pays off instead.
arxiv-2603-02889:
Jarosław Pawłowski and Mateusz Krawczyk teach a neural network to read a quantum device's rulebook from its measurements. Their 2026 paper targets solid-state quantum simulators, whose behavior follows an energy rule set called a Hamiltonian. Finding those rules from lab data is normally slow, expert work.

Their physics-informed autoencoder bakes the scattering rules of quantum transport straight into its decoding half, so learned summaries must stay physically sensible. Trained on simulations, it characterized a chain of three quantum dots from transport data alone. The model generalized beyond its training range and coped with noisy measurements, as real labs require. It did weaken when the parameter space grew too large or varied, marking where the method needs care.
arxiv-2603-02989:
Jiayi Wang and Steve Tonneau plan footsteps for two-legged robots in real time without chopping the world into a grid. Classic A-star search needs reachability chopped into discrete steps, while exact optimization handles smooth constraints but slows down fast, especially with turning. Their 2026 framework, CASSR, keeps the constraints continuous inside the search.

Convex, smooth descriptions of the robot's leg reach travel through the search tree as it grows. A new cost-to-go estimate, built on a geometry algorithm, keeps the search aimed well. In tests, plans of up to thirty steps arrived in well under a second. The method beat grid-based A-star by up to one hundred times and also outperformed a commercial optimization solver.
arxiv-2603-03289:
Ji-Eun Byun and Se-Hyeok Lee offer a new way to judge how reliable an industrial process plant is. Plants for chemicals, gas, and energy must keep material flowing through linked stages, yet older tools like fault trees often ignore flow continuity and layout. Their 2026 system function measures the maximum flow a plant can still process, given its structure and stage order.

The function builds on maximum-flow methods and is solved with linear programming, then feeds estimates of failure probability and component importance. Two benchmark cases test it, including a gas supply plant. Layout changes guided by the importance scores cut the failure probability by up to one fifth. The authors present the framework as a practical aid for risk-informed plant planning.
arxiv-2603-03489:
Raz Heppner and four colleagues simulate a shock wave squeezing through a narrow spot in a pipe. Such constrictions appear in engines and natural channels, and the reflected and transmitted shocks they create decide downstream behavior. Their 2026 study varies blockage, constriction length, and shock strength systematically, comparing two shapes: an abrupt rectangular step and a smooth sinusoidal narrowing, the two limiting cases.

Validated large-eddy simulations resolve the full transient, not just the end state. For rectangular steps, the reflected shock's strength depends mainly on blockage, barely on length, while the transmitted shock does feel length. Smooth constrictions couple the two strongly, governed by the wall's local slope. The start-up inside the constriction unfolds far more slowly than the shock's passage, through reflections, separation, and reorganization. Simple semi-empirical formulas fitted to the trends predict both shock strengths across the whole parameter range.
arxiv-2603-03589:
Arnab Phani, Elias Strauss, and Sebastian Schelter sketch infrastructure for machine learning pipelines written by agents rather than people. Language models now generate, test, and refine whole data science pipelines, producing thousands of executions. The popular Python ecosystem was built for humans working interactively, one step at a time, and its slow interpreted core buckles at that scale. Their 2026 vision paper proposes stratum, a system that splits planning from execution.

Stratum accepts pipelines from agents or humans through the usual Python libraries, then compiles batches of them into optimized execution graphs. Those graphs run across heterogeneous backends, including a new runtime written in Rust for speed. Early prototype experiments speed large-scale pipeline search by more than sixteen times. The paper lays out the architecture, key design decisions, and open research problems.
arxiv-2603-03689:
A measurement from the CMS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider listens for the spin of gluons inside particle jets. Gluons, the carriers of the strong force, are spin-one particles, and their polarization should imprint angular patterns when a gluon splits into a quark-antiquark pair inside a jet. This 2026 analysis, using proton collisions recorded by CMS in 2022, goes hunting for that imprint.

Jets are unclustered step by step to expose their inner branching history, and a novel selection isolates the intermediate gluon splittings of interest. The measured polarization-sensitive observable is then compared against two standard shower simulators, each run with and without spin-induced angular correlations. The data side clearly with the models that include gluon polarization, and strongly disfavor those that leave it out. The result validates a subtle quantum chromodynamics effect inside the parton shower.
arxiv-2605-00089:
Bruno Bucciotti, Paolo Creminelli, Alessandro Longo, Warin Patrick McBlain, and Enrico Trincherini study what superluminality can even mean in gravitational effective field theories. A healthy theory should not allow faster-than-light signals, but with gravity there is no fixed Minkowski light cone to compare against. Their criterion is asymptotic: can the theory make signals outrun what the spacetime's asymptotic structure allows?

They analyze signal propagation in black hole backgrounds with higher-derivative operators. In more than four dimensions, effective light cones can produce genuine asymptotic superluminality, which can bound the theory's validity. In four dimensions the asymptotic causal structure proves identical to Schwarzschild's: prompt light rays ignore the corrections, and no asymptotic time advance is possible for any such theory. They also discuss two ways to define superluminality in four dimensions.
arxiv-2605-00189:
Alberto Bressan, Laura Caravenna, and Wen Shen study what smoothed versions of conservation laws look like up close, right where the true solution breaks. Conservation laws govern quantities such as traffic density or gas flow, and their solutions can form shocks, sharp jumps in the state. Many approximation schemes exist, from added viscosity to numerical grids, and broad convergence results are known.

The open question is local: near a shock, a shock collision, or the birth of a new shock, what pattern does an approximation settle into? The authors argue that, after a careful rescaling of space and time near such a point, the approximations approach a specific eternal solution defined for all space and time. They give precise results in the vanishing viscosity case, the scheme where a small smoothing term fades away.
arxiv-2605-00289:
Gayathri Viswanath and 10 co-authors report spectroscopic monitoring of a young giant planet still gathering material, Delorme 1 (AB)b. The companion has about thirteen times Jupiter's mass and circles a pair of stars on a wide orbit. Helium emission lines can reveal how gas falls onto such an object, a view hydrogen lines do not fully give.

The team analyzed thirty-three high-resolution spectra from a major telescope in Chile. Seven helium lines stood out clearly, changing from visit to visit. Several lines split into a narrow part near rest and a broader part shifted toward the red, a shape like that seen in young accreting stars but narrower. The authors trace the narrow part to gas just after the accretion shock, near the planet's surface, and the broad part to the shock front itself.
arxiv-2605-00389:
Mohammad Raihanul Bashar and 3 co-authors add game design to a virtual reality trainer for ultrasound-guided catheter insertion. VR simulators are common in procedural medical training, but many chase realism while giving trainees little formative feedback along the way. The team's simulator answers practice attempts with aligned sights and sounds: progress indicators, guidance, and rewards.

Studies with twenty-four novices and twelve clinicians compared the gamified trainer in use. Gamification cut task time, improved usability scores, and lowered the workload trainees reported. Novices described clearer goals and greater confidence, while experienced clinicians said the pacing of their work improved. The authors conclude that game-style feedback can serve as effective formative feedback in VR medical training, not merely as decoration on top of it.
arxiv-2605-00589:
Taro Kimura and Sanchita Sharma study reflection symmetry for Dirac operators on a finite warped cylinder, a curved tube used as a clean model in spectral theory. Their operator is twisted by a complex line bundle whose holonomy, the phase picked up around the tube, is a parameter. Boundary conditions follow the Atiyah-Patodi-Singer rule, standard for such problems.

They prove the reflection lifts to a unitary symmetry of the twisted setting exactly when twice the holonomy parameter is an integer. In that matching case, reflection pairs up the angular modes, the paired boundary blocks match exactly, and its trace sits on the single self-paired zero-mode sector. They then let the setting vary. With fixed trivial holonomy the family keeps an O(2) equivariance, and its spectral flow splits into named parts. With varying holonomy that equivariance breaks, and only a parity sign survives.
arxiv-2605-00789:
Xihao Chen, Yangyang Guo, and Roger Zimmermann present LightKV, a way to shrink the key-value cache that large vision-language models keep during inference. The cache speeds decoding, but vision tokens from the prefill stage consume large amounts of GPU memory. LightKV reduces that load by exploiting redundancy among vision-token embeddings, guided by the text prompt.

Cross-modality message passing gathers useful information across vision tokens and compresses them step by step during prefill. In tests on eight open models and eight benchmarks, keeping only about half the vision tokens halved the vision cache and cut computation by up to forty percent. General performance held up, and LightKV beat existing baselines by a clear margin.
arxiv-2605-00989:
Yuval Grossman, Guglielmo Papiri, and Stefan Schacht study CP violation induced by neutral kaon mixing in a specific charm meson decay, D-zero to two neutral kaons. CP violation measures a fundamental asymmetry between matter and antimatter behavior. The question is whether kaon mixing, a well-known source, can contribute noticeably to the asymmetry expected in this decay channel.

The authors show the kaon mixing contribution arises only together with second-order weak interactions in the D decay. They estimate the effect at a very small level, negligible compared with current experimental sensitivity and with the expected contribution from CP violation in the charm sector itself. Similar reasoning, they note, can be applied to other systems where such mixing effects might be suspected.
arxiv-2605-01189:
Chandrasekaran and five co-authors present NEURON, a neuro-symbolic system for grounded clinical explainability in health forecasting models. Adoption in clinics is blocked because strong models act as black boxes without grounding in medical concepts or a clear account of their logic. NEURON joins structured data views based on the SNOMED CT medical ontology with machine learning models, bridging raw data and medical nomenclature.

A retrieval-augmented language model layer merges feature scores and per-patient notes into clear plain-language explanations. Tested on MIMIC-IV data for acute heart failure mortality forecasting, NEURON improves discrimination over the base range. It also greatly beats SHAP-based accounts on human-aligned metrics. The authors present the system as a scalable route to trusted connected health uses.
arxiv-2605-01489:
Tianshi Zheng and seven co-authors build research agents that can do frontier science, not just look facts up. Deep research agents learn by hunting information, but science problems hide in sparse, scattered papers and demand heavy computation, so graph-built or browsing-built training data fall short.

Their framework, SciResearcher, makes the training data itself: it synthesizes varied concept and computation tasks grounded in academic proof, and drills information hunting, tool use, and long chains of steps. Fine-tuning plus agentic reinforcement learning on that data yields SciResearcher-8B. At its size it sets a new mark on a hard biology and chemistry bench, beats several larger closed agents, and posts double-digit gains on hard graduate-level biology and literature test sets. The authors offer the pipeline as a scalable route to scientific agents.
arxiv-2605-01689:
Khalid Mahmud Labib, Saad Waheed, Bakhtiar Nafis, and Shabbir Ahmed watch a lithium-ion battery age by turning its dynamics into a network and reading the network's decay. Circuit stand-ins with fixed parts cannot follow the shifting chemistry inside a wearing cell, so the team work from operating data alone.

A control-aware mode decomposition first extracts the battery's modes from the data. The mode matrix becomes a weighted adjacency matrix, a graph whose nodes are dynamic states and whose links carry their coupling strength. Graph measures, connectivity and a modularity proxy among them, then track structure across aging stages. The healthy battery reads as one tight, coherent web. With wear, the web thins, fragments, and grows uneven. The authors offer the graph view as an interpretable gauge of system-level aging that no single voltage curve shows.
arxiv-2605-02389:
Joost Van Veen, Luise Prielinger, and Sebastian Feld improve reinforcement learning for routing circuits in distributed quantum systems. Scaling one quantum processor is hard, so qubits are spread across smaller linked modules. Compilation then means placing, routing, and using qubits across modules, with state-dependent choices about when and where to create shared remote states for remote operations.

Building on a 2024 framework by Promponas and colleagues, the authors introduce an agent with a new action-space formulation and effective action masking. Action-space engineering, shaping what moves the agent may choose, is their lever for faster, better policies. A broad numerical comparison tests the new approach against the earlier one across circuits.
arxiv-2605-02589:
Hedi Tabia and eight co-authors survey how machines learn useful representations from optical coherence tomography images of the retina. This scan type gives sharp, non-invasive views of retinal layers and is now central to eye care. Clinics produce huge volumes of scans, and automated reading promises less reliance on scarce expert labels and more consistent results across devices.

The survey organizes the field by learning style. Covered areas include supervised networks, self-supervised and semi-supervised methods, generative approaches, three-dimensional modeling, multimodal learning, and large pretrained foundation models, including vision-language systems. For each area the authors trace main contributions, note limits that persist, and follow links between older and newer work. The review serves as a map for researchers entering retinal image analysis.
arxiv-2605-02789:
Mario Rodríguez Béjar and two co-authors present FunFuzz, a fuzzing framework that uses language models to hunt compiler bugs. Fuzzing feeds a program crafted inputs to trigger faults, and model-written inputs can be well structured. But results swing with the starting prompt and random sampling, wasting effort on repeated inputs.

FunFuzz runs several isolated searches in parallel, like islands, and migrates strong candidates between them to keep variety. Starting prompts come from documentation, with topic-specific instructions per island, and prompts adapt under feedback as the run goes. Candidates are ranked by new compiler coverage, and compiler-internal failure signals flag crash inputs. In day-long campaigns on two major compilers, the framework reached higher coverage than prior model-driven baselines and found more distinct failures.
arxiv-2605-02889:
Roman Gorazd introduces gluing diagrams, a combinatorial tool for building maps between shift systems on directed graphs, and applies them to a classic group theory problem. Higman-Thompson groups can be viewed as the full symmetry groups of such shifts. Whether two of them are isomorphic was conjectured by Higman, and existence of the isomorphisms was later proved, but an explicit construction was missing.

Gluing diagrams construct homomorphisms between the shift pseudogroups, and the paper establishes which diagrams give isomorphisms. The constructive procedure for Higman-Thompson groups follows Euclid's algorithm, the ancient method for common divisors, repurposed as a recipe for gluing. The diagrams also lift isomorphisms to higher arity, giving explicit witnesses where theory previously gave only existence.
arxiv-2605-03689:
Mert Tiftikci, Amir Molzam Sharifloo, and Mira Mezini introduce CGFuse, a framework that gives pre-trained language models direct access to the structure of program code. Language models read code as token sequences, so they miss control flow and data dependencies that a graph represents naturally. Earlier fixes extracted graph features or added them to prompts, losing information along the way.

CGFuse instead fuses graph-derived representations at token level inside the model's intermediate layers. A graph neural network learns the structural features, and the language model keeps its fine-grained detail during generation. The authors present the work as the first systematic exploration of deep token-level graph-language fusion for structure-aware code generation.
arxiv-2605-03989:
Dutao Zhang and Tian Liao present Experience-RAG Skill, a pluggable retrieval layer that sits between an agent and a pool of retrievers in retrieval-augmented generation systems. A single fixed retrieval pipeline is often assumed to serve all tasks, yet factoid question answering, multi-hop reasoning, and scientific fact checking prefer different retrieval strategies. The skill chooses among them per task.

The proposed skill analyzes the current scene and consults an experience memory. It selects a suitable retrieval strategy and returns structured evidence to the agent. Under a fixed candidate pool, it achieved a strong overall ranking score across three BEIR datasets. Those cover natural questions, multi-hop questions, and scientific fact checking. It outperformed fixed single-retriever baselines and stayed close to Adaptive-RAG-style routing. The authors argue picking the retrieval strategy belongs in a reusable agent skill.
arxiv-2605-04189:
Brandon Lit, Anthony Maocheia-Ricci, and Thomas Driscoll compare how software testing tools show their results to the people who run them. Their study covers fifty tools and test harnesses across four well used programming languages, most with text output and a few with visual screens.

The team records the shared parts of these outputs, how results are laid out, and how colour is used in both text and visual tools. Their findings point to clear trends that tool makers can follow, so test results become easier to read, scan, and act on.
arxiv-2605-04289:
Andrea Britto and five co-authors build realistic models of United States power transmission grids entirely from public data. Detailed grid data are restricted for security reasons, which limits research, so an open route to full models has clear value.

Their five-stage pipeline pulls infrastructure from OpenStreetMap, rebuilds the network layout, estimates electrical values from official plant data, and spreads hourly demand across buses using census population. It then solves power flow for models of all forty-eight mainland states plus six multi-state regions. Most state models converge under the strictest settings, and costs and losses look close to real market outcomes.
arxiv-2605-04689:
Tao Gu and three co-authors explore a bridge between logic and computation, linking a completeness proof for intuitionistic logic to the programming technique of continuation-passing style. Their setting is proof-theoretic semantics, where the meaning of a logical statement is given by the rules for proving it.

They focus on base-extension semantics. They analyse a known completeness proof through the lenses of Kripke and Heyting semantics. They also use natural deduction and the lambda calculus, on the computing side. Their analysis shows that written forms of continuations capture basic ideas about meaning and use. Proof-theoretic semantics makes those ideas precise. The two traditions, they suggest, describe one thing from two sides.
arxiv-2605-04789:
Jun-Hua Gu and thirteen co-authors describe the design and commissioning of an upgraded radio telescope built as a testbed for the Square Kilometre Array era. Complex digital architectures in modern arrays create new instrumental effects, and strategies for handling them need a working platform before the giant array is fully operational.

The upgraded system adds a digital backend capable of forming beams in real time. The team demonstrates it with interferometric observations. High-time-resolution pulsar measurements confirm its sensitivity and stability. As a case study, they characterise a sawtooth-like spectral artefact. It is introduced by the two-stage channelisation used in similar low-frequency systems. They use both simulations and real data, to guide future calibration.
arxiv-2605-04889:
Robert Hao and three co-authors prove a new partition identity in the Andrews-Gordon family, which concerns ways of writing whole numbers as sums under set rules. Earlier work by Andrews treated parity conditions, where even or odd parts appear an even number of times. Two cases were settled, each with its own product form.

Hao and colleagues handle the remaining mixed-parity case using Bailey's lemma, obtaining an identity whose product side matches one earlier case. They also derive a recurrence by fixing peaks in related lattice paths, which supplies a combinatorial reading the sum form lacked. The identity is then proved analytically, completing this branch of the parity story.
arxiv-2605-04989:
Ali Shibli, Andrea Nascetti, and Yifang Ban test how best to adapt large geospatial foundation models for mapping wildfire burn areas from Sentinel-2 satellite images. Such maps support damage assessment, emissions modelling, and fire-climate research. The open question was which fine-tuning style survives shifts in place and time.

Using thousands of wildfire events across the United States and Canada, they compare full fine-tuning, decoder-only tuning, and low-rank adaptation for three leading models. Low-rank adaptation gave the strongest generalisation across domains while updating under one percent of parameters. One model paired with that method achieved the highest accuracy and the largest gain over full tuning.
arxiv-2605-05089:
Anatoly Krestenko and three co-authors treat decentralised basis trading, holding a spot asset while shorting its perpetual contract, as a collateral control problem. The strategy must split capital between spot inventory and derivative margin under on-chain liquidity and execution frictions. Getting that split wrong risks liquidation or wasted carry.

A static analysis shows a risk-constrained rule gives a more robust benchmark than the pure economic optimum, with required collateral rising under volatility stress. A dynamic extension sets an asymmetric intervention band, driven by solvency below and by carry losses versus rebalancing costs above. Live routed execution and historical backtests validate the execution layer of the design.
arxiv-2605-05189:
Nicholas Barnfield and four co-authors find sharp capacity limits for linear associative memories, asking how many key-value pairs a square matrix memory can store and retrieve. The answer depends on the retrieval rule, not just the number of free entries. Under Gaussian embeddings, they prove a sharp threshold for the strictest rule, where every target must beat its strongest competitor.

Above the threshold they construct a memory that retrieves everything, and below it they prove no data-dependent linear memory can. The logarithmic cost in the threshold is the unavoidable price of winner-take-all decoding. For weaker top-list retrieval they introduce a tail-average margin measure and characterise the high-dimensional behaviour of learning with it exactly.
arxiv-2605-05289:
Daniel Paradiso, Sarah Vallejo, and Eric Coughlin explain the origin of mass ejection in failed supernovae, the quiet collapses of massive stars that form black holes without a bright explosion. Neutrinos escaping the newborn neutron star launch a weak shock into the star's outer layers, producing a faint transient as it breaks out. Two self-similar solutions describe that shock, mixing outward ejecta with fallback onto the black hole.

The authors show the stronger-shock family is unstable, with its Mach number growing slowly away from the self-similar prediction, while the weaker family is stable. Above a reachable mass-loss threshold the shock strengthens toward the strong limit. Ejection, they conclude, is governed mainly by neutrino mass loss relative to the mass the shock encloses.
arxiv-2605-05589:
The Heisenberg chain is the textbook example of an exactly solvable quantum magnet. Oliver R. Bellwood and William J. Munro ask a sharper question: can its finite-size ground states be written down symbolically at all? They analyze exact Bethe ansatz solutions for chains of up to twelve sites, tracking the algebra behind the numbers.

The algebraic degree of the magnon phases and Bethe roots grows at a different rate than that of the energy and wavefunction. For ten or more sites, the Bethe roots and energy become Galois unsolvable. Exact solvability, in other words, does not guarantee a usable closed-form answer.
arxiv-2605-05689:
Diffusion models can predict how a graph will change, but sampling them is slow and sometimes unstable. Shaozhen Ma and four co-authors present GCCM, which pairs generative graph prediction with a contrastive consistency model. Consistency training shortens sampling to few steps, yet the authors find it can collapse into a shortcut that satisfies the constraint without learning the prediction.

Their contrastive component guards against that degenerate solution. The model learns conditional distributions over target graphs given an input graph. The combination aims at competitive accuracy with stable, cheap sampling at inference time.
arxiv-2605-05789:
Hiding secret text inside an image is an old trick with new stakes: hidden instructions can be aimed at large AI models. Zhen Sun and four co-authors build SADBench, a benchmark that stages this contest directly. It measures an attacker's ability to inject harmful secrets through steganography and a defender's ability to catch them through steganalysis.

The benchmark spans four core tasks covering both sides of the fight. Existing evaluations treated attack and defense separately or not at all. By scoring them together, SADBench shows how the threat evolves as each side improves.
arxiv-2605-06289:
Heegeon Yoon and Heeyoung Kim build a multimodal generative model for learning from partly labeled, class imbalanced data. Models trained on skewed data favor majority classes, and semi supervised learning makes it worse: pseudo labels for unlabeled items are predicted from the same skewed labeled set, spreading the bias further. Most existing remedies also assume a single input modality, ignoring the complementary signals that multimodal data offers.

Their model uses a separate encoder per modality with latent variables shared across modalities, joined by a product of experts rule. Student t distributions replace Gaussians in the prior, encoder, and decoder to fit the heavy tailed latent patterns of imbalanced data. A new training objective built on a power divergence covers labeled and unlabeled data together. Benchmark results beat baseline methods.
arxiv-2605-06389:
Cheng Chi and Yan Wang present a proof concerning families of sets with no s pairwise disjoint members. The maximum size of such a family is tied to the Erdős matching conjecture, a classic extremal combinatorics problem. Frankl and Kupavskii had conjectured an exact formula for a certain range of set sizes.

The authors show that, for each fixed m at least three and all sufficiently large s, the extremal families have a specific weighted form based on a small set L. That confirms the Frankl-Kupavskii conjecture in that range. For m equal to three they pin down the full range, extending earlier work.
arxiv-2605-06589:
Wilfrid Gangbo, Sebastian Munoz, Jeremy Wu, and Zhaoyu Zhang develop a careful solution theory for mean field game systems on finite graphs when individual noise is present. The extended system couples a master equation and a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation on the probability simplex. Its shape comes from discrete optimal transport, where an entropic equation appears as a gradient flow on the graph.

A key step proves positivity stays in a measured way for the discrete continuity equation, ruling out solutions hitting zero at the boundary in finite time. That yields smooth solutions on the open simplex with no boundary rule imposed. As an application, the discrete system recovers a Nash equilibrium reading through Markov chains on the graph.
arxiv-2605-06889:
Francisco Chen, Yiran Wang, and Yunpeng Shi improve global camera pose finding by enforcing consistency among triples of cameras. Structure-from-motion pipelines locate cameras from pairwise translation directions. Pairs estimated on their own can look locally plausible yet clash with each other. Their TriDE method treats triangle consistency as a cheap, higher-order check on each direction, avoiding a costly global nonlinear search that hinges on its starting point.

Message passing between directions and their weighted triangles refines weak estimates by spreading trustworthy information. The authors prove a phase-transition bound for exact recovery under a plausible corruption model. On real image graphs, direction accuracy improves by a large margin, and downstream camera locations get better. Local estimates thus link to global geometry in a practical way.
arxiv-2605-07289:
Soh Kumabe and Yuya Uezato study how hard it is to match text against regular expressions that contain backreferences, a feature of most real matching engines. The question matters because slow matching enables ReDoS attacks, where crafted input strings exhaust a server. Famous outages at Stack Overflow and Cloudflare came from exactly this weakness.

The pair prove strong limits. For the general problem, no algorithm can run much faster than a certain power of the input length, assuming a standard complexity hypothesis. The problem is also hard in a parameterized sense. For a restricted one-use form, though, they give a fast algorithm running in near-linear time. Their tools include suffix trees and factorization forests.
arxiv-2605-07389:
A. Azamnouri and five co-authors study teamwork problems inside machine learning teams in the semiconductor industry. Such teams mix engineers, data scientists, and domain experts with different goals and jargon, which makes long-term rollout harder. Hardware settings add strict data rules, long cycles, and tight coupling to plant processes.

Talking with twelve staff at a global chip company, the team found sixteen common challenges, with unclear roles and duties ranked most serious. They also collected habits staff found useful against those problems. The findings match known issues in cross-field work, but show how hardware constraints reshape them.
arxiv-2605-07789:
Sora Kang and six co-authors study how people actually make everyday decisions in conversation, to design conversational AI that works the way people do. Most systems reason from data, but people lean on heuristics and social moves in natural talk. The team analyzed nine hundred fifty-five real Korean conversations about food and travel decisions, coding them with a decision-making codebook.

People mostly satisfice rather than optimize, drawing on internal knowledge and conversational strategies to manage mental effort. A frequency-efficiency mismatch stood out: the commonest heuristics keep exploration flowing, while rare rule-based strategies are the ones that drive decisions to resolution when closing. The authors map how these patterns transfer to human-AI interaction and derive design lessons from them.
arxiv-2605-07889:
Louis Seyfritz and two co-authors hunt for warning signs before a giant solar flare. On October 3, 2024 the Sun produced an X9.0-class flare from active region NOAA 13842, and instruments had been watching for hours beforehand, a rare chance to study the pre-flare phase. The team analyzed spectroscopic data from the IRIS satellite, centered on a silicon emission line.

Time-series and wavelet analysis found two bands of periodic oscillation during the pre-flare hours, around seven to ten minutes and eighteen to twenty-one minutes, enhanced near the polarity inversion line. Line measures there also rose steadily from three hours before the flare, tipping into strong non-thermal velocities and blueshifts about fifteen minutes before onset. The pattern fits a slow destabilization of the coronal magnetic field, perhaps a flux rope activating, before rapid reconnection.
arxiv-2605-07989:
Wilhiam de Carvalho and four co-authors dissect dynamic operating envelopes: the import and export limits assigned to customers on radial distribution networks. They ask how the envelopes should be computed and shared out. As rooftop solar and electric vehicles stress low-voltage grids, these envelopes decide who may use how much network capacity. The calculation details turn out to matter a great deal.

Envelopes shift significantly with the power flow model used, with whether thermal or voltage limits bind, and with whether the import or export case is being computed. The team proposes a new algorithm, LACE, designed for transparent, scalable computation that can run on larger networks or alongside other optimization engines. Simulations span standard test feeders and a realistic Belgian low-voltage feeder with real-world data.
arxiv-2605-08289:
Fan Zhang, Shiming Fan, and Hua Wang argue that forecasting models should forget most cross-variable links. In multivariate series, real links depend on the current state. They also come with noise. Dense interaction layers can amplify fake correlations. They can smooth representations until predictions turn unreliable in the hard cases.

Their MS-FLOW framework treats interaction as a capacity-limited flow. The flow passes through a sparse bottleneck. Only a few key dependency paths stay open. Cross-variable signals pass under a strict communication budget. The routing keeps the links that matter for the present regime. It drops the spurious ones that dense models would amplify.
arxiv-2605-08389:
Mingyu Liu, Sihan Huang, Yijia Fan, Yinlin Yan, and coauthors fix a subtle flaw in zero-shot composed image retrieval. A user supplies a photo plus a text edit. The system must find the edited target. No labeled training triplets exist. Lightweight projection methods are cheap. But they treat the edit text as a label for the target image. They miss that it is a change applied to the source.

The authors show that one adapter trained for both jobs creates a conflict. Endpoint matching fights transition learning. DeCIR separates them. Paired forward and reverse edit tuples are built from image-caption pairs. They train distinct low-rank modules for endpoints and for semantic transitions. The bottleneck goes away.
arxiv-2605-08489:
Musabbir Ahmed Arrafi, Malik Ali, Nicholas Stiffler, and Krishna Bhavithavya Kidambi model race car dynamics with a memory that respects physics. At the handling limit, simulators built on simple assumptions miss nonlinear behavior. Purely learned models can drift into states no real car can reach. They can also fail when track conditions change, and a race car gives no second chances at speed.

DynSSM couples two learned parts with a structured vehicle model at the core. State-space sequence modeling and recurrent encoders capture long and short dynamic patterns. Tire and vehicle settings adapt inside bounded ranges to stay plausible. A small patch term absorbs what the physics misses. The hybrid targets accurate, adaptable dynamics for high-speed racing controllers.
arxiv-2605-08689:
Xiaodong He and four coauthors build graph foundation models that treat network structure itself as the transferable knowledge. Graphs from different domains clash in both shape and node features, blocking one model for all. Their structure centric approach views graphs as metric measure spaces and learns geometric bases that form a shared coordinate system for structure.

Graphs align to those bases through optimal transport distances, while a structure aware re-encoding unifies node features without fixed dimensions or per dataset preparation. Across graph level and node level tasks, the model generalizes within and across domains better than earlier graph foundation approaches. Graph learning gains a path toward general models grounded in shape rather than surface features.
arxiv-2605-09089:
Abhishek Kumar, Riya Tapwal, Carsten Maple, and Mark Hooper build a detector for forged identity documents, the kind uploaded when people open bank or telecom accounts online. Attackers may swap the photo, edit text fields, or do both, and general forgery detectors are not built for the fixed layout of such documents.

Their system, FLiD, first finds the face and text regions with a tuned detector, then reads each region with a small frozen image model and a compact classifier. Tested with repeated cross-checks, it beat a whole-document baseline by a wide margin on error rates. It also used far fewer trainable parts and far less computing than general detectors, suiting places with tight resources.
arxiv-2605-09289: Thin plates that do not fit Euclidean geometry — curved by growth or heat — vibrate in strange modes. Joseph C. Roback, Carlos E. Moguel-Lehmer, and others study the dynamical geometric modes of non-Euclidean plates. The 2026 paper is elasticity theory for warped sheets.
arxiv-2605-09489: The signed bipartite graph SB(3,n) — with all its symmetries — cannot host a Hamiltonian cycle when n is even. Shisheng Li proves it with a clever sign-of-permutation argument. The 2026 paper is graph theory with a satisfying parity punchline.
arxiv-2605-10089: Lithium body salts — coordination, screening, emergent length scales — seen from a small-scale perspective. Amaury Coste, Eva Zunzunegui-Bru, Ambroise van Roekeghem, and others provide it. The 2026 paper is battery man-made science at small-scale clarity. It sees battery body salts patiently molecule by molecule.
arxiv-2606-00089:
Or asks a question about robot prediction systems in this 2026 arXiv paper: can a predicted motion be accurate on average yet physically impossible? Physical AI models output rollouts and plans, and low prediction error does not guarantee a proposal could run. Or formalizes physical admissibility as a gate before control. Before running, each plan is checked against kinematic and dynamic conditions and horizon consistency rules, with rejections explained by component.

Experiments used the PushT benchmark from the LeRobot collection, with rigged tests. One-step error and dynamics residuals each separated valid from invalid proposals well, while kinematic checks alone performed weakly. The gate scored strongly while adding step-level attribution for its calls. In replay tests, the filters prevented 87 to 89 percent of invalid proposals while keeping progress almost intact. Passing the gate is not a certificate, Or stresses, but failing it identifies a concrete violation.

arxiv-2606-04089:
Wynne Turner presents in 2026 a new way to clean up noisy covariance matrices, the error tables that cosmology analyses depend on for honest parameter estimates. When the data vector is huge, as in three-dimensional Lyman-alpha forest surveys, the matrix built from data subsamples cannot even be inverted.

Turner's method projects the noisy matrix onto the pattern basis of a mock-based reference, then builds a weighted correction from a second basis trained by a classifier on simulations. The patch captures correlation structure the first pass missed. Tested on mock data the classifier never saw, the method reconstructed matrices far better than the current smoothing fix. It also recovered cosmological parameter ranges much closer to those from the true covariance.
arxiv-2606-04289:
Karthik Shivaram and colleagues develop in 2026 a weakly supervised method to find social media posts that criticize partisan news outlets, a signal tied to hyperpartisanship and distrust of media. Labeled examples are scarce, so they cannot train a classifier the ordinary way.

Instead, several noisy labeling rules, drawing on post content and on each user's history of sharing news, vote together to train the classifier. Applying it at scale, they found criticism spiking around polarizing events, including the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election and the 2017 Charlottesville rally. Criticism also became more likely after users had been exposed to unreliable, hyperpartisan media. The authors offer the method as a health monitor for the information ecosystem.
arxiv-2606-04489:
Wu and colleagues speculate on the wider social effects of mediated social touch, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A hug from afar, or from the past, shows the promise. Such systems can reduce loneliness and give emotional support. The authors argue that research has focused on these direct benefits. It has neglected broader social and technical impacts, both welcome and harmful.

They use the Future Ripples method. This is a structured speculation exercise. They ran three workshops with 24 participants. The group included potential users, domain experts, and haptics researchers. Participants envisioned future scenarios, opportunities, and threats. They also proposed concrete responses. The analysis organized the results into four themes and three distinctive challenges. The authors map those challenges onto the record-synthesize-reproduce pipeline. This points to intervention points for designers. It also gives lessons on applying Future Ripples to new technology.
arxiv-2606-04689:
Ramkumar, Innan, and Shafique replace the classical decision head that labels relations in images with a small quantum circuit, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Datasets are heavily long-tailed. Classical models lean on dataset statistics, predicting frequent relations instead of fine-grained ones. Yet the predicate classifier remains a large classical module with high parameter cost.

Their hybrid system puts a Quantum Predicate Head inside an existing scene graph network. It is trained with weighted cross-entropy. The best four-qubit head uses amplitude embedding and strongly entangling layers. It compresses 4,096-dimensional pair features into a 16-dimensional quantum representation, a 256-fold reduction. It reaches a mean recall at 100 of 57.25 percent against 41.1 percent for the classical reference. It uses only 96 trainable quantum parameters. Scaling to eight qubits keeps strong long-tail performance at 55.38 percent. Depth analysis exposes an expressibility-versus-runtime trade-off.
arxiv-2606-04789:
Rather studies the independence polynomial of zero divisor graphs, in a 2026 arXiv mathematics paper. A graph's independence polynomial encodes, in its coefficients, how many independent sets it has of each size. Counting them is NP-hard in general, so theorems matter. The graphs here come from commutative rings: vertices are zero divisors, joined when their product is zero.

Rather demonstrates that the sequences of these polynomials are unimodal, rising then falling, and log-concave, so the unimodality conjecture holds for the independence polynomials of some zero divisor graphs. He also delineates the polynomial's zeros, locating the annular regions of the complex plane where they lie. The ring's arithmetic shapes the graph, and the polynomial's shape, in turn, certifies properties that are invisible from the graph alone.
arxiv-2606-04889:
Pala, Toh, and Poria stop rewarding every word of a good answer equally, in a 2026 arXiv paper on reinforcement learning for reasoning. Methods like GRPO broadcast one sequence-level advantage to all tokens, or pay for costly process reward models to supervise step by step. Flawed reasoning steps and filler words are reinforced as strongly as valid logical inferences. Their method, GRAIL, reweights the advantage token by token using gradient-activation saliency.

Tokens that matter get more weight; filler gets less. Across five models from the Qwen3, R1-distilled, and OctoThinker families, GRAIL outperforms GRPO, improving accuracy by an average of 3.60 percent and Pass@3 by 3.05 percent. The gains demonstrate that fine-grained reasoning alignment is achievable without process-level supervision, using only signals already inside the model. That makes the method cheap to adopt wherever group-relative reinforcement learning is already used to teach mathematical reasoning.
arxiv-2606-05289:
Arhum Ansari, Deep Mazumdar, and Brijesh Thakkar show that core structural properties of cosmological correlators descend from flat-space physics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their starting point is a framework in which correlators in de Sitter and anti-de Sitter space are written as flat-space scattering amplitudes dressed with propagators that encode the curved background.

Working inside that dressed representation, the authors derive cosmological cutting rules for spinning correlators from the flat-space optical theorem, which ties the imaginary part of an amplitude to intermediate processes. They obtain the cosmological tree theorem from the Feynman tree theorem. They lift the BCFW recursion relations into the curved setting through the same dressing. Flat-space soft theorems are shown to reproduce the soft limits of the curved-space correlators. The analysis finds indications of an emergent universal structure in the subleading soft limits.
arxiv-2606-05489:
Esmat and colleagues tackle a tuning problem in visual search in their 2026 arXiv paper. Modern search systems pair an image index with many linked settings. Older tuning tools treat each setting as if it stood alone. That habit breaks down when the settings affect each other. The team instead uses a large language model, a program trained on text, as the tuner. Their test case is finding pictures of people acting on objects.

The model tuner plans its search in phases and learns from every past trial. On the HICO-DET test set it beat a leading tuning tool by about a third on a score that balances speed and quality. It also gave more than fifteen times the throughput of a rival search system. Tests on two other data sets and a second database system confirmed the gain.
arxiv-2606-05989:
Nagesh, Pasha, Kumar, and Narahari test two exponential graph numbers that predict molecular energy in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chemical graph theory squeezes a molecule into indices from atom-bond structure. Gourava indices weight bonds by atom degrees; exponential variants sharpen their sensitivity. The study works out both the sum-connectivity and product-connectivity versions for benzenoid hydrocarbons, the fused-ring family behind many dyes and drugs.

The two indices correlate strongly with each other across the compounds. Fits against pi-electron energies, a key molecular property, proved very tight. Correlations exceeded zero point nine nine nine in the reported fits. The product-connectivity variant fit slightly better, landing closer to optimal least-squares values. Such accuracy lets chemists estimate electronic properties before synthesis or heavy computing. Structure-property studies gain two checked descriptors. The authors present the product form as the more promising of the pair for precision work.
arxiv-2606-06189:
Lindsay Burke and co-authors design a bus network that routes itself like slime mold in this 2026 arXiv paper on public transit. Demand responsive transit drops fixed routes and sends vehicles where riders actually request trips, which suits sparse areas. Central scheduling, though, tends to be costly and unreliable. Slime molds, though brainless, grow efficient networks toward food, and the team borrows that trick for routing.

In their system, buses allocate passengers and arrange transfers through a continual cooperative bidding process, with no central dispatcher. A slime mold inspired algorithm reshapes routes as demand shifts. Simulations on real street maps from OpenStreetMap covered suburban, urban, and semi rural settings. Against a fixed route network, the swarm system raised passenger delivery rates by twenty eight, forty nine, and one hundred one percent across the three settings. Walking time for riders fell by more than seventy five percent in every case.
arxiv-2606-06689:
Light based quantum computers have a quiet weakness: plain glass can delay and mix pulses of light, but it can never multiply them. Soh proves what changes when one nonlinear element joins the loop. His 2026 arXiv paper studies quantum reservoir computing, where a physical system does the hard processing and only a simple readout is trained.

The added element is a Kerr medium, whose effect on light depends on the light's own brightness, placed inside a delayed feedback loop. Each trip around the loop lets a pulse interact with its own past, so one mode does the work of many. Soh proves a strict gap. A linear reservoir with any number of modes hits a ceiling on the cross time patterns it can form. The single Kerr mode faces no such ceiling. Its reach grows with loop depth at no extra hardware cost.
arxiv-2606-07089:
A robot that plans with imagined video still has to decide how to think. Yinzhou Tang and co-authors give their world action model a choice of thinking modes in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models predict future observations to guide robot actions. Text reasoning suits big task transitions. Visual reasoning suits fine, delicate manipulation.

Their AdaWAM switches between the modes as context demands. A light dynamic router triggers the right kind of reasoning autonomously. During high level shifts, the model reasons in words. During precise contact work, it reasons in pictures. Tests ran on simulated suites and real robot platforms. AdaWAM beat leading embodied policies on long, complex tasks. It also cut wasted computation by skipping needless reasoning. The authors liken the design to dreaming only when necessary. Future work may add touch and depth senses, and let the router learn its own boundaries.
arxiv-2606-07189:
A photon can briefly behave like a bundle of quarks and gluons, and physicists need maps of that inner structure. Chithirasreemadam and colleagues provide new maps, called VALO1.0, in this 2026 arXiv paper. These parton distribution functions state how likely a photon is to reveal each constituent at a given energy share. They matter for predicting photon-driven reactions at colliders.

The team fitted world data on the photon structure function measured in electron-positron scattering, using one hundred Monte Carlo replicas to track experimental uncertainty. A five-parameter starting form, with simplified flavor assumptions, produced stable quark distributions at both accuracy orders studied. The gluon distribution was well determined at the higher accuracy order but remained largely unconstrained at the lower one. Uncertainties stayed modest above one percent of the photon momentum and grew below it, where data are sparse.
arxiv-2606-07689:
Fan Zhang and colleagues introduce Struct-Searcher, a research agent that keeps its evidence organised as a changing graph, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Deep research agents gather online information to answer hard questions, now across text and images together. Most simply pile up evidence in a line, which handles contradictory sources badly.

Struct-Searcher borrows belief revision theory, a formal account of how beliefs should change when new evidence conflicts with old. Its structural graph is updated as evidence arrives, so conflicts between text and image sources are faced rather than buried. Across several benchmarks and five backbone models, the workflow raised accuracy by about seventeen percent on average in relative terms on BrowseComp-VL. It also beat the strongest rival systems on three multimodal search benchmarks, and it works as a plug-in with different underlying models.
arxiv-2606-07789:
Cerqueira and co-authors build a fairer way to benchmark concept drift detectors, in this 2026 arXiv paper for KDD. Concept drift is the moment a data stream's patterns change, quietly degrading any model trained on the old pattern. Detectors exist to flag that moment. Comparing them has been messy, because studies used toy data, incompatible metrics, and hidden tuning choices.

The framework injects controlled changes into real datasets through Monte Carlo trials, keeping real-world complexity while making the true drift points known. Its scoring is timing-aware, adding an F1 detection score and a normalised detection time that can be compared across streams. The authors also urge tuning each method while leaving one dataset out, to reward robustness. They benchmark fourteen widely used detectors on seven real datasets across four drift types, under both abrupt and gradual change, and publish the baselines.
arxiv-2606-07889:
Pandya, Zhang, and Lyu name and measure a failure pattern in coding agents in this 2026 arXiv paper: strained coherence. Sometimes an agent states a problem in its reasoning, then proceeds anyway, acting against information it registered. The pattern matters: it marks failures the agent had the means to avoid. It resembles reward hacking, where the agent names the gap between a proxy and the goal, then optimises the proxy regardless.

The team defines the pattern and builds a judge that reads trajectories and flags spans. On forty-four trajectories from a benchmark, flagged runs failed ninety-four percent of the time. Unflagged runs failed forty-six percent, a forty-seven point gap. At matched selectivity their detector reached ninety-four percent precision, beating a lexical baseline at eighty-eight percent. A replication on a second family pointed the same way, more weakly, because many trajectories held no reasoning to read.
arxiv-2606-08089:
Yang Qu and Rong Ma solve a Waring-type problem for a quirky family of integers, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Waring's problem asks how many k-th powers are needed to write every large number. The summands here are D. H. Lehmer numbers. Relative to an odd prime p, a number a counts if a plus its modular inverse is odd. The inverse is the number that multiplies with a to give one modulo p.

For any fixed odd prime, they prove two results. Every sufficiently large integer, except possibly those congruent to fifteen or sixteen modulo sixteen, is a sum of fourteen fourth powers of Lehmer numbers. Dropping the congruence restriction costs two more summands: every sufficiently large integer is a sum of sixteen fourth powers of Lehmer numbers. The counts sit close to the Waring number for fourth powers, sixteen. Thinning the allowed summands barely raises the price.
arxiv-2606-08189:
Zhang and Chen prove a result in quantum information theory in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their subject is steering, the effect where measurements on one particle seem to fix the state of a distant partner particle. A state is called entangled when two particles share linked behavior that no separate description can capture. The authors ask whether every weakly mixed entangled state of a kind called rank two can be steered using only the simplest measurements, known as projective measurements.

The answer is yes, in at least one direction, for systems of any finite size. When both sides have equal effective size, steering works in both directions. The proof is geometric rather than based on testing a steering inequality, a numerical test for the effect. It locates a boundary point where a measurement outcome must land, and shows that this contact itself certifies steering.
arxiv-2606-08289:
