Juan Pablo Ferreira studies how national statistical offices can estimate totals for small subpopulations in this 2026 arXiv paper. These offices use a uni-weight approach: one set of survey weights, independent of the variable measured, produces estimates for many parameters and many domains, meaning subpopulations of interest. The paper examines regression trees, simple models that split data by thresholds, as the assisting model, focusing on unplanned domains.

Two strategies are compared. One fits a single tree at the population level and derives universal weights usable for any domain. The other fits a separate tree for each domain. Ferreira shows both estimators can be written as weighted sums whose weights do not depend on the measured variable. This preserves the uni-weight property and additivity, so domain estimates still sum to the population total. The analysis is design-based, resting on the survey design itself.
arxiv-2606-08489:
Hoyer reviews a perturbative approach to bound states in the theories of the strong and electromagnetic forces, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Bound states, particles held together as hadrons or atoms, differ from scattering states, yet textbooks on quantum field theory barely cover them. Hoyer's method rests on canonical quantization with the temporal gauge fully fixed, which imposes Gauss's law on physical states. As Dirac pointed out, this implies electron states include a longitudinal gauge field, and that field determines the instantaneous potential binding the state.

The same structure applies to quarks and gluons in quantum chromodynamics. An instantaneous confining potential arises for color-singlet quark-antiquark states. It needs a non-vanishing boundary condition on the longitudinal field at infinity. Following Gribov, the strong coupling may freeze at a perturbative value when the confining potential dominates.
arxiv-2606-08789:
Grabovsky and Truskinovsky extend a symmetry method to elastic bodies whose motion develops shocks, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Elastodynamics describes how deformable solids move and vibrate. Its solutions make an action quantity extreme, but they can also form shocks, abrupt jumps in strain and speed. Emmy Noether's approach turns symmetries of the action into integral rules over the whole body. The authors adapt it to solutions with shocks.

They derive new integral rules involving the body's kinetic and elastic energies. For the allowed solutions, those obeying an entropy condition, the equalities turn into inequalities. The striking finding concerns energy storage. Even though material speed drives how energy spreads through the process, the kinetic energy can be removed entirely from the formula for stored elastic energy. That removal holds even when shocks are present, through their generalized Noether rules.
arxiv-2606-09189:
Tai shows brain-signal AI models leak private attributes through their embeddings even when standard privacy checks pass, in this 2026 arXiv paper. EEG foundation models turn brain recordings into reusable embeddings. Releases are audited one endpoint at a time: raw reconstruction, membership inference, or identity linkage. Tai audits 3 models, BIOT, LaBraM, and EEGPT, under all 4 endpoints jointly, finding leaks single-endpoint audits miss.

The decisive test is cross-encoder transfer. A ridge decoder trained on one frozen encoder transfers, via a fitted linear bridge, to held-out-subject splits of every other encoder, its confidence bound at least 0.081 across all 6 directions. He proves when such bridges must exist, introduces a disagreement score positive in all 8 test cells, and shows a membership audit reaching only 0.50 to 0.70 AUC. Standard defenses, including differentially private training at useful noise levels, left the channel unchanged. The framework turns scattered checks into one release decision.
arxiv-2606-09689:
Jack Kelley speeds up a wave solver by pairing two tricks that each cut cost in this 2026 arXiv paper. The target is the Helmholtz equation, the steady form of the wave equation, on a two-dimensional grid. Such solves feed sonar, speech tech, and scans. The Operator Fourier Transform rewrites the task as a sweep over a fake time of Schrödinger-type solves.

Those inner solves carry the main cost, most of all at fine grids. Kelley's fix is a low-rank cross method, Cross-DEIM, which works with a thin slice of the full data. Low-rank methods beat the growth of cost with size when the answer has hidden thin structure. The pair is tested on classes of wave problems where that structure shows. For those, the joint method cut costs by a large margin.
arxiv-2606-09989:
Saito and his team study what makes supercurrents flow without resistance in quasicrystals, in a 2026 arXiv paper on condensed matter physics. Quasicrystals have ordered but non-repeating atomic patterns, and their electron states can be critical: neither spread out nor sharply trapped. The property in question is superfluid weight, which measures how strongly the material expels magnetic fields. Part of it comes from ordinary band motion, and part from quantum geometry.

Using both real-space and momentum-space methods, the team separates the standard part from the quantum geometric one, which depends on the quantum metric, a measure of distance between quantum states. They find the superfluid weight is dominated by the geometric part in quasiperiodic systems with critical states. That dominance reveals a basic link between superconductivity and critical states in quasicrystals. The result suggests geometry, not just electron mass, controls superfluid response in these materials at zero temperature.
arxiv-2606-10089:
He and colleagues build theory for flow matching, a leading method for training generative models, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning theory. Flow matching learns a velocity field that carries noise into data, and neural networks parameterize that field in practice. The authors establish convergence guarantees for gradient descent when the velocity field is an over-parameterized two-layer ReLU network. They also derive generalization bounds for the conditional velocity-field matching objective, controlling how training error transfers to unseen data.

Building on those bounds, they provide Wasserstein-distance guarantees for the samples the learned flow generates, bounding how far the generated distribution sits from the target. Extensive experiments on synthetic data and real-world image benchmarks validate the theoretical results. The work gives flow matching, widely used in image generation, a firmer mathematical footing comparable to earlier theory for diffusion models.
arxiv-2606-10189:
Beloborodov proposes an origin for the fast radio bursts seen from a Galactic magnetar, in a 2026 arXiv paper on high-energy astrophysics. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, and kilohertz perturbations in an active magnetar grow into monster radiative shocks at about one hundred million centimeters from the star. The shock generates X-rays and a semi-coherent radio precursor that strongly interacts with the magnetospheric plasma ahead of it.

The precursor falls in the gigahertz band and peaks as the shock reaches about a billion centimeters. Escaping the magnetosphere is not guaranteed: the burst is absorbed unless the plasma density near the light cylinder is far below typical expectations, so observers need some luck. The shock's X-rays follow the radio by a millisecond, matching the paired radio and X-ray activity detected from SGR 1935+2154.
arxiv-2606-10289:
Taylor introduces a cleaner notation for the math behind modern estimation on rotating and moving bodies, in a 2026 arXiv paper on applied math. Matrix Lie groups, which describe rotations and rigid motions, appear more and more in estimation problems for robotics and navigation. Working with them requires many derivatives, and the usual matrix notation makes them clumsy and error-prone. His proposal uses tensors with Einstein summation notation, a compact shorthand from physics where repeated indices imply sums.

Applying tensors and Einstein notation to matrix Lie derivatives is novel, even though both tools are well known in other fields. Clearer notation reduces algebra mistakes when engineers build filters and tuners on rotation groups. The paper shows the notation on the standard tasks users need, aiming to lower the barrier to adopting Lie group methods in estimation tools.
arxiv-2606-10489:
Abdelkader, Fiorino, and Pellier re-examine PlanGPT in this 2026 arXiv paper, a study of whether large language models can do automated planning. Planning means producing a sequence of actions that carries a system from a starting state to a goal, and problems are usually written in the formal PDDL language. PlanGPT was presented as a leading language-model planner. The authors reran its experiments and added two measures the original work lacked, plan cost and generation time.

The verdict is deflating. On plan cost, PlanGPT performs slightly worse than a simple greedy search strategy, though it does better in certain domains. Its generation time also compares poorly once its resource demands are counted. The authors stop short of declaring language models hopeless for planning, noting room for improvement and newer reasoning models. Still, their central finding stands: the celebrated system is no better than greedy search overall.
arxiv-2606-10689:
Lublinsky and Tzarfati analyse a chiral plasma in strong magnetic fields through holography in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chiral plasmas, in the early universe, quark-gluon plasma, and Weyl semimetals, host anomaly-driven transport, where the axial current is not conserved. The authors put the plasma in an arbitrarily strong magnetic field plus an electric field, resum gradients to all orders, and express both currents through thirteen transport coefficient functions. The functions are computed in a holographic model, a Maxwell-Chern-Simons theory in a black hole spacetime, a laboratory for strongly coupled plasma.

For negative magnetoresistance, no phenomenological relaxation time is needed: the non-uniformity of the electric field plays that role instead. For chiral magnetic waves, earlier work suggested dissipationless modes above a threshold field. Including the electric field kills those modes; two remain, one overdamped, one propagating with dissipation. Both results sharpen comparisons with real data.
arxiv-2606-10789:
Ghosh tackles zero-shot activity recognition from wearable sensors in this 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. The goal is recognising activities never seen in training, by matching sensor embeddings against text descriptions of activities. The obstacle is a modality gap: sensor and text embeddings occupy separate regions of their shared space. Testing 7 configurations on PAMAP2, with 14 seen and 4 unseen activities, Ghosh shows the gap is created at training time by the encoder's objective, not by inference choices.

Training toward label-name text prototypes leaves sensor embeddings at mean cosine similarity 0.30 to their targets. Swapping in richer activity descriptions as targets raises that to 0.69, and the gain transfers across inference methods. The best configuration, contrastive training plus inverted softmax, reaches 73.2 percent accuracy and 0.583 macro F1 on unseen classes, against 58.3 percent and 0.34 for the baseline; running recall rises from zero to 74 percent. Richer descriptions blur prototype separability, a documented warning.
arxiv-2606-11089:
Yucheng Guo and the MEGAFLOW team measure the size of cool gas clouds around galaxies in a 2026 arXiv paper, their survey's fourteenth. The circumgalactic medium, a galaxy's gas halo, holds cool gas near ten thousand degrees in discrete clouds of unknown size. The team stacks magnesium absorption lines, dips carved into background light, against two kinds of background sources.

Background galaxies span a few kiloparsecs, while quasars are effectively points, under a hundredth of a parsec. When the source is smaller than a cloud's coherence scale, partial covering makes median and mean absorption part ways. Against galaxies the two agree; against quasars they differ significantly, especially beyond one hundred kiloparsecs from the foreground galaxy. Large background galaxies, near 6.6 kiloparsecs in radius, match the galaxy stacks, while small ones near 1.5 kiloparsecs diverge. Together the contrasts pin the clouds' coherence length at roughly two to seven kiloparsecs, confirmed by a toy model.
arxiv-2606-11189:
Tong Xie and five co-authors reinterpret supervised fine-tuning in a 2026 arXiv paper. Standard fine-tuning maximizes the likelihood of every demonstrated token, treating it as the one-hot target, the only correct continuation. Yet observed tokens can be non-unique, noisy, or at odds with the pretrained model's knowledge, so strict fitting can be suboptimal.

The authors recast the problem as target distribution design. Their Q-target framework splits supervision into two choices: how strongly to rely on the observed token, and how to spread the remaining probability over alternatives. Many known fine-tuning variants turn out to be implicit settings of those choices. Their Target-SFT method builds the training objective from the desired target distribution. It outperformed rivals across the ten reasoning dataset-model settings. Target design, the authors argue, is a more basic fine-tuning principle, opening a wider search space than loss tweaking.
arxiv-2606-11389:
Baxendale proves a 2004 assertion about a noisy oscillator in a 2026 arXiv paper. The system is a nonlinear oscillator with small friction and small additive noise, a cubic restoring force driven by white noise. Arnold, Imkeller, and Sri Namachchivaya stated without proof that the top Lyapunov exponent scales like a positive constant times epsilon to the two-thirds power as the small parameter vanishes.

Baxendale proves that scaling law for the exponent, which measures how fast nearby trajectories separate. Positivity means the linearized system is unstable despite damping: noise continually excites the oscillator and the cubic term stretches perturbations. The proof uses the Furstenberg-Khasminskii formula and the oscillator's Hamiltonian structure in the zero-noise limit. The result confirms the unusual two-thirds power, neither the naive friction scale nor the noise scale, as the correct balance. It closes a twenty-year gap in the stochastic stability literature.
arxiv-2606-12089:
Bo Li, Shen Zhang and Ren Zhang show that lawless quantum systems are in fact critical in this 2026 arXiv paper. Non-Hermitian systems, whose energy operator is not self-adjoint, can evade Anderson localisation, the disorder-driven trapping of electrons in ordinary one-dimensional materials. Their states spread through the whole system instead.

The authors prove these spread-out states are not blandly extended but critical, in the same universal class as one-dimensional random Dirac fermions. The bridge is spectral winding, a property of the complex energy spectrum, linked through a Hermitisation trick to topological Anderson transitions. The states show universal power-law correlations, the fingerprint of Dirac criticality. In Hermitian systems this criticality appears only at finely tuned transition points. Here it emerges on its own, as a direct result of spectral topology, with no tuning required. The result unifies this spreading under a single mechanism.
arxiv-2606-12289:
Pietro Barbiero and co-authors propose a standard theory for making AI models interpretable, modeled on physics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Interpretability, explaining how a model computes, lacks any general theory for designing methods from first principles. The literature is split, with inconsistent evaluation. Their Standard Interpretable Model, SIM, starts from premises: statements of what it means for a target user. From premises it derives symmetries, then constraints, shaping a Lagrangian, the energy-like function borrowed from mechanics.

Its minima are the optimal such models for the stated premises. Two routes reach them: adjust an opaque model's parameters toward interpretability, or build the constraints straight into the model. Tests show the framework identifies and fixes limits of existing methods, including concept-based approaches. It also exposes new directions and shapes core interfaces. The aim is a shared foundation for a scattered field.
arxiv-2606-12389:
L. Linke and co-authors squeeze extra cosmology from galaxy distortions by counting triplets as well as pairs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Weak lensing, the slight shearing of galaxy images by intervening mass, maps the dark universe. Standard two-point analyses mostly pin down one parameter combination, leaving matter density and clumpiness entangled. Third-order statistics capture non-Gaussian features that can break that degeneracy. The team jointly analyzes both orders in the Kilo-Degree Survey release, KiDS-Legacy.

Second-order signals come from COSEBIs statistics over wide scales; third-order from aperture mass moments on smaller scales. The joint fit gives matter density near 0.297 and a clumpiness measure of 0.806, with tightened errors. The figure of merit in the key parameter plane more than doubles versus the two-point analysis alone. The third-order results pass consistency tests and agree with the two-point constraints and with Planck measurements.
arxiv-2606-12589:
Melnik and Podzolkova ask whether the Milky Way's resonance rings pull hard enough to matter, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The galactic bar's gravity organizes stars into elliptical rings: outer rings near its outer Lindblad resonance, an inner ring near corotation. As stars pile into the rings, the rings' gravity should perturb the motions that created them. The authors add that feedback to a 2D Galaxy model with bar, bulge, disk, and halo.

They represent each ring's radial force with fitted polynomials, matching numerical differentiation of the potential within about six percent. Three model variants, no ring gravity, all rings, and outer rings only, let them isolate the effect. The verdict is modest: ring gravity has little effect on how epicyclic motions, stars' orbital wobbles, adjust near the outer resonance. The bar, not the rings it spawns, runs the kinematics. That simplifies interpreting the velocity data Gaia measures near the resonance.
arxiv-2606-12689:
Aswal and colleagues warn that patterns inside latent reasoning models do not explain how those models think, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Latent reasoning models replace written chain-of-thought with continuous hidden states, called latent thoughts, that carry intermediate computation. Earlier studies decoded search-like patterns from these states and treated them as evidence of reasoning. The authors test 2 such models, Coconut and CODI, against controls lacking the proposed mechanisms.

The patterns also appear in the controls, in untrained models with forced thought positions, and do not always affect behaviour. Causal interventions on the hidden states show latent-thought use is graded rather than all-or-nothing. The effect concentrates in low-rank directions, a small set of influential axes whose geometry grows more structured as their influence rises. The conclusion is blunt: latent thoughts are hidden computation, not hidden explanation, and mechanism claims need controls plus causal tests.
arxiv-2606-12789:
Fensore and colleagues ask how finely categories should be split when building benchmarks for retrieval-augmented generation systems, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, answers questions by retrieving texts and then writing a reply grounded in them. Benchmarks sort questions along axes, but builders lack evidence on how many categories a dimension needs.

Their HieraRAG framework defines granularity as the level with the most discriminative power, the widest spread of answer quality across categories. As a case study they generate 5,872 QA pairs from the FineWeb corpus across 3 dimensions, question complexity, answer type, and linguistic variation. Each sits at 3 levels of fineness with 2, 4, or 8 categories. Testing a BM25 plus Falcon-3-10B setup, they find complexity gains from the finest split, while answer type and linguistic variation peak at medium granularity. A Coherence Ratio metric shows fine splits divide categories unevenly, scoring 0.40 for complexity against 1.44 for answer type.
arxiv-2606-12889:
Chooi revisits the polling miss of the 2024 United States presidential election using the data defect correlation framework, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Polls predicted a Democratic lead, yet Trump won, echoing 2016. Chooi applies the framework to the 60,000-respondent Cooperative Election Study, matched to the United States adult population.

The analysis finds that non-response bias against Trump voters persists at the order of magnitude as in 2016, with a correlation of minus 0.0030 compared with minus 0.0045, even after sample matching. There is evidence of positive response bias for Harris voters once turnout is taken into account. As in 2016, polling errors scale with state population size, and sample sizes shrink by over 99 percent in the largest states. Chooi proposes a bias correction using defect correlations and turnout rates, cutting root-mean-square error from 0.13 to 0.05 using prior election data, comparable to post-election weighting at 0.09.
arxiv-2606-13389:
Micallef and Petrovska propose richer ways for students to declare AI use in this 2026 arXiv paper. Universities require declarations when students use tools, but yes-or-no statements capture little. Saying that a tool was used hides whether it planned an essay's structure or wrote the text itself. The authors argue transparency protects integrity, builds AI literacy, and shifts the conversation from policing toward workplace practice. They develop task-specific declaration frameworks built for a computer science department from a taxonomy of AI usage.

One framework covers writing-focused activities, the other coding assessments. Each separates usage by stage, telling apart planning an essay's structure from writing its text, or improving code from writing it. Students must reflect on their process rather than tick a box. Their position argues that such disclosure should replace binary statements across education. The authors present the frameworks as templates for other departments.
arxiv-2606-13489:
Andriulli proposes a filtering plan for the matrices of electromagnetics in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tracking how radio waves scatter needs solving integral equations, whose discretisation yields dense matrices that are costly to handle. A filter can regularise and compress them, speeding iterative and direct solvers. Earlier filters were built for 2D problems such as the electric field equation. This work extends the idea to 3D, the setting of real devices.

The filter cuts the spectrum of the integral operator's kernel, the Green's function. A form from the spherical Hankel transform gives the approach an analytical basis rather than a heuristic one. The author gives semi-analytic and numerical evidence of the filter's impact on solver response. This matters because 3D simulations of this kind are memory-hungry, and compressing the operator without losing detail widens the scope of such work.
arxiv-2606-13789:
Hotnisky and co-authors present COUNTESS, a search pipeline that hunts planets crossing in front of their stars in data from the TESS space telescope. Most of the sky gets short TESS visits, which limits sensitivity to planets with periods beyond about ten days. The northern continuous viewing zone is watched far longer, opening a window on slower orbits. Their 2026 arXiv paper applies the pipeline to that zone and releases a uniformly checked catalog of planet candidates.

The team built a uniform catalog of three hundred ninety-one thousand and fifty-nine stars using Gaia and 2MASS data. They then searched twenty-six thousand stars with TESS light curves. The pipeline recovered one hundred fifteen of one hundred fifty-nine known objects of interest. It also found ten new planet candidates that passed the vetting tests. Two are statistically validated sub-Neptunes, planets smaller than Neptune but larger than Earth.
arxiv-2606-13889:
Jørstad, Myers, and Pasterski explore entanglement inside a pocket of flat space built within holography. Holography relates a gravitational bulk to a quantum theory on its boundary, with entanglement entropy read from minimal surface areas. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses Coulomb-branch solutions describing shells of D-branes, whose depths contain a flat-space bubble, as a controlled setting.

The flat-space region carries less entanglement than the standard vacuum. It also holds fewer effective infrared degrees of freedom, meaning fewer active low-energy variables. Internal Ryu-Takayanagi surfaces, the bulk surfaces computing the entropy, show the same pattern. Holographic complexity, a measure of how hard the boundary state is to prepare, behaves similarly. The results give concrete evidence on how flat regions imprint on boundary entanglement, guiding the still-missing theory of flat space holography.
arxiv-2606-14089:
Zhu and colleagues field-test a two-armed robot picking apples from a tree's top and bottom at one stop. Labor shortages press growers, and fresh apples need individual handling to avoid bruising. Their 2026 arXiv paper stacks the arms vertically, replacing multi-tree repositioning with single-tree stops. Perception uses foundation models, Grounding-DINO with EfficientViT-SAM. A temporal-logic policy coordinates both arms around one vacuum source.

Field trials ran in two Washington orchards on Nicoter and Envy trees in the 2025 harvest. Across one thousand seven hundred thirty-eight arm cycles it succeeded on eighty percent of attempts, averaging seven point five three seconds per cycle. Indoor tests reached three point six five seconds per attempt, one point seven six times the serialized speed. Fruit quality held: ninety-one point two percent kept the top Extra Fancy grade, bruise rates two point four to four point nine percent.
arxiv-2606-14289:
Pekka Malo and co-authors build a 2026 arXiv scheme for studying population-based optimizers. These methods improve a whole set of candidate answers at once. They mix rules like mutation, selection, and recombination. When one rule changes, it is often unclear which promises still hold.

Their operator calculus treats each update rule as an operator. An operator is a math action on the group. The calculus says how separately checked effects combine. Under stated conditions, the leading changes simply add up. That gives reusable blocks for proofs about convergence. The scheme splits three goals apart. It separates finding a good answer, keeping it, and raising the group's mean score. Tests on nonconvex problems show a twist. A rule can worsen the mean score yet still yield better final answers.
arxiv-2606-14489:
Catalá, Valero, and Rodrigo build a quantum classifier in a 2026 arXiv paper. Its job is to detect phase changes in strongly correlated matter. The target is a shift between two states. One is a Fermi polaron, a particle dressed by its surroundings. The other is a molecular bound state. Their classifier is physics-informed and variational. Its circuit mimics time evolution of an effective Hamiltonian. So learned values keep a clear physical meaning.

The classifier finds the best measurement protocol on its own. It picks the evolution time and bath strength that sharpen Ramsey fringe contrast. It cleanly separates the condensate regime from the pairing regime. The team ran it on the QRed quantum processor in Barcelona. Despite hardware noise, the phase order stayed intact. Gate cost grows only linearly with system size. That scaling avoids the memory wall of classical simulation.
arxiv-2606-14589:
Wu documents silent failures in a production AI agent system in a 2026 arXiv longitudinal study. The system is a personal-assistant runtime running since March twenty twenty-six, with about forty scheduled jobs, eight model providers, and thousands of tests and governance checks. Over eight weeks, Wu recorded twenty-two incidents with full postmortems, where one pattern, an error signal never reaching a human in usable form, appeared at least twenty-eight times.

The resulting taxonomy has five classes, from platform quirks to operational blind spots. One class is unique to language-model systems: the model rewrites a failure into fluent, plausible narrative delivered as if true, which Wu calls fail-plausible. About seventy percent of silent failures were caught by humans watching outputs, not by tests, and audits blocked regressions but prevented nothing in advance. The paper closes with a defense framework and design principles.
arxiv-2606-15289:
Mu models helical carbon coil arrays as tunable microwave absorbers in a 2026 materials paper. The coils are tiny carbon springs with a three-dimensional chiral shape. Their geometry lets them interact strongly with microwaves across the gigahertz range. Working on quartz substrates, Mu builds a coarse-grained electrodynamic model of the arrays. A simple resonance rule links the absorbing frequency to the coil pitch. The study compares bare coils against coils with a carbon anchoring layer beneath.

Without the layer, strong absorption occurs only at one special coil thickness. Reflection at the air interface caps performance away from that thickness. Adding an anchoring layer of tuned thickness changes the input impedance the wave sees. That restores impedance matching and boosts absorption at the chosen frequency. The layer thus acts as an active design knob for the device. The paper offers fabrication guidance for lightweight, high-performance microwave absorbers.
arxiv-2606-15389:
Sun and coauthors improve diffusion inversion by rescheduling its timesteps in a 2026 machine learning paper. Diffusion models generate images by removing noise step by step. Inversion runs that process backward, mapping a real photo to the noise it would have come from, which enables editing with the model. The standard fast inverter introduces errors, and the authors show the error size follows a curved pattern across the schedule, worst at the earliest and latest steps.

Their scheduler answers with nonuniform spacing: wide steps where errors are small, fine steps where they grow, arranged by a global rescaling plus a local dynamic programming search. It bolts onto existing inversion methods with no extra parameters and no added compute. Experiments on reconstruction and editing show consistent gains in fidelity. The work is a reminder that in iterative algorithms, where the steps fall can matter as much as how each step is computed.
arxiv-2606-15489:
Kjellgren and colleagues present a quantum computing method in 2026 for calculating the ground and excited states of molecules. Their approach, called orbital-optimized multistate contracted VQE, uses spin-adapted operators, meaning operators built to respect the spin symmetry of the starting states. Excited states govern how molecules absorb light, so getting them right matters for spectroscopy and for designing photoactive materials.

In simulation, the team finds that the circuit parameters needed for accurate results grow about linearly with the number of states included. Doubling the states doubles the required circuit length, while adding orbital optimization barely changes the parameter count. They also give a circuit implementation, pair it with error mitigation, and run it on real quantum hardware. There, absorption spectra for two benchmark molecular systems come out correctly only when error mitigation is applied, showing the method works but stays noise-limited.
arxiv-2606-15589:
Tong and colleagues ask in 2026 whether code helps algorithmic reasoning because of its structure or because a machine runs it. Tool-augmented models beat plain language reasoning, but the comparison confounds two changes: the representation and the executor. The team separates them with a middle route: the model writes executable code, then simulates it in context to answer.

On a forty-task verifiable benchmark, real code execution beats natural-language reasoning by about thirty-two points. The middle route, by contrast, lands within a fraction of a point of plain language reasoning, so the code representation alone explains almost nothing. A reconstruction test, translating code back into language traces, confirms the two representations carry similar value. A simple decision-theoretic model pins down when execution dominates overall risk. For tool design, the win comes from handing the trace to a reliable external executor, not from thinking in code.
arxiv-2606-15689:
Kumar and colleagues compare five large language models as automated code reviewers in 2026, testing whether bigger models review better. The benchmark covers 150 code reviews: one hundred synthetic bugs injected by mutation, and fifty real bug-fix pull requests mined from eight major open-source repositories. Models range from Claude Sonnet and Haiku to GPT and open alternatives.

The smaller, cheaper Haiku beats the larger Sonnet on F1 score, 0.365 against 0.343, with eighteen percent higher recall and better qualitative marks on every dimension, at roughly a third of the cost per review. Synthetic tests flatter everyone: on real pull requests the best model's F1 collapses to 0.066, against 0.847 on synthetic cases. Diff size dominates outcomes, with scores falling steeply once changes exceed about one hundred fifty lines. All models show near-zero recall on performance bugs. For production reviewing, the authors recommend the small model plus deterministic rules where models fail.
arxiv-2606-15889:
Rosenthal and colleagues present SiGnature in 2026, a gesture-generation framework aiming at gestures both meaningful and true to a speaker's personal style. Co-speech systems have mastered rhythm, but meaningful gestures, like iconic shapes or pointing, are rare and hard to learn. Unlike latent-space methods, SiGnature diffuses motion in explicit joint-rotation space, keeping every joint directly editable.

Its core, Joint Motion Integration, is training-free: at inference it injects any external motion sequence into the diffusion process, finding the active joints that carry the meaning. The backbone then fills in the remaining body motion, posture and flow, in the target speaker's learned style. Experiments and user studies report state-of-the-art smoothness and more natural motion than latent baselines, without the stitched look of cut-and-paste methods. The authors note limits: no facial expressions yet, and windowed processing is not real-time.
arxiv-2606-15989:
Papathanasiou and colleagues introduce MED-VAE in 2026, a multi-encoder-decoder variational autoencoder that aligns neural activity across subjects without requiring shared stimuli. Standard alignment needs every subject to see the same stimuli, excluding naturalistic experiments with little overlap. MED-VAE instead anchors each subject's encoder to a common scaffold from a pretrained network, so encodings meet in a shared latent space by construction.

On the Natural Scenes Dataset, the common spaces show better semantic organisation and higher cross-subject alignment than standard methods, and generalise well to held-out stimuli where standard methods degrade. Decoding back into each subject's own neural space preserves the stimulus-driven signal, so the shared space is not bought with information loss. The alignment enables cross-subject prediction, shown by decoding images from a new subject's brain activity. For neuroscience, such shared manifolds are candidate evidence for principles different brains hold in common.
arxiv-2606-16189:
Bakkaoui studies a structured family of prime numbers in a 2026 paper, labeling every claim by its proof status. Every prime above three is plus or minus one modulo six. The family generalizes that fact: primes are written using parameters k, m, a sign, and an offset q, around a hexagonal base value. Each prime above k plus one gets a canonical triple with the smallest offset.

Two unconditional pillars anchor the work. Structurally, for every prime divisor of twice k, the family satisfies a fixed congruence that ignores the offset entirely. Constructively, Pocklington-Lehmer certificates prove primality unconditionally for a smooth subfamily, backed by filters removing about 87 percent of candidates early. A certified prime with 29,998 digits demonstrates the machinery at record scale. Other laws, on sizes and modular distribution, are tagged conditional on standard hypotheses such as the Riemann hypothesis, or marked heuristic.
arxiv-2606-16789:
Yan and colleagues analyze soliton solutions of the Satsuma-Mimura equation in a 2026 paper on integrable systems. The equation belongs to a family built around the Hilbert transform, and its algebraic solitons can be tracked by following their poles in the complex plane. A qualitative picture of that pole system was left open in earlier work.

The authors first complete the pole dynamics analysis, describing how the poles move and interact. They then test three ways of perturbing the equation. A first-derivative perturbation keeps the system exactly linearizable and yields an explicit shifted soliton. A second-derivative perturbation reduces to the original equation under a scaling change, giving pole asymptotics and the soliton profile. The third perturbation, involving the Hilbert transform itself, is genuinely harder. For it they derive first-order perturbation equations and run a short-time numerical simulation with an explicit Euler scheme.
arxiv-2606-17189:
Wise and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on stellar bars in galaxies. Bars are long star structures that torque gas toward a galaxy's centre. Their role in shutting down star formation has long been debated. The study uses the JWST CEERS survey and spans from the nearby universe to redshift two.

The sample holds well over a thousand galaxies and is complete above a set mass. The team repeats the analysis with COSMOS-Web data as a check. Early barred galaxies tend to form stars actively, with low central concentration. The barred but quiet share rises steeply over the last ten billion years. Results match the TNG50-1 simulations for longer bars, suggesting bar-driven inflows may help galaxies grow quiet.
arxiv-2606-17289:
Zeng, Griffiths, and Lake, of Princeton University, present a 2026 arXiv paper asking whether a language model can discover the concept of zero on its own. Real mathematical discovery needs a strong kind of generalisation, forming structures never seen in training. Arithmetic with zero is their test case, since models trained without zero examples must invent a genuinely new and powerful idea rather than copy a pattern from data.

Models of GPT-2 size failed to generalise to zero at test time, no matter how much language pretraining they had received first. After training on tens or hundreds of examples involving zero, the same models improved substantially on the held-out task. Language pretraining still helped, cutting the number of zero examples needed by roughly half in their runs. The result frames language as a scaffold that eases, but does not replace, direct evidence for new concepts.
arxiv-2606-17889:
Korte and colleagues ask when splitting a learning system into modules actually helps it learn task after task, in a 2026 paper. Continual learning must stay plastic enough to absorb new tasks while stable enough to keep old skills, and modular designs promise both. The team compared a task-partitioned recurrent network with a single network on a sequence that revisits an earlier task.

The answer depended on the shape of the learned representations. When representations were high-dimensional and weakly constrained, both designs performed alike and modularity added little. In a lower-dimensional regime, the modular network pulled clearly ahead. It formed task-specific subspaces that overlapped for similar tasks and separated for unlike ones, cutting interference. Extra tests with deeper networks left the pattern intact, tying the benefit to dimensionality rather than depth.
arxiv-2606-18089:
Kong and colleagues argue that teaching language models to reason works because training splits reasoning into reusable parts, in a 2026 paper. The standard recipe pairs supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, and the pair plainly works, but why the combination beats either stage alone was unclear. The authors model a reasoning trace as a cascade of hidden choices that pick atomic modules, both skills and routing steps that reuse earlier results.

Within that model, the two stages play asymmetric roles. Fine-tuning supplies the raw module material inside its example traces, while reinforcement learning pulls those traces apart, identifies the atomic modules, and learns to recombine them for new problem shapes. Controlled experiments back the theory: models recombined extracted modules to solve configurations never shown whole. The frame gives post-training research a concrete target, the compositional structure itself.
arxiv-2606-18489:
Ferdian and colleagues present GHOST-CAT, a neural network that turns echocardiograms into moving three-dimensional meshes of the heart's left ventricle, in a 2026 medical imaging paper. Ultrasound is the workhorse of cardiac imaging, but its volumetric form suffers low contrast, a conical viewing window, and acoustic shadowing, making manual analysis variable between readers.

Their two-stage network combines convolutional networks, graph convolutional networks, and transformers to produce meshes that stay topologically consistent and temporally coherent across the heartbeat. Tested on one hundred held-out three-dimensional echo studies against reference segmentations from magnetic resonance imaging, it beat leading methods. Overlap scores were strong for the chamber cavity and the heart muscle, and surface errors were a few millimeters. The meshes support automatic calculation of clinical measures such as volume, mass, and strain, and can feed biophysical digital twin models. The code is shared.
arxiv-2606-18589:
Chen and colleagues present DREAM-Chunk, a test-time method that makes robot action-chunking policies react better when the world does not follow the plan, in a 2026 robotics paper. Vision-language-action models often commit to a short sequence of actions at once, but executing that chunk open-loop is brittle under stochastic dynamics and hardware errors.

DREAM-Chunk samples several candidate chunks from the existing policy, rolls each one forward inside a lightweight learned world model that works in latent space. It executes actions from the chunk whose dreamed future best matches what is actually observed. No extra policy fine-tuning is needed. On a simulation benchmark its gains grew with action noise and with the number of candidates. Across four manipulation tasks on two real robot platforms it improved performance under execution noise, partial observability, and external pushes.
arxiv-2606-18989:
Ye and colleagues build G-IdiomAlign in 2026, a test of how well language models match idioms across tongues. Idioms are hard because their sense is figurative, not the sum of their words. Word-for-word swaps thus fail often. Each idiom in the test is tied to an English gloss from Wiktionary. That gloss gives a clear sense to aim for, and a vetted reference set backs fair scoring.

Two test modes are given. One is multiple choice with typed wrong options to sort error types. The other asks for free generation, with and without the gloss, to isolate its effect. Across many models, a pull toward literal translation is the top failure mode. It is worst for low-resource target tongues. Glosses help generation in a steady way, yet scores stay modest overall. Work on one model hints gains sit in a few attention heads.
arxiv-2606-19089:
Scherl and colleagues present ART-VS in 2026, an adaptive tiling method for visual servoing with vision transformer features. Visual servoing steers a robot by matching live images to a target view. Self-supervised transformer features give training-free positioning with strong generalization. Coarse patch features are stable but imprecise, while high resolution adds many patches for only small robustness gains under disturbance, a poor trade.

ART-VS adapts feature granularity to servoing progress in two phases. A coarse phase at native resolution aligns the view stably. A tiled high-resolution phase then matches only local neighborhoods to sharpen accuracy. With no task-specific training, the method reaches high convergence under perturbation, beating standard and full-resolution servoing by wide margins. It also cuts positioning error sharply versus the standard approach, runs far faster, and uses less memory than full resolution. Real grasping tests confirm the gain.
arxiv-2606-19489:
Ya Wang and Adrian Paschke propose Concept Flow Models in 2026, a design for image classifiers that must explain themselves. Concept Bottleneck Models force a network to decide through human-readable concepts, such as shapes or parts. When the concept count nears the embedding size, spare detail leaks through and the stated reasons stop being honest.

Wang and Paschke swap the flat bottleneck for a decision tree built from concepts. Each inner node weighs a small local set of concepts and narrows the class step by step. Hierarchies grow from visual embeddings, and soft weights train through probabilistic walks down the tree. On standard benchmarks the models match flat bottleneck accuracy while using far fewer concepts per decision. Each prediction leaves a stepwise trail that auditors can follow and check.
arxiv-2606-19689:
Matt Oddo, Indira Sowy, Stephen Kobourov, and Tamara Munzner present Syndesmoscope in 2026, a network exploration system built on invariant plots. Node-link diagrams and matrices can show wildly unlike patterns for one network under different layouts. Invariant plots instead surface the same pattern for the same topology every time.

Syndesmoscope places a force-directed view beside three geometry-based panes. Those panes encode dense-sparse gradient, geodesic eccentricity, and spectral bisection. A new invariant plot, kSnakes, rests on density decomposition. Two interactions link the panes: leapfrogging highlights one selection across views. Hopscotching extends selections hop by hop through the topology. Usage scenarios span 72 diverse networks. Paired views reveal patterns no single view exposes, the authors show. A live demo invites readers to test the linked exploration themselves.
arxiv-2606-19789:
Bodas, Dorsman, Mandjes, and Ravner allocate processor cores to flexible jobs whose speed-ups stay unknown, in a 2026 study. Malleable jobs can change their core count mid-run, letting a scheduler rebalance a busy machine. Jobs fall into two classes, each with its own speed-up curve and hidden parameters.

The goal is a policy minimising the long-run mean number of jobs in the system. Within each class, active jobs share cores equally. An alternating scheme estimates the hidden parameters, then re-solves a Markov decision process for the class split. The estimator rests on state-dependent gaps between job departures. It is proven strongly consistent under any fixed allocation policy. Two learning algorithms pair that estimator with dynamic programming policy updates. Numerical experiments show the learners tracking good allocations as evidence accrues.
arxiv-2606-19889:
Wentao Pan and five colleagues build SurgVista in 2026, a world model that imagines surgical video far ahead. Robot surgery policies need training data, yet expert demonstrations cost dear and live trials risk patients. World models generate future frames from actions, but surgical ones fail in two stubborn ways.

Visible tool contact often fails to deform tissue in a spatially consistent way. Prediction errors also compound over long rollouts, rotting image quality step by step. Deformation Consistency Regularization extracts scene-point paths from training videos. Contrastive learning then enforces cross-frame coherence on those paths. Drift Adaptation Training perturbs conditioning frames with realistic drift, hardening long rollouts. A new benchmark, SurgWorld-Bench, scores tool-motion accuracy and tissue-response fidelity separately. Gains over leading methods widen as the prediction horizon grows.
arxiv-2606-19989:
Dian Li, Zekun Wang, Yaoru Wang, and Jiahong Yan present Online Dynamic Batching for language model training in 2026. A training sample's true cost appears only after preprocessing, tokenization, and visual-token expansion, so offline batch builders work blind and waste capacity on padding. Their system moves batch formation to the data loader, the point where real lengths are known, while keeping distributed training steps aligned across machines.

The alignment requirement is formalized as a distributed group alignment problem, with proofs of deadlock-free, bounded completion. No model, optimizer, or kernel changes are needed. On public Qwen3-VL fine-tuning runs, throughput rises roughly two- to four-fold over fixed batching at comparable quality, approaching offline oracle methods. Heterogeneous multimodal training, where lengths vary wildly, benefits most.
arxiv-2606-20189:
Maciej Wozniak and six colleagues pretrain LiDAR perception for self-driving cars by distilling knowledge from camera-based vision foundation models, but with the teacher's internal structure left in. Their 2026 paper, HilDA, notes that current distillation treats the teacher as a black box and matches only frame-wise features. That wastes the teacher's layer-by-layer semantics and the motion information inside LiDAR sequences. HilDA distills hierarchically instead, aligning features across several teacher layers for progressive semantic learning, plus global context distillation for scene-level meaning.

A second ingredient, a temporal occupancy diffusion objective, pushes the LiDAR backbone toward spatiotemporal consistency, so it captures both the semantic what and the geometric where of a scene. Pre-trained this way, models reached state-of-the-art results on cross-modal distillation benchmarks. They also beat earlier distillation approaches on 3D object detection, scene flow, and semantic occupancy prediction.
arxiv-2606-20389:
Ziyuan Tang and Chenxi Xiao present CoLI, an open-source continuum robot platform designed so other labs can actually reproduce it. Their 2026 paper tackles the field's reproducibility problem. Soft, bendable continuum robots promise safe, compliant manipulation, but complex fabrication, tricky kinematic modeling, and awkward control interfaces keep designs locked in their home labs. CoLI's arm is printed as a single compliant structure by multi-material 3D printing.

Control comes through an isomorphic teleoperation interface that maps directly at the actuator level, removing the need for explicit kinematic modeling and giving a singularity-free mapping. The platform also supports imitation-learning-based autonomous control, so demonstrations gathered through the interface can train policies. For a field where every group's robot is a one-off, a printable standard platform could do for continuum robotics what reference designs did for drones.
arxiv-2606-20689:
Rahul Patel and Nirjala Jarpula present NeoJaundice-AI in 2026, a phone-based tool to screen newborns for jaundice without a blood test. Jaundice, caused by excess bilirubin, affects many newborns. India alone records about 15 million cases a year. Early detection can save lives. Yet rural clinics often lack labs and equipment. Their system uses photos of skin and eye whites to estimate severity in under three seconds, with no internet needed.

A dual-branch EfficientNet model analyzes the skin image and the eye-white image apart. It then fuses deep features with handcrafted color statistics. The output gives both a four-class severity label and a bilirubin level. A synthetic generator also creates training examples. It shifts color channels to mimic bilirubin yellowing on normal skin. Phone screening could help front-line workers triage babies fast, while keeping blood tests for cases that need confirmation.
arxiv-2606-20789:
J Zanazzi and three colleagues study dynamical tides in 2026 as a cause of patterns in hot gas planet periods. Sub-Saturn planets cluster at three to six day periods, forming a Neptune ridge. Jovian planets pile up at similar periods. Sub-Saturns are scarce inside three days, a Neptune desert, while Jovians are not. During high-eccentricity migration, tides excite fundamental modes inside a planet. Those modes store orbital energy.

The open question is how mode energy returns to the planet interior. Simulations show close passes excite modes at supersonic speeds, shocking gas envelopes. Shocks can circularize orbits, creating clusters near the ridge and pile-up. They can also unbind mass. Sub-Saturn cores can be left in the desert after losing envelopes. One tidal process thus links three observed patterns, giving observers a physical story for why planet mass and period cluster as they do.
arxiv-2606-20989:
Emmanuel Sérié presents OxyMake in a solo 2026 paper, a workflow engine that decides reruns by content rather than file timestamps. Make-like tools ask whether a job must rerun by comparing modification times. That proxy is broken. A checkout or backup restore rewrites times without changing content, causing wasteful reruns. Worse, a stale output can look newer than its inputs and be reused silently.

OxyMake replaces the proxy with a content-addressed cache key. A BLAKE3 hash covers rule source, input content, parameters, environment, and platform. The decision survives timestamp churn. It can also travel across machines and shared caches on the same platform. Undeclared inputs stay invisible to the key, a limit stated plainly. Correct caching matters for science and software builds, where a phantom rerun wastes hours and a stale reuse can quietly corrupt every result downstream.
arxiv-2606-21189:
Yitian Zhou and ten colleagues propose TF-SNO in 2026, a spectral neural operator that adapts its frequency response as a partial differential equation evolves. Non-stationary equations appear across science. Their dominant frequencies and energy distribution drift over time. Many spectral operators apply one shared response at every rollout stage. That mismatches time-varying spectra and hurts long runs.

Learnable time-frequency gating sits inside the spectral blocks. Compact statistics from the current state, in both frequency and physical space, generate modulation coefficients. The spectral response then evolves with the dynamics. No explicit time input is added, keeping model complexity low. Adaptive blocks are embedded to capture multi-scale features and improve long-horizon stability. Tests cover six non-stationary benchmarks in one and two dimensions. Adaptive spectra could extend neural solvers to systems whose character changes as they run.
arxiv-2606-21889:
Wang and You study ranking-and-selection problems in 2026, where a decision maker must pick the best options from noisy, costly measurements. Two complications break the usual single-winner template. Sometimes several answers are simultaneously correct, and sometimes a noisy estimate temporarily admits no valid answer at all, as when estimated preferences form a cycle with no overall winner.

Their unified framework rests on answer-wise acceptance sets, a restricted likelihood-ratio stopping rule, and a decomposition that separates candidate answers from pitfalls. From these parts they build ENDS, a general procedure combining estimation, nomination of candidates, pitfall detection, and cost-aware sampling. The authors derive explicit formulas that instantiate ENDS for several concrete problems, including multi-fidelity selection and finding a Condorcet winner from pairwise comparisons. Extensive numerical experiments show the recipe does well on a broad range of pure-exploration problems.
arxiv-2606-22089:
Waggener and Tamil present BAC-JEPA in 2026, a label-efficient framework for tracing breast arterial calcification on screening mammograms. Those calcium deposits are an emerging imaging marker of cardiovascular risk, but quantifying them needs pixel-level outlines that experts are expensive to produce. BAC-JEPA sidesteps human training masks by manufacturing its own: synthetic deposits are inserted into real mammogram backgrounds with exact masks.

The generator samples arterial graphs, disease burden, appearance, and hard negatives such as non-arterial deposits and metal objects. Synthetic images train self-supervised vision transformer models with a high-resolution decoder. Drawing on over seventy-five thousand studies for background selection, the larger backbone reached an intersection-over-union of 0.5325 on held-out synthetic data. On a human-labelled benchmark, image-level scoring from its maps reached an area under the curve of 0.8719, showing useful transfer without any human pixel-level training masks.
arxiv-2606-22189:
Li documents, in 2026, a complete small language model pipeline run on a single NVIDIA L20 graphics card, and releases the resulting model as L20-Edu-135M. Strong public models of this size are usually trained on hundreds of billions of tokens on large clusters. Li's 134.5 million parameter model instead received about thirteen billion pretraining tokens, mostly educational web text plus a smaller mixture for mathematics, code, and reasoning.

The study details the architecture, data quality gates, near-deduplication, benchmark-overlap removal, fine-tuning with weight interpolation, and reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards. On a six-task harness the model scores a mean of 0.415, reaching eighty-seven percent of SmolLM-135M's score with about two percent of its token count. One negative result stands out: direct reward-based training lowered grade-school mathematics accuracy instead of raising it.
arxiv-2606-23189:
Anmol Goel and Iryna Gurevych test whether computer-use agents respect contextual privacy in a 2026 paper. These agents act for a user across email, calendars, and task lists. Working across apps is useful, but it invites a subtle leak. Information gathered in one context can surface in another where it does not belong. The authors call the standard contextual integrity, and they build a benchmark that turns it into scored scenarios. Three failure modes are targeted: pulling in forbidden items sitting next to the target, oversharing personal state on vague prompts, and sending content to the wrong recipient.

Goel and Gurevych evaluate fifteen frontier agents. Twelve of the fifteen leaked in over half of their scenarios. Average leakage ran near sixty-eight percent. The same failures persisted when agents acted end to end in the environment.
arxiv-2606-23489:
Qi Sun and colleagues generate three-dimensional meshes with an equivariant flow matching model in a 2026 graphics paper. Meshes are a standard representation of 3D shapes, built from vertices and triangular faces. Generating them directly is hard because the representation has built-in symmetries: reordering vertices or faces changes nothing about the shape. A generator that ignores those symmetries wastes capacity relearning them. The team's MeshFlow treats the mesh as a triangle soup, a loose collection of triangles. It learns to generate that soup with a flow matching model built on equivariant optimal transport, so the symmetries are respected by design.

Sun and colleagues present MeshFlow as a way to get clean, usable triangle meshes straight from a generative model. The equivariant design addresses the permutation invariance of vertices and faces head on. The work appears in the SIGGRAPH 2026 conference papers.
arxiv-2606-23789:
Gibbs and colleagues report a third giant planet discovered in the Beta Pictoris system, in a 2026 paper on exoplanet astronomy. Beta Pictoris is a young nearby star famous for its debris disk and two previously imaged planets. Imaged systems with more than two planets are exceptionally rare. Such systems are prized because sibling planets share one birth disk.

The new planet, Beta Pictoris d, turned up unexpectedly in Webb telescope spectroscopy and was confirmed by a second round of observations. Its spectrum shows clear methane, carbon monoxide, and water absorption, and its measured radial velocity matches its orbital position. Orbit fitting places it beyond thirty astronomical units, wide enough to carve the disk's inner edge. Models put its mass at roughly two to four times Jupiter's. It is the first planet found by spectral template matching.
arxiv-2606-23889:
Desai, Yao, Porwal, and Lee teach Walmart's sponsored search to read the hidden intent inside short grocery queries, in a 2026 paper on information retrieval. A query like a bread brand name may silently encode a gluten free need, and a snack brand may want its protein bars shown for keto searches that never mention it. Missing such signals wastes the few ad slots available. INSPIRE represents intent as structured attributes: brand, flavor, dietary needs, ingredients, subtype, and cuisine.

A large language model annotates products with these attributes, acting as teacher. A lightweight student model is fine tuned to predict them at catalog scale. Predicted intents are then folded into the query and product embeddings of a dense retrieval system, so matching respects intent as well as wording.
arxiv-2606-24089:
Hou and colleagues teach a bipedal-wheeled robot to climb long staircases smoothly. It is a machine that walks on two legs ending in wheels. Earlier teacher-student training setups lose touch with the robot's dynamics. They also encode terrain shape incompletely. So performance on continuous stairs lags behind slopes and single steps. Their 2026 framework, DynaWM, adds two stabilising ingredients to the representation the student controller learns.

A learned world model acts as a regulariser. It forces the internal representation to predict forward dynamics, and so retain full terrain geometry. A momentum target encoder supplies steady distillation targets. That prevents the representation from collapsing when the teacher keeps changing. Visual checks show the encoder organising terrain features in a clear hierarchy. In simulation and on real hardware, Hou's method delivers better terrain adaptability and smoother motion. The robot handles varied continuous staircases that defeated earlier controllers.
arxiv-2606-24289:
Igra, Sopin, and Yu build a flow that pushes dynamical systems downhill from order into chaos, in homage to the second law of thermodynamics. Given any smooth one parameter family of vector fields transitioning from order to chaos, can a single flow realise that transition on its own trajectories? Their 2026 construction, the Entropy flow, answers by coupling the original dynamics to a drift through parameter space.

Defined on the product of phase space and parameter space, the Entropy flow carries each initial condition toward more disordered, complex states. Tested against the three classical routes to chaos, period doubling, the Ruelle-Takens-Newhouse route, and intermittency, the construction behaves exactly as hoped. Using the Conley index from forcing theory, the authors also connect the Entropy flow to bifurcations topologically. Igra's team gives the vague idea of a route to chaos a concrete dynamical vehicle that travels it.
arxiv-2606-24589:
Khandelwal builds a red-teaming pipeline that does not trust its own judge. Scaling adversarial evaluation needs hard inputs, and confirmation that the failures found are real. A single judge is fast, but cannot flag its own leniency or settle close calls. AdversaBench mutates seed prompts with five operators, attacks a target model, then confirms each failure through a three-judge panel with a meta-judge breaking ties.

Dozens of seeds run across reasoning, instruction-following, and tool-use categories, expanded from a pilot to cover temporal reasoning, strict formatting, and tool edge cases. Every seed produces a confirmed failure. Operator effectiveness varies sharply by category, a pattern invisible in totals. Binary failure rates also hide difficulty: instruction-following seeds need more than twice the attacker iterations of the other categories. Writing alone in 2026, Khandelwal argues red-teaming should report effort and category structure, not just whether a model broke.
arxiv-2606-24789:
Juul Sanders, Sebastiaan Brand, Arend-Jan Quist, and Tim Coopmans speed up the normal form algorithm behind a quantum decision diagram. Decision diagrams store vectors compactly by merging equivalent pieces, which speeds linear algebra. In quantum circuit simulation the vectors are quantum states. One variant, the LIMDD, merges vectors up to local invertible maps such as Pauli gates. Theory promises exponential advantages for such diagrams, but the complex normal form procedure is only partly implemented in existing tools.

The new algorithm targets Pauli LIMDDs. For a diagram node with a single child, worst case cost drops from cubic to quadratic in the qubit count. Nodes with two distinct children keep the cubic bound. The authors implement the method inside QolDDer, a simulator written from scratch in C and C plus plus. On Clifford circuits it realises the proven advantages and runs far faster than existing LIMDD simulators.
arxiv-2606-25189:
AI agents in production run inside harnesses, software that is meant to enforce policies like running tests before a commit. Yusheng Zheng and eight colleagues identify the gap. Policy intent is stated in loose natural language. Enforcement, though, must act on concrete system actions. Tool level guardrails miss actions that bypass the tool layer entirely.

Their system, ActPlane, lets the agent declare policies close to the task, then enforces them inside the operating system kernel, covering every execution path. A small information flow control language expresses policies about event ordering and data flow across events. Built with eBPF, ActPlane returns semantic feedback instead of opaque sandbox errors. Across policies from an empirical study, coding benchmarks, and safety benchmarks, compliance improves, including on indirect paths that tool interception cannot see. The overhead runs roughly two to eight percent.
arxiv-2606-25389:
Teams of agents that learn task after task tend to forget old coordination skills or lose the flexibility to gain new ones. Yuchen Xiao and colleagues propose COMAD in 2026, a framework for continual cooperation learned entirely from stored multi agent data. An autoencoder first mines reusable coordination skills from mixed behaviour logs. A density based estimator then judges which skills are worth reusing, and a multi head policy is steered by the skills it selects.

Because the skill library keeps growing instead of staying fixed, new tasks add skills without overwriting old ones as badly. Theory shows the method approximates the optimum of the continual skill discovery problem it defines. Across several multi agent benchmarks, COMAD transferred skills both forward to new tasks and backward to old ones better than the baselines tested.
arxiv-2606-25889:
Gregor Humar and colleagues report an experiment on false vacuum decay, the process where a metastable state collapses into a lower-energy one through growing bubbles of the new phase. Cosmologists use the same picture for the early universe. Instead of a cosmic setting, the team stages the process inside a programmable quantum annealer holding more than four thousand qubits.

A two-dimensional quantum Ising model on the annealer encodes the false vacuum as an aligned spin state. At one chosen field strength, single spin flips along a seeded bubble's edge become resonant, so the bubble expands in a constrained but rapid way. Domain growth turns out nearly ballistic, far outpacing new bubble formation, while the boundary widens more slowly in a pattern matching Kardar-Parisi-Zhang universality, a known class of roughening behaviour.
arxiv-2606-26089:
Abdelrahman Elabd, Eilam Gross, Dmitrii Kobylianskii, and Benjamin Nachman release Parnassus, a fast particle detector simulator written in Python. Simulating detectors with Geant4 is accurate but slow. Reconstruction chains add more cost. Parnassus swaps in interchangeable detector models that run on graphics processors. Neural models imitate the expensive simulation chains. Simpler parametric models follow the Delphes recipe of bias and smearing.

Two CMS detector models headline the release. One uses a flow-matching neural network. The other reimplements the Delphes CMS card in PyTorch. ATLAS and ALEPH parametric cards join them, plus a neural ALEPH model for the older LEP setting. Every backend shares one process-agnostic interface. Nex C. X. Stuhlmüller and Marjolein Dijkstra determine what physical neural networks need in order to learn. Physical computing lets matter itself do the calculating as it relaxes to a steady state, promising huge energy savings. Many proposed physical networks are linear, though. Linear systems cannot perform the nonlinear operations real learning demands. The authors show nonlinearity alone is still not enough.

Without them, the network cannot emphasise useful paths or quieten useless ones, and nontrivial computation fails. Tianlong Wang, Yuhang Wang, Weibin Liao, Xin Gao, Xinyu Ma, Yang Lin, Yasha Wang, and Liantao Ma steer a reasoning model toward truth while it is still thinking. Volume 1 of the Proceedings of the American Society for Psychical Research appeared in 1889, covering 1885 to 1889. The American society followed the London model, gathering reports of ghosts, trances, and thought transfer. Figures such as Richard Hodgson and William James shaped its early work.

Reports describe sittings with mediums, tests of claimed powers, and cases sent in by the public. The writers weighed fraud, faulty memory, and chance before accepting any claim as real. The volume shows American psychical research at its start, when trained scholars tried to bring strict method to claims that most scientists of the day dismissed.
attar-bird-parliament-fitzgerald-1889:
Farid ud-Din Attar, a Persian Sufi poet of the twelfth century, wrote the Conference of the Birds as a long allegory in verse. Edward FitzGerald, known for the Rubaiyat, rendered it in 1889 as Bird Parliament. His version was the first English translation of the work.

The birds of the world gather and set out under the hoopoe to find their king, the Simorgh, beyond distant mountains. Most fall away on the road, and the thirty who arrive find the king in a mirror of themselves. The poem maps the soul's journey toward God with wit, story, and sorrow.
baco-verulamius-alchemicis-philosophis-q: Baco Verulamius alchemicis philosophis quid debuerit, 1889. Bacon's debt. This book preserves that study. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
bentham-principles-morals-1789:
Jeremy Bentham published An Introduction to the Principles of Morals and Legislation in 1789. Bentham founds utilitarianism, the view that right acts bring the greatest happiness to the greatest number. His principle of utility judges every law and act by its effects on pleasure and pain. The felicific calculus is his scheme for weighing those effects.

Bentham defines crimes, punishments, and the aims of law with reforming zeal. He attacks vague talk of natural rights and sympathy as guides to legislation. The book became utilitarianism's founding text in English. Law reformers across the world took up its program. Its demand that laws justify themselves by results still shapes policy debate.
bernard-eales-life-works-vol1-1889:
Samuel Eales translated and edited the Life and Works of Saint Bernard, and the first volume appeared in 1889. Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux in the twelfth century, was the most commanding churchman of his age. He founded scores of monasteries, preached the Second Crusade, and advised popes and kings across Europe.

Volume 1 opens with Bernard's life, drawn from early accounts by those who knew him. It shows a monk who ruled much of Europe's public life from a cloister cell. His influence rested on preaching, letters, and a fearsome gift for rebuke. Eales made the Latin sources readable for English church readers of the Victorian age. The later volumes of the set carry Bernard's own letters, sermons, and treatises in the same translation.
bernard-eales-life-works-vol2-1889:
The second volume of Eales's Life and Works of Saint Bernard appeared in 1889, the same year as the first. Where the opening volume told Bernard's life, this one gives his letters in English. Bernard wrote to nearly everyone who mattered in twelfth-century Christendom, and his letter bag was enormous.

Popes, kings, bishops, and abbots all received his counsel, his comfort, or his sharp rebuke. The letters show how a monk with no army or office could steer the politics of an age through words alone. They also reveal his pastoral side, guiding monks and laypeople in the life of prayer. Eales's translation opened this correspondence to English readers who had no Latin, and it remains a vivid window on the medieval church.
bernheim-suggestive-therapeutics-1889:
Hippolyte Bernheim made the trance a tool of the ward in Suggestive Therapeutics, in English from 1889. Bernheim led the Nancy school in France. He held that the trance is no strange state, but keen heed to a healer's words. By such words, he claims, pain, dread, and bad wonts can be eased in sick folk of all kinds.

Case past case fills his proof. His school beat the great Paris school in their long row. The book is the flag of that win. It made trance craft a part of true care.
blavatsky-voice-of-the-silence-1889:
H. P. Blavatsky said she took The Voice of the Silence from an old book of gold rules. It came out in 1889, late in her life. The prose reads like verse. Short, grave lines urge the soul to spurn pride, greed, and self love on the path up.

The path leads to a vow to help all who live and strive. That call to pity is the heart of the book. It is the most loved prayer text of her creed. Seekers still read a page a day from it. Short lines make the book fit a coat pouch with ease. Many fans kept it so, as a daily guide for the path.
brentano-vom-ursprung-sittlicher-erkennt:
Brentano delivered the lectures behind On the Origin of Moral Knowledge in Vienna, and the German text appeared in 1889. The work is his ethics in brief, one of the shortest books ever to found a school of moral thought. Brentano asked how we know right from wrong, and answered through the emotions.

He argues that some feelings are felt as correct, the way some judgments are seen as true. Love of the good and hatred of evil, when rightly aimed, give moral knowledge its ground. The analogy between logic and ethics runs through the whole argument. Brentano's students carried the idea across Europe, and the book still anchors debates about whether value can be known rather than merely felt.
burgoyne-light-of-egypt-vol-1-1889:
Thomas Burgoyne set down the lore of a hid band in The Light of Egypt, Vol. I, out in 1889. The band was the Hermetic Brotherhood of Luxor, a foe to the creed of Blavatsky. Burgoyne, its scribe, lays out its scheme of stars, souls, and man's long rise through the ages.

Charts of the stars and rules of fate fill the tome. The band taught by post, in hid grades of drill. This book is its school text, first half. It shows a whole rival scheme of the occult in full dress. The band sold its lore in grades, each locked till paid and sworn. This tome was the prize its keen pupils worked to earn.
burgoyne-light-of-egypt-vol-2-1889:
Thomas Burgoyne rounds out his band's school text in The Light of Egypt, Vol. II, out in 1889. The scan here comes from a print run of 1900. The Hermetic Brotherhood of Luxor taught its lore by post in hid grades. This tome takes up where the first left off, in stars, souls, and fate.

More charts, keys, and rules for growth fill the pages. Read with the first tome, it gives the band's whole creed. The band is gone, yet its scheme still draws fans. These two tomes are its chief mark. The band's foe creeds mocked its claims as mere made up lore. Yet pupils kept the tomes, and collectors now prize them as rare finds.
chelmsford-three-witches-apprehension-15:
Chelmsford saw a third great witch case in 1589, and The Apprehension and Confession of Three Notorious Witches tells it. The pamphlet follows the Essex town's earlier trials of 1566 and 1579. By now the printed trial report was a known form in England.

It records how the three women were taken, what they were asked, and what fate the court gave them. Arrest, questioning, and judgment unfold in order, as the law of the day allowed. The series of Chelmsford prints shows local justice turning into national news. Printers knew fear and wonder sold, and this case fed both.
cia-0000009389:

A captured officer sighted at war's end drew close attention, since officers' names were well documented. Officials could test the claim against prisoner lists with unusual precision. cia-0000009589:
