His key find was regression to the mean: very tall parents tend to have children closer to average height. He showed the same pull toward the middle in seeds, stature, and other measured traits. That simple pattern became a base tool of statistics and of the study of inherited traits. His methods let later workers treat inheritance as a thing that could be counted.
gao-gaoreports-b-295589: Park Tower Management filed a March 2005 twin protest — two dockets — and GAO's combined ruling answers both. The property firm's double claim faced one referee. Two filings, one even-handed verdict. The verdict covered both claims. The referee was even. The answer was even.
gao-gaoreports-b-295989: Front Line Apparel Group took its June 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-296489: Digital Healthcare took its August 2005 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Health firms get the same full hearing as all.
gao-gaoreports-b-297789: Three printers fought one March 2006 battle — Goodway, NPC, and Hutchison — and GAO's combined ruling settles the claims. The firms challenged the award, and the call weighs each claim. Joint filings get one careful answer. Joint filings get one careful answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-297889: AshBritt doubled its March 2006 protest — two case numbers, one debris-removal fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-298889: U.S. Dynamics Corporation took its December 2006 contract fight to GAO, and this ruling is the verdict on the claims. The firm said the agency's award was unfair, and the call tests the protest. Every challenger gets the full fair-play hearing.
gao-gaoreports-b-302789: Coast Guard electronic certification got a fiscal ruling in this July 2005 GAO call, which tests the procedures. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the procedures were legal. The law had the final word. The procedures had to be legal.
gao-gaoreports-b-303689: A chemistry council donation to NIEHS got a fiscal ruling in this September 2005 GAO call, which tests accepting the gift. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the donation was legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-310489: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Superlative Technologies, Inc. Decided January 4, 2008, it reviews whether the agency ran a fair competition. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts. The full text sits with this description in the library.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-189: The troops' HR software needed more polish in 2005, and GAO's report says the people-system project had gaps. The review flags what was missing. The troops' personnel system deserved the polish. The polish had to come. The gaps were flagged.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-289: Environmental justice needed more EPA attention in 2005, and GAO's report says clean air rules should consider fairness. The findings demand the equity. The report warns that the poor neighborhoods deserved clean air. The attention had to be devoted. The poor neighborhoods deserved clean air.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-789: Native American health care was not always available in 2005, and GAO's report says the Indian Health Service left gaps. The findings document the shortfall. The report warns that the tribes deserved reliable care. The gaps had to be closed. The tribes deserved reliable care.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-189: Reservation phone service lagged in 2006, and GAO's report looks at the gaps in Native telecom. The findings map the dead zones. The report warns that the tribal lands deserved a dial tone. The reservations deserved connection. The dead zones needed mapping.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-289: Fishermen deserved a voice in 2006, and GAO's report says plain rules and a plan would bring them to the table. The findings prescribe the invite. The report warns that the nets' owners should help write the rules. The voice had to be heard.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-389: Radiation detectors were reaching U.S. ports in 2006, and GAO's report says DHS had made progress deploying the equipment. The findings give the credit. The report warns that the atomic gateways needed guarding. The progress had to continue. The atomic gateways needed guarding.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-989: Navy shipyard consolidations needed to pay off in 2006, and GAO's report says improvements were required to realize the benefits and handle funding changes. The findings demand the follow-through. The report warns that the merged yards had to deliver. The consolidations had to work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-889: A papers-please rule was dropping the insured in 2007 — GAO's report says states blamed the citizenship proof mandate for enrollment slides among eligible kids. The findings document the paperwork purge. The report asks whether the fraud fight was worth the children it cut.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-89: The homeland's round-the-clock watch centers needed better teamwork in 2007, and GAO's report says collaboration could improve at the multi-agency hubs. The findings press for the joint effort. The report warns that separate screens showing the same threat still missed the picture. The centers had to act as one.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-189: This 2007 report from the Government Accountability Office looks at nuclear Nonproliferation: DOE's Program to Assist Weapons Scientists in Russia and Other Countries Needs to Be Reassessed. Working for Congress, GAO checks how federal programs spend money and whether they deliver results. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-289: The Government Accountability Office dug into utility Oversight: Recent Changes in Law Call for Improved Vigilance by FERC in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Findings like these push agencies to fix the problems GAO reports.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-389: This 2008 GAO report takes a hard look at health Insurance: Most College Students Are Covered through Employer-Sponsored Plans, and Some Colleges and States Are Taking Steps to Increase Coverage. Congress relies on GAO for straight fact-finding on federal programs. Its conclusions can shape how agencies run their programs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-589: GAO published its findings on equal Employment Opportunity Commission: Sharing Promising Practices and Fully Implementing Strategic Human Capital Planning Can Improve Management of Growing W in 2008. GAO digs into federal programs at Congress's request and reports back what it learns. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-889: The Government Accountability Office dug into federal Courthouse Construction: Estimated Costs to House the L.A. District Court Have Tripled and There Is No Consensus on How to Proceed in this 2008 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. Reports like this give Congress the facts behind funding and reform choices.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-89: The Government Accountability Office dug into defense Trade: State Department Needs to Conduct Assessments to Identify and Address Inefficiencies and Challenges in the Arms Export Process in this 2007 report. Its findings feed into Congress's hearings and new laws. The library keeps it in the public record of federal watchdog work.
gissing-nether-world-1889:
George Gissing knew London poverty from the inside, having lived in cheap rooms on a tiny income. He set The Nether World, published in 1889, in the slums of Clerkenwell. Gissing wrote it as a plain record of working-class life, without the consolation of a happy plot.

Families crowd into courts and workshops, fighting over wages, drink, and a small inheritance that promises escape. A returned emigrant's money stirs hope in several households, but the money mostly spreads new misery. Gissing refuses villains and heroes; the trap is the world itself. The novel stands among the bleakest and most honest pictures of Victorian slum life.
glanvill-saducismus-triumphatus-english-:
Joseph Glanvill, a fellow of the Royal Society, wrote Saducismus Triumphatus to defeat Sadducism, his age's doubt about spirits. This edition of 1689 appeared after his death, with fresh material added. Glanvill offers full and plain evidence concerning witches and apparitions, gathered like a scientist's casebook.

His most famous case is the Drummer of Tedworth, a poltergeist that beat drums in a Wiltshire house. Glanvill treats testimony for ghosts as data, to be weighed like any observation. The book is science's strangest defense of the spirit world. It shows the new philosophy of experiment turned, in earnest, toward proving that witches exist.
glauber-works-1689:
Christopher Packe gave England the complete Glauber in 1689, translating The Works of Johann Rudolf Glauber, the famous German chemist. Furnaces, mines, metals, saltpetre, and the mending of barren land all fall within his restless program. Glauber wrote from decades at the bench, and his pages smell of the laboratory.

New philosophical furnaces open the collection, designs meant to work metals cleanly and cheaply. Later parts teach the separation of metals, the making of salts, and ways to enrich poor soil. The volume stands as the great seventeenth-century chemical corpus in English, prized by historians of early industry and craft.
gore-lux-mundi-1889:
Charles Gore edited Lux Mundi, the 1889 essay collection that brought biblical criticism inside Anglo-Catholic faith, and shocked Victorian England. Gore, later a bishop, gathered younger Oxford churchmen to write on faith in a new age of science and history. The book's title means Light of the World.

The essays accept evolution and the critical study of scripture while holding fast to the incarnation and the sacraments. Gore's own essay on the Holy Spirit and the church set the volume's daring, loyal tone. Lux Mundi split church opinion and marked the start of a more open Anglo-Catholicism.
grinnell-pawnee-hero-stories-and-folk-ta:
Before his Blackfoot tales, Grinnell spent time among the Pawnee of Nebraska, who shared their hero stories and folk tales with him. His 1889 book prints what he heard, making it one of the earliest published collections of Pawnee narrative.

The tales tell of Tirawa, the great power behind the world, and of heroes who fought monsters and won sacred gifts for the people. Grinnell also describes the morning star sacrifice and the warrior societies that guarded tribal life. These stories carry the Pawnee view of courage, duty, and the sacred, recorded before the tribe's old order broke apart.
hartmann-principles-of-astrological-geom:
Franz Hartmann taught an old art of fate in The Principles of Astrological Geomancy, his guide of 1889. Geomancy reads fate from marks in earth or dots cast at chance. Scribes of old joined those marks to the stars. Hartmann bases his rules on Agrippa, a sage of the age of print's dawn.

Steps, charts, and worked cases fill the guide. A keen fan could cast a chart by its rules at once. The art had near died out by his day. Hartmann's guide is the chief text of its late new life. Casters cast four rows of dots, then read the forms they make. Hartmann shows each step with care, so a new hand can learn fast.
hering-guiding-symptoms-vol9-1889:
Volume IX of Hering's Guiding Symptoms, from 1889, stands second to last in the ten-volume row. By now the editorial hands are practised, and the pages hold the same dense, well-sorted wealth. Each remedy's record runs from mental signs down to skin, fever, and sleep.

Hering began the harvest of provings decades before, and his name still heads the work. The grading signs, his own device, mark what practice confirmed most often. For the working homeopath the set served as both library and tool, and this volume carries its full share of the load.
hobson-physiology-of-industry-1889:
Hobson wrote The Physiology of Industry in 1889 with the businessman A. F. Mummery. It was Hobson's first book, and it launched the heresy he defended for the rest of his life. Orthodox economics taught that saving was always a virtue and spending a danger; the two authors argued the opposite could be true.

They claim that saving can outrun the need for new capital goods, leaving goods unsold and workers idle. Thrift, pushed too far, then causes the very slumps it was meant to prevent. The economics profession tried to bury the book, and Hobson was shut out of academic posts. Decades later, Keynes praised it by name as a seed of his own theory. The volume remains a landmark of dissent inside economics.
janet-automatisme-psychologique-1889:
Pierre Janet maps the hid mind in L'Automatisme psychologique, his French thesis of 1889. Janet was a young sage at work in the wards of Paris. His sick wrote, spoke, and acted with no sense of their own deeds. He calls such acts the work of a split off part of the self, out of the main mind's sight and rule.

Cases fill the book, each probed with great care. His scheme came ere Freud's fame and fed it in part. In French, the book is a root text of mind science. Its reach is vast.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luntz-10189:
Luntz, the name of a family traced back to Worms, is treated in a genealogical entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Family tradition holds that Elijah, sixth in line from Moses, son of Joselman Loans, left Worms around 1700. He settled in the small town of Kelm and became its rabbi. His descendants spread across Lithuanian Jewish life.

The article follows the main branches of the family. One line produced Elijah of Krozhe, a wealthy and pious Talmudist whose descendants took the name Rabinowitz. Another son, Ezekiel, served as rabbi of Shavli from about 1749 until 1808. A later descendant, Wolf Luntz of Riga, became a communal worker and a founder of Russian Zionism. The entry also clarifies that Abraham Moses Luncz of Jerusalem does not belong to this family. It is a period record of how one Worms family branched out.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahler-eduard-1:
Eduard Mahler, an Austrian astronomer, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in Cziffer, Hungary, in 1857, he finished school at Vienna in 1876. He studied mathematics and physics at the university there, graduating in 1880. From 1882 he shared the labors of the astronomer Oppolzer. In 1885 he joined the royal commission on the measurement of degrees.

The article says his true field became chronology, the science of dates. Early interests in Oriental history, Assyriology, and Egyptology turned into a lectureship at Budapest. Sweden and Norway gave him a royal gold medal in 1889. Since 1898 he had served at the Hungarian National Museum. His books study eclipses named in the Bible and in the book of Nahum. He also wrote a biblical chronology and extended the standard tables comparing Muslim and Christian dates. The entry honors a scholar who dated the ancient world by its skies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattithiah-b-he:
Mattithiah ben Heresh, a Roman tanna of the second century, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906 by the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Ismar Elbogen. Born in Judea and probably a pupil of R. Ishmael, he left for Rome after his ordination, driven by Hadrian's persecution. There he founded a school and a Jewish court that soon won real standing in the capital.

His surviving legal rulings try to soften the Sabbath laws where the sick are concerned, but the entry says his gift was chiefly for the Haggadah, the homiletic side of tradition. One of his sayings stands in the Pirke Abot: "Meet each man with friendly greeting; be the tail among lions rather than the head among foxes." A later legend shows him triumphing over a temptation set in his path by Satan.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meisel-10589:
Meisel is the name of a Bohemian family. A team of eight contributors traces it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Mordecai Marcus Meisel, the rich “primate” of Prague, made the name famous above all. The family seems to have come from Cracow, where a printer of the name flourished in the late sixteenth century. Prague documents, though, carry the name back to 1477.

The article proceeds person by person. Frummet Meisel, the second wife of Mordecai, helped build the Meisel Synagogue and loaded the synagogues of Prague with her gifts. Yet a chronicle claims her husband divorced her on his deathbed over his will. Her tombstone names the house of her father, not her husband. Judah Löb Meisel reopened the Cracow printing house of his father-in-law in 1663 and worked it for seven years. The entry then turns to Mordecai himself, born at Prague in 1528.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mephibosheth-10:
Mephibosheth was the lame son of Jonathan and grandson of Saul. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price give him a careful reading in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article first untangles his name. Chronicles calls him Merib-baal. The books of Samuel call him Mephibosheth. The change swaps "shame" for Baal, like Ishbosheth for Esh-baal. After the disaster at Gilboa, his fleeing nurse dropped the child. He was crippled for life. David restored Saul's estate to him, for Jonathan's sake. David kept him as a perpetual guest at the royal table.

The Absalom revolt clouded everything. Ziba reported that his master stayed in Jerusalem. The master hoped for the throne, Ziba said. Mephibosheth met the returning David unwashed and unkempt. He blamed Ziba's deceit. David was perplexed between the stories. He split the estate between the two men. The entry reports that judgment. It does not resolve it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michaelis-johan:
Johann David Michaelis, born at Halle on February 27, 1717, was a Christian Orientalist whose work shaped the scholarly study of the Bible. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He was the grandnephew of the Hebraist Johann Heinrich Michaelis and was educated at Halle, with study journeys to England and Holland.

After lecturing at Halle on Semitic languages and Bible interpretation, he spent nearly fifty years as a professor at Göttingen, from 1746 onward. His teaching covered Old Testament exegesis, Hebrew antiquities, Mosaic law, and the Semitic tongues. The article credits him with a Hebrew grammar of 1745 and a supplement to the Hebrew lexicons of his day, among much else.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-el:
Mordecai ben Eliezer Jonah was an Austrian commentator who lived at Lemberg in the later sixteenth century, recorded by Wilhelm Bacher and S. J. Levinson in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His single known work is an ethical discourse on the Shema, the daily confession of God's unity. It was published at Prague in 1618 under the title Petil Tekelet.

The book falls into three parts, and their order is the man's theology in outline: first the love of God, second abstention from sin, and last the problem of misfortune. The entry is four lines long, resting on Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue, Fürst, and Benjacob. Some scholars survive as a shelf-mark and one well-built book.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahshon-ben-zad:
Nahshon ben Zadok was gaon of Sura from 874 to 882, succeeding Mar Amram ben Sheshna. The Jewish Encyclopedia article is by its editorial committee and S. Mannheimer. He explained hard words in the Talmud in the order of the tractates. A work on ritual slaughtering is ascribed to him, though the ascription is doubted.

His fame rests on the calendar. Nahshon found that the weekdays of the festivals repeat in a cycle of two hundred forty-seven years. He set the years out in fourteen tables, the Iggul that still bears his name. He and his son Hai also opposed the Kol Nidre prayer. His responsa, in terse Aramaic, won him great respect.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-navarra-abram-1: Abram Navarra was a rabbi at Casale in Italy. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote his brief entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He held that post in the year 1650. No other facts of his life are given here. His responsa, or legal answers, survive only in manuscript. They rest in David Kaufmann's collection at Budapest. Others are held by the Jews' College at London.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-hampshire-1:
New Hampshire was one of America's thirteen original states. Cyrus Adler wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. A record names Aaron Moses at New Castle in 1693. Lists later name Joseph Levy and William Levi. Levi served as a private in the Revolution. Proof of their Jewish origin, though, is lacking.

Abraham Isaac settled at Portsmouth after the Revolution. Brewster calls him that town's first known Jew. He gained much property and built himself a house. He died on Feb. 15, 1803, and his stone still stands. By 1904 Manchester held two Jewish congregations. Portsmouth and Nashua held one congregation each. The state's Jews were put at 1,000 to 1,200. Its whole population then stood at 411,588.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nordlingen-1158:
Nördlingen is a Bavarian city of Swabia. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It stayed a free city until 1803. Jews likely lived there in the twelfth century. Documents name them only from the thirteenth onward.

A tale of a massacre in 1290 is false. A city clerk invented it about 1549. Real woes came under Rindfleisch and the Black Death. In 1384 rioters wiped out the whole community. The Swabian union demanded the ringleaders' banishment for it. The king settled the quarrel for 3,500 florins. Expulsion edicts followed across the fifteenth century. The last, in 1506, was enforced in full. No Jew resided there again until 1860. A congregation formed ten years after that return.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ollendorf-gusta:
Gustave Ollendorf was a French critic of art and state officer. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Paris on March 4, 1850. He died at Saint-Cloud on September 19, 1891. Chief Rabbi Zadoc Kahn gave him his Jewish schooling.

In the war with Prussia he served in the Paris guard. In 1871 he joined the state staff for schools and fine arts. He rose fast in that work over the years. He founded a youth group just after the war's close. In time he ran the bureau for museums and shows. He helped plan the great Paris fair of 1889. His books treat the care of the fine arts in France. He also wrote notes on the Paris art shows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-peine-11989:
Peine is a German town in the province of Hanover. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Jews lived there as early as the fourteenth century. The town once belonged to the bishopric of Hildesheim.

In 1428 the bishop pawned the town's Jews to Hildesheim. The price was six hundred Rhenish gulden. Later bishops granted letters of protection to the Jews. By the eighteenth century over forty families lived there. They kept their own rabbi under Hildesheim's chief rabbi. Only about a hundred Jews remained by 1904.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-phasael-12089:
Phasael was the elder brother of Herod the Great. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Their father Antipater set him over Jerusalem. Herod, the younger son, took Galilee instead. Josephus calls him a brave and noble man.

Jewish elders twice charged the brothers before Antony. Both times the charges failed for Herod's skill. Antony then made the two men tetrarchs. When Antigonus struck with Parthian help, Phasael held the walls. Lured into the Parthian camp, he was seized. He killed himself rather than face disgrace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pisgah-always-w:
Pisgah was a mountain of Moab east of the Jordan. The Executive Committee and J. F. McLaughlin wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Israel camped by it on the journey north. Balak offered sacrifice on its height. Below its slopes lies the Dead Sea shore.

Pisgah is famed above all for Moses' end. From its top he viewed the promised land entire. He saw Gilead, Naphtali, Judah, and the western sea. Then he died there, as Deuteronomy tells. The peak is now placed at Ras Naba. Its ridge looks down the whole Jordan valley.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prophets-and-pr:
Prophets and prophecy in Israel are the subject of a long article by Emil G. Hirsch, J. Frederic McCurdy, and Joseph Jacobs. It appeared in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Many old peoples had prophets of their own, they note. Yet the word took its common sense from Israel alone. Hebrew prophets stand without match in their work and sway.

The article is built in two large parts. The first traces how prophecy grew over time. It starts with the names used for the prophet's task. The Greek word means one who speaks forth. The second part turns to the words the prophets left. It weighs their books, their times, and their weight for later faith.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-tusfa-ah:
Rabbah Tusfa'ah was a Babylonian teacher of the seventh set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a pupil of Rabina the First. He was of an age with Rabina the Second. Their names stand side by side in the Talmud at times. A few free rulings of his own have been kept.

One ruling treats how long a woman may bear a child. He held the term may stretch from nine to twelve months. That ruling stands in the tractate Yebamot. His chief work in the tradition is named at the entry's end. The writers trace his place at the close of an age.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-resh-kallah-126:
A resh kallah was a high officer in Babylonian academies. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Only the president, or gaon, ranked above him. Sura and Pumbedita each had seven such officers.

The article says they sat in the first row facing the gaon. Each stood over ten members of the great assembly. Their name comes from the kallah study months. In those months they explained the gaon's chosen topics. They taught students in the first three weeks. A resh kallah read Scripture at an exilarch's installation. Sons could succeed fathers, even as minors. The entry shows how the academies ordered their teaching ranks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rocamora-isaac-:
Isaac de Rocamora was a Spanish monk, physician, and poet. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born about 1600 to Marano parents at Valencia. He died at Amsterdam on April 8, 1684.

The article says he was educated for the Church. As Vicente de Rocamora he became a Dominican monk. He served as confessor to the Infanta Maria of Spain. In 1643 he openly adopted Judaism and took the name Isaac. He studied medicine and settled in Amsterdam. There he practiced and directed philanthropic societies. He judged a poetry academy founded by Manuel de Belmonte. None of his poems in Spanish or Latin survive. His son Solomon also practiced medicine in Amsterdam.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosh-ha-shanah-:
Rosh ha-Shanah, here, is the eighth treatise of the Mishnah order Mo'ed, not the holiday itself. Wilhelm Bacher and Ludwig A. Rosenthal wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. It sums up the tractate's rules on the calendar and the feast.

The tractate opens with four different new years in Jewish reckoning. It tells how witnesses reported the new moon to the Sanhedrin, even on the Sabbath. Old bonfire signals once carried the news of a new month as far as Babylon. Later chapters give the form and use of the shofar, the ram's horn. They also fix the order of the New Year service.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sadducees-hebre:
The Sadducees were the party of Temple, priesthood, and the written Law in ancient Judaism. Kaufmann Kohler wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia, working alone. They stood directly opposite the Pharisees in views and practice.

The name points to the Bene Zadok, sons of Zadok the high priest. Zadok served under David and Solomon, and his line long ran the Temple. The entry says the priestly party sank under Greek influence in Seleucid times. Its members grew worldly, even Epicurean, in the Hasidim's hostile telling. In time the name covered all aristocratic circles tied to the high priests.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-saphir-sigmund-:
Isidore Singer and Samuel Krauss wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Sigmund Saphir. He was a Hungarian journalist. Saphir was born in Hungary in 1806, though some say 1801. He died at Pesth on October 17, 1866. His uncle was Moritz Gottlieb Saphir, the humorist. Sigmund edited several German papers in Pesth.

His Pesther Tageblatt ran from 1839 to 1845. His uncle wrote for it. The paper sometimes carried pieces of Jewish interest. One told the legend of Judah ha-Levi's death. Saphir also edited the Pesther Sonntagszeitung. No complete set of that paper is known to survive. Its pages often held comic sketches of Jewish life. With Count Majláth he edited Iris, a yearbook of poetry. It ran in 1840 and 1841. Ludwig August Frankl was among its contributors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schnabel-louis-:
Cyrus Adler wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Louis Schnabel. He was an Austrian teacher and journalist. Schnabel was born at Prossnitz, in Moravia, on June 29, 1829. He died at New York on May 3, 1897. He studied at various yeshibot and at the University of Vienna. He taught at Prossnitz, Boskowitz, and Vienna.

From 1854 to 1863 Schnabel taught in Paris. He worked in Derenbourg's school for boys and Madame Cahn's school for girls. In 1869 he emigrated to America. He ran the Hebrew Orphan Asylum of New York. He also founded Young Israel, a magazine that lasted eight years. In 1875 he led the preparatory school for the Hebrew Union College. From 1890 he taught English to Russian immigrants. He had been Emma Lazarus's Hebrew teacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-segelmessi-siji: Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Judah ben Joseph Segelmessi. He was an African writer of liturgy. He flourished about the year 1400. He came from Segelmesa, in Morocco. Two of his seliḥot, penitential prayers, still survive. Each bears his signature, Judah ben Joseph Segelmessi. One opens with the words Eleh kokebe marom. The other opens Mah e'eseh le-ẓedati. Dukes printed part of the second prayer in a German journal. The entry rests on Fuenn, Landshuth, and Zunz.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shiraz-13589:
Shiraz is a Persian city, capital of the province of Fars. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the city. It was founded in 693 by Mohammed, brother of al-Hajjaj. Persian tradition says Jews settled there very early.

Benjamin of Tudela counted 10,000 Jews at Shiraz in the twelfth century. A later traveler, Chardin, visited in the seventeenth century. He found Jews making wine for European companies there. Non-Muslims then enjoyed religious liberty, he reports. Yet poems by Babai tell a harsher story, the entry notes. Shiraz Jews suffered the same persecutions as other Persian Jews. Attacks struck them hard in the early eighteenth century. The entry balances traveler praise against local lament.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-b-ezron-: Simeon ben Ezron was a leader in the Jewish war against Rome in the year 66. Richard Gottheil and Samuel Krauss wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was of noble descent, Josephus reports in his war history. He sided with Eleazar ben Simeon, the Zealot leader of the revolt. He may be the same man as Simeon ben Arinos in Josephus. Josephus also praises a Simeon ben Ari for bravery in that war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sisera-13789:
Sisera was the general of King Jabin of Hazor. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. In the days of Deborah he invaded northern Israel. Deborah ordered Barak to meet him with 10,000 men. The battle took place by the river Kishon, where Sisera lost.

Sisera fled alone and on foot from the field. A Kenite woman named Jael took him into her tent. She gave him milk when he asked for water. While he slept, she drove a tent pin through his temple. The Midrash adds wild tales of his vast strength and voice. It says his descendants later taught children in Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-society-for-the:
The Society for the Promotion of Culture Among the Jews of Russia was founded in 1863. Herman Rosenthal and A S Waldstein wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It began at St Petersburg in December of that year. Joseph Yozel Günzburg became its first president. His son Horace served as first vice-president.

Its stated aim was to spread culture among Russian Jews. It worked to spread knowledge of the Russian language. It published useful books and journals in Russian and Hebrew. It also helped young Jews pursue knowledge and the sciences. For years its membership stayed below 250 men. After 1880, riots and new limits drove more Jews to self-help.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-studenzki-moses:
Moses Studenzki was a Polish physician born at Zbarasz in Galicia. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. His father, Aaron Polak, was rabbi of that town. Moses studied Hebrew and Talmud under him until fourteen. He died at Warsaw about 1876.

Studenzki later attended the yeshiva of Brody for three years. At seventeen he went to Warsaw for secular study. He finished his medical training at Berlin in 1834. Back in Warsaw he practiced as a top-grade physician. In 1846 he also qualified in childbirth care. His 1847 book treats children's diseases in Hebrew and German. A second work guides readers on hygiene and health. The entry joins rabbinic schooling with modern medicine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-swine-12289:
The swine stands among the Bible's unclean animals. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. English versions render the Hebrew hazir as swine. Leviticus and Deuteronomy both forbid its flesh. Isaiah brands eating it as a mark of apostasy.

Wild boars still swarm the Jordan thickets near Jericho. Psalm 80 calls the boar the swine of the woods. Talmudic speech avoided even naming the animal. Speakers said another thing in its place. Tyrants forced Jews to eat swine as a torment. Breeding or keeping swine was flatly forbidden. Yet its haunches counted as a delicacy to others. The entry gathers law, proverb, and custom around one shunned animal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tables-of-the-l:
The Tables of the Law are the stone tablets of the Ten Commandments. Emil G. Hirsch and Wilhelm Bacher wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article in 1906. God called Moses up the mountain to receive them. Exodus calls them tables of testimony, written by God's finger. The writing covered both sides of the stones.

Moses came down carrying the two tables himself. Seeing the golden calf, he smashed them in anger. God then ordered two new stones hewn like the first. On them God wrote the covenant words again. Moses placed the new tables inside the Ark at Horeb. They still sat there when Solomon dedicated the Temple. Rabbinic tales measure the stones at six handbreadths. The entry follows the tablets from mountain to Temple.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-teixeira-pedro-:
Pedro Teixeira was a Portuguese traveler born at Lisbon. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. His parents were Maranos, secret Jews under Christian rule. He was educated and a close observer of places. He died around the mid-seventeenth century.

Teixeira traveled eighteen months through the Philippines and China. His routes reached parts of America as well. After two years at Lisbon he set out again. That scientific journey crossed India and Persia. His 1610 book tells Persia's kings from Persian sources. It also reports on Jews of Aleppo and Bagdad. Notes on Jewish monuments fill its pages too. Later travelers used it as a working guide. An English translation carried it to new readers. The entry honors a Marano who mapped the East.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tibni-14389: Tibni was a rival king of Israel during the gap between Zimri and Omri. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote this brief Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. When Zimri died after a seven-day reign, Israel split in two. One half backed Omri, and the other backed Tibni, son of Ginath. Verses in Kings suggest Tibni ruled half the kingdom for four years. Omri's side won in the end. Tibni died, and Omri took the throne. The Septuagint adds a brother, Joram, who backed Tibni and died with him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-trebino-tremino:
Tomas Trebino de Sobremonte was a martyr burned by the Inquisition in 1649. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was burned at Mexico, or possibly Lima, on April 11. He had once been reconciled by the Inquisition. New charges came in 1642 during another trial.

He and his wife Maria Gomez were denounced then. He sat in an Inquisition dungeon until his death. The inquisitor may have wanted his fortune, the article hints. Of 109 prisoners, he alone was burned alive. He died without a groan, mocking his tormentors. He joked that the wood cost them nothing, since his money bought it. De Barrios honored him in two sonnets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-united-states-1:
Jewish life in the United States receives the encyclopedia's largest country treatment here. Cyrus Adler, Herbert Friedenwald, Herman Rosenthal, Judah David Eisenstein, and Joseph Jacobs wrote it, published in 1906. Only Russia and Austria held more Jews under one government. The article sorts its vast material under thirteen headings.

Immigration waves come first in the plan. Cities and states follow in order of settlement. New York, Newport, and New England lead that long list. Relations with the federal government get their own section. Education, philanthropy, and religious development follow in turn. Military service and civil rights are treated next. Persecution drove most Jewish immigration, the authors stress. The first settlers came from Spain and Portugal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-vessillo-israel:
Il Vessillo Israelitico, the Hebrew Banner, was an Italian Jewish monthly. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The paper continued the Educatore Israelita, founded in 1853. When editor Giuseppe Levi died in 1874, Flaminio Servi took over. Servi moved the paper from Vercelli to Casale.

Early issues held essays by leading scholars. Steinschneider and Berliner were among the contributors. Later the paper's literary quality declined. Still, it kept one clear strength. Its life stories of Italian Jews remain valuable. Servi's son Ferruccio modernized the paper after 1904. In 1905 it absorbed the review Lux of Leghorn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wasker-silleman:
Silleman Abajee Wasker was a Beni Israel soldier in India. Joseph Jacobs wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His English name was Solomon Abraham. He died about 1850. He enlisted in 1809 in the Third Regiment Native Light Infantry. He served thirty seven years in all.

Wasker fought at Puna, Multan, Kittoor, and Gujarat. He rose to sirdar bahadur, the top native rank. He also won the first class Order of the Star of India. For twenty five years he commanded the Beni Israel regiment. He retired from the army in March 1846. The entry honors a long, decorated career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-widal-fernand-g:
Fernand Georges Widal was a French doctor. He was born at Paris on March 9, 1862. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this short entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. From 1886 he demonstrated research in pathological anatomy. He then ran a bacteriology course for two years. That course sat in Professor Cornil's laboratory.

In 1895 Widal became a visiting physician in Paris. In 1904 he joined the medical faculty as instructor. He now serves as physician to the Hôpital Cochin. He also leads the medical clinics there. His essays treat infectious diseases in depth. Erysipelas, heart, liver, and nerve diseases fill his list.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolff-joseph-14:
Joseph Wolff (died 1900) was a Russian historian of Poland and Lithuania. Isidore Singer and Julius Gottlieb wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Saint Petersburg, he was the son of a book dealer. He caught a love of old tales of the past as a boy.

He went to school in his home city and then to Leipsic. There he gave his time to Polish and Lithuanian affairs. His books list the high lords of the grand duchy. They run from 1386 to 1795 in one large work. A second book traces the kin line of Gediminas. A third treats the princes of the Lithuanian-Russian lands. The Academy of Cracow made him a member by post. His books still serve those who study that lost world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yishai-jesse-be:
Yishai ben Hezekiah was an exilarch at Damascus in the late 1200s. Joseph Jacobs and M. Seligsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He stood as a strong shield for the works of Maimonides. Foes of that sage were on the march in his day.

One foe was the mystic Solomon Petit of Acre. Yishai warned that man to stop his attacks at once. He set the ban as the price for more abuse. Petit paid no heed to the threat from Damascus. In 1286 Yishai called the rabbis to act with him. Rabbis of Safed joined the call to cast Petit out. The writ bore the seal of the exilarch at its head. That seal showed a lion with a raised hand above it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zuckermandel-mo:
Moses Samuel Zuckermandel was a German rabbi and Talmudist known for editing the Tosefta. Isidore Singer and Newell Dunbar wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Ungarisch-Brod, Moravia, on April 24, 1836. He served as rabbi in Pleschen, Prussia, and in 1898 became a lecturer at Breslau.

His fame rests on the Tosefta, an early companion work to the Mishnah. He published its Erfurt manuscript in 1876, then a full edition from the Erfurt and Vienna manuscripts in 1880-82. Later books gather biblical sayings from the prayer book. One adds a word list and grammar for the Hebrew verses in that prayer-book volume.
judge-yoga-aphorisms-of-patanjali-1889:
William Q. Judge turned the Yoga Aphorisms of Patanjali into English in his book of 1889. Patanjali was a sage of old India. His brief lines map how to still the mind by drill, breath, and deep thought. Each line is terse, like a knot to be untied by a guide.

Judge adds glosses that link the drill to his creed. The book brought the lore of yoga to fans of the occult in the West. It helped spark the West's long pull to yoga. Plain, short, and deep, it still gets read. Patanjali's lines are so brief that no fan reads them bare. Judge's glosses give the new fan a hand through each hard knot.
kalidasa-shakuntala-jones-1789:
Sir William Jones translated Kalidasa's Shakuntala into English in 1789, and the text here follows the London edition of 1790. His Sacontala, or The Fatal Ring, was the first Sanskrit drama ever Englished, or put into any European tongue. King Dushyanta loves the hermit girl Shakuntala, gives her a ring, then forgets her under a curse.

The lost ring, found in a fish, restores the king's memory and the lovers' hope. Jones's version stunned Goethe, Herder, and the young Romantics with its freshness. It opened Sanskrit literature to the West almost at a stroke. Scholars still mark the translation as a turning point in world reading. Jones worked from a Bengal recension with native scholars at his side.
kingsford-clothed-with-the-sun-1889:
Anna Kingsford's bright visions fill Clothed with the Sun, a book set in print in 1889, past her death. Her friend Edward Maitland shaped her notes for the press. Kingsford held that she saw truths of the faith in dreams and trance. She cast those truths in terms of her own creed of Christ.

She reads old myths and texts as codes for the soul's life. Her views exalt the wife side of God, a bold stand then. The book is the seer's own record. Fans of deep Christ lore prize its strange glow. Maitland, her friend and aide, kept her notes with great care. His hand in this book lets her voice reach fans past death.
l-or-et-la-transmutation-des-metaux-1889:
G. Théodore Tiffereau wrote L'Or et la Transmutation des Métaux, published in Paris in 1889. Its title means gold and the transmutation of metals. The book joins a series on the hermetic sciences.

Tiffereau was called the alchemist of the nineteenth century. The volume gathers his memoirs and lectures on making gold. An opening piece treats Paracelsus and alchemy more broadly. Readers meet a modern believer defending an ancient claim with his own reported experiments. Adolphe Franck adds weight with an opening study in the volume. Two voices thus frame Tiffereau's bold claims about gold.
liebeault-sommeil-provoque-1889:
Ambroise-Auguste Liebault treats induced sleep in Le sommeil provoque, in French from 1889. The Nancy school's founder argues that suggestion, not magnetic fluid, works the cure. A country doctor's quiet clinic taught Europe that words themselves could heal, a claim his case books support in patient, humble detail.

Bernheim and others carried the Nancy method into the world's clinics. Liebault writes without show, letting rows of cures speak for him. His work marks a founding moment for suggestion-based hypnotherapy in medicine. Modern psychotherapy traces one of its clearest roots to this modest book, written far from Paris by a doctor who charged the poor nothing.
life-and-death-of-john-of-barneveld-advo:
Motley's fourth volume carries the Barneveld story through 1610 to 1612. Dutch commissioners now negotiate with King James in England. Prince Maurice takes command of troops besieging Julich, which surrenders. Matthias becomes King of Bohemia as old Emperor Rudolph dies.

At Leyden, Vorstius replaces Arminius, deepening the religious quarrel. Bitterness grows steadily between Barneveld and Prince Maurice. James dreams of a Spanish marriage for his heir. Motley links church disputes, court plans, and battlefield news together. Spain's James dreams, church appointments, and marriage projects intertwine throughout. Maurice and Winwood confer as the Arminian dispute sharpens Dutch politics.
lightfoot-apostolic-fathers-1889:
Joseph Barber Lightfoot, bishop of Durham and a giant of Victorian scholarship, published The Apostolic Fathers, Part 1, in 1889. The Apostolic Fathers are the earliest Christian writers after the New Testament itself. Lightfoot's edition became the definitive English treatment of Clement, Ignatius, and Polycarp.

He prints the Greek texts with long introductions, translations, and notes that settle dates, authorship, and church order. Clement's letter to Corinth and Ignatius's letters on his road to martyrdom anchor the volume. New Testament scholars still begin serious work on these writers from Lightfoot's pages. His notes weigh every old claim about the texts before trusting it.
locke-letter-concerning-toleration-1689:
John Locke wrote his Letter Concerning Toleration in Latin exile in Holland, and William Popple's English translation of 1689 is the text here. Locke had seen England tear at itself over religion for a generation. His letter asks what business the magistrate has with the care of souls, and answers: none at all.

A church, for Locke, is a free society of men joining to worship as they judge best. Force can make hypocrites, never believers, so persecution fails even at its own aim. The letter became the charter of liberal toleration, read wherever church and state are argued over. Its calm logic still does work in every debate on religious freedom.
mathers-key-of-solomon-the-king-1889:
Mathers's Key of Solomon the King, published in 1889, translates the Clavicula Salomonis from manuscripts in the British Museum. The Key is the central Solomonic grimoire, the most copied handbook of ceremonial magic in Europe. Mathers's version is the foundational English edition.

It gives the full working system: the choice of hours, the making of wands, swords, pentacles, and robes, and the conjurations for each task. Planetary seals and prayers crowd its pages in Mathers's careful hand. Occultists of the Golden Dawn and after built their practice on this English Key. Every tool in the book must be made, blessed, and used at its proper hour.
meiji-constitution-1889:
Japan promulgated the Meiji Constitution in 1889, the charter of the Empire of Japan. Itō Hirobumi, who had studied constitutions in Europe, took the Prussian model and adapted it to the Chrysanthemum Throne. The emperor granted the constitution to his people as a gift from the throne, timed to the modernization drive that was remaking Japan.

The text makes the emperor sacred and supreme, holder of sovereignty, while creating an elected Diet to share in lawmaking. Rights of speech, religion, and property are promised, but only within the limits of law. Ministers answer to the emperor, not to parliament, which left the army a dangerous freedom. Itō's charter carried Japan to great-power status and ruled until 1947. It stands as the constitution of Japan's modern age, Western forms bent to imperial rule.
memoirs-of-the-court-of-marie-antoinette:
Volume six of Campan's memoirs opens at chapter five, in spring 1791. The King, tired of the Tuileries, hopes to return to St. Cloud. His household and his dinner have already gone on ahead.

The guard mutinies, shuts the gates, and bars his carriage at one. Two men near the carriage are ill treated by the crowd. All that March the Queen makes secret plans for a flight. Campan buys clothes in secret, a few at each shop, for the escape. A trunk of clothes goes to an aunt at Arras for the flight. Any place in Austrian Flanders could be her first safe stop.
minor-law-books-jolly-1889:
Julius Jolly translated the Minor Law-Books for the Sacred Books of the East in 1889. The volume, number thirty-three in the series, holds the law codes of Narada and Brihaspati. Hindu law beyond the famous Manu is the subject here.

Narada's code treats courts, contracts, debts, and ordeals in practical detail. Brihaspati's fragments add rules on procedure and evidence for judges. These texts date from the early centuries of the common era. They show ancient Indian justice actually at work, case by case. Jolly specialized in Hindu law throughout his scholarly career. His volume remains the standard English source for both lawgivers.
moby-dick-or-the-whale-pg2489:
Call me Ishmael: Herman Melville's novel opens with the most famous summons in American fiction. Ishmael has little money and nothing to interest him on shore. A damp, drizzly November in his soul sends him to sea. Sailing, he says, is his substitute for pistol and ball.

He describes New York's crowds of water-gazers leaning over the bulwarks. Landsmen penned in lath and plaster all week, they crowd to the water's edge on Sundays. Ishmael ships aboard the Pequod, whose Captain Ahab hunts the white whale. This text presents the novel plainly, chapter by chapter, from that first loomings onward.
morse-american-geography-1789:
Jedidiah Morse published The American Geography in 1789, the year the United States Constitution took effect. Morse, a Connecticut clergyman, saw that the new nation had geography books written in Britain but none of its own. He set out to describe the young republic for its own citizens.

The book surveys each state's land, rivers, towns, trade, and people, with maps and tables of numbers. It also covers the wider continent beyond the states' borders. Morse wrote with open pride in his country, mixing hard fact with patriotic hope. The work earned him the title of father of American geography, and later editions grew with the nation through the years of expansion.
mulford-thoughts-are-things-1889:
Prentice Mulford was a California humorist, journalist, and gold-country storekeeper who turned late in life to spiritual teaching. His Thoughts Are Things, published in 1889, gathers his New Thought essays on the power of mind. The title states his whole doctrine in three words.

Mulford teaches that thoughts are real forces that draw health, wealth, or ruin toward the thinker who holds them. Fear and hurry repel good fortune; calm, expectant thought attracts it as mental causation, spirit acting as law. His essays, plain and funny by turns, seeded the law-of-attraction teaching that followed.
new-physiognomy-or-signs-of-character-as:
Samuel R. Wells edited the Phrenological Journal, and his New Physiognomy reads character from outward signs. The sampled title page is a New York printing dated 1875, though the record says 1889. Wells published it himself on Broadway, with entry in 1866. The book claims more than one thousand illustrations.

Wells holds that character shows through temperament and outward forms. Above all, he says, it shows in the human face divine. A line from Ecclesiasticus on the title page backs him: a man may be known by his look. Shakespeare is quoted to the same point, that the heart can be seen in the face.
openalex-w1489768389:
Nelson Durán, Priscyla Marcato, and three co-authors wrote this study. It appeared in the Journal of Nanobiotechnology in 2005. The team studied a fungus called Fusarium oxysporum. Several strains of the fungus met silver ions in solution. The question was how the fungus makes silver nanoparticles.

The fungus reduced silver ions outside its cells. That process formed a stable silver hydrosol, they report. The particles measured only tens of nanometers across. A nitrate-linked enzyme and a quinone shuttle drove reduction. The authors note strong potential as antibacterial material. Fungal synthesis offers a clean route to nanoparticles.
openalex-w2049309389:
Renata Teles Vieira, Leonardo Caixeta, Sergio Machado and colleagues reviewed early-onset dementia. Their paper appeared in 2013. Early-onset dementia begins before old age. It differs from the dementia of later life. Cases are common enough to matter, yet often missed.

The team searched major medical databases for studies. They covered work published from 1985 to 2012. They compared early and late onset forms. Nerve-degenerating diseases were the most common causes. Alzheimer's disease was prominent among them. Reported rates varied widely between studies. Rates rose with age within the younger groups. The authors stress better recognition and diagnosis. Families face the disease during working years.
openalex-w2069283089:
Anna Stewart Ibarra, Sadie Ryan, Efrain Beltran and colleagues studied dengue mosquito patterns in Ecuador. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2013. Dengue is the fastest spreading tropical disease. Climate and human behaviour both shape mosquito numbers. Their relative weight depends on local conditions.

The study took place in the city of Machala. The team measured mosquito presence in homes. They gathered climate data and household social data. Water storage and housing conditions mattered locally. Weather patterns also shaped mosquito abundance over time. The mix of factors varied across neighbourhoods. Control efforts should target local drivers, they argue. Blanket campaigns may waste scarce resources.
openalex-w2123160589:
G. Aad and colleagues in the ATLAS Collaboration published this measurement in the European Physical Journal C in 2014. They checked how well the ATLAS detector rebuilds the paths of muons, the heavy cousins of electrons. Every later ATLAS result depends on knowing that rebuilding step, its success rate, and its errors.

The team used proton collision data from 2011 and 2012 at the Large Hadron Collider. They measured muons from known particle decays and compared the data with computer simulations. Over most of the range studied, rebuilding worked more than ninety-nine times in a hundred. The authors give momentum accuracy ranges and corrections that other ATLAS analyses should apply.
openalex-w2793318989:
Rossana Perrone and Ana C. Silva studied hormone control of social status in a weakly electric fish, in Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience in 2018. Their species, Gymnotus omarorum, fights fiercely over territory in single-sex and mixed pairs. After a contest, winners stay aggressive while losers signal submission in a set sequence of moves and electric pulses. That sharp split makes the fish a strong model for dominance studies.

The study examines vasotocin, a hormone tied to social behavior across vertebrates. Its title reports that vasotocin shapes dominance and submission differently depending on the fish's status. Such status-based control needs distinct brain and hormone paths for winners and losers. Electric signals give researchers an unusually readable window into those states. Seeing how one molecule pushes both aggression and submission may teach lessons that generalize widely. Social hormones rarely act the same way on the powerful and the defeated.
openalex-w2809443489:
Laura Turnbull, Marc-Thorsten Hütt, and Andreas A. Ioannides lead this 2018 review in Applied Network Science, on connectivity in complex systems. Many fields, from neuroscience to ecology, now describe their systems through connectivity. Each field developed the idea inside its own walls. The review asks whether one shared approach could serve them all.

The authors examine four challenges any connectivity study faces. First, choosing the basic unit whose connections get mapped. Second, separating structural links from functional ones. Third, understanding behavior that emerges from the whole network. Fourth, actually measuring connectivity in practice. Insights come from six disciplines, including computational neuroscience, geomorphology, and systems biology. The team proposes a common toolbox built on network methods. Shared tools, they argue, would let fields learn from each other's hard-won lessons.
openalex-w2898372989:
Karen Böhmwald, Nicolás M. S. Gálvez, and Mariana Ríos, with Alexis M. Kalergis, reviewed brain effects of respiratory viruses in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2018. Viruses like RSV, influenza, coronavirus, and metapneumovirus fill hospitals every winter. They hit young children, the elderly, and the immunocompromised hardest. All cause bronchiolitis and pneumonia, but their reach may extend past the lungs.

The review examines neurological alterations these infections can produce. The blood-brain barrier is the brain's first defense line against invading pathogens. Its endothelial cells, astrocytes, and supporting structures decide what gets through. When respiratory viruses breach or bypass that barrier, the central nervous system suffers. The authors gather evidence on how such infections reach and affect the brain. Clinicians often miss these complications while treating the lungs. The review argues the nervous system belongs in the clinical picture.
openalex-w2952488689:
Ignácio Aguilar, Andrés Legarra, F. Cardoso, and colleagues published this short paper in Genetics Selection Evolution in 2019. It adds formal p-values to a popular method for scanning cattle genomes for genes tied to traits. Their test case is birth weight in American Angus cattle.

Single-step genomic prediction gives estimates of gene effects, but it lacked a proper testing framework. The authors derived fast algorithms that turn those estimates into p-values for single markers. On a dataset with almost two million animals in the pedigree, the computation took negligible time and showed no statistical inflation. The markers that passed strict significance cutoffs matched those explaining the most genetic variance, making p-values a general tool for finding trait loci.
openalex-w3030870789:
Mohammad Siddiqui, Rubén Morales-Menéndez, Xiaodi Huang, and Nasir Hussain wrote this review in Brain Informatics in 2020. It surveys machine learning methods for detecting epileptic seizures from brain signals. Epilepsy is a serious long-term brain disorder that these signals can reveal.

Brain signals are captured by EEG sensors on the scalp or by electrodes on the brain itself. The signals are complex, noisy, and ever-changing, and they pile up in huge volumes. Machine learning classifiers can sort them and flag seizures while also exposing useful patterns. The review's main challenge is choice: which features to extract and which classifier to trust. The authors organize recent methods by feature type and by model family.
openalex-w3040739689:
Gilberto Pastorello, Carlo Trotta, Eleonora Canfora, and colleagues published this data paper in Scientific Data in 2020. It presents FLUXNET2015, a global dataset of how ecosystems exchange carbon dioxide, water, and energy with the air. Tower instruments at each site breathe with the landscape, day and night.

The set joins records from two hundred twelve sites, totaling more than fifteen hundred site-years through 2014. Independent site teams shared their data, which was checked and processed by uniform methods so sites can be compared. The release includes filled time series, estimates of plant uptake and ecosystem respiration, and uncertainty figures. Modelers and field scientists use it to test how the living world drives climate.
openalex-w3111916089:
Ingrid Arevalo-Rodriguez, Diana Buitrago-Garcia, Daniel Simancas-Racines, and colleagues published this systematic review in PLoS ONE in 2020. It examines false-negative results from first RT-PCR tests for COVID-19. A false negative means an infected person tests negative at first, then positive on a later test.

Such misses matter: wrongly cleared patients may skip isolation and spread the virus. The team searched major medical databases and COVID-19 evidence collections for studies reporting first-test misses. Two reviewers screened and extracted the data independently, and study quality was graded with standard tools. They pooled the miss rate with a statistical model and rated the certainty of the evidence. The review gives testing programs a firmer grip on a hidden risk.
openalex-w3167454989: Samlesh Chand, Kaylash Chaudhary, Avinesh Prasad, and Vishal Chand studied why students do poorly in mathematics at two secondary schools in Fiji. Their 2021 case study appeared in Frontiers in Applied Mathematics and Statistics. It covers Ba and Tavua Secondary Schools and the causes students and teachers perceive. The preserved sample holds the opening pages on the value of mathematics, with no readable abstract or findings.
openalex-w7208818989:
Everaldo Antonio de Jesus and Graciela Celsa Zarate Miranda examine study and work inside the prisons of Brazil's Federal District, through the lens of human rights. A prison sentence takes away freedom of movement, they stress, not a person's other fundamental rights, so education and dignified work cannot be treated as favors or mere control tools. Their documentary study reads the constitution, the penal execution law, court decisions, and the district's own prison work and education plans.

The Federal District has a real structure in place: the prison administration, the education department, and a prisoner-worker support foundation act together. Offerings include adult education, sentence reduction through reading, vocational courses, and work inside and outside the walls. Limits persist, however, and the authors' critical reading asks whether provision on paper matches the reintegration the system promises.
openalex-w7212994189:
Rogerio Ribeiro Costa leads a team on self-defense classes for women as a public shield in Brazil's north. That wide land holds states where men kill wives and mates at grim rates. The team read the laws and class plans of the north states from 2021 to 2025. They set them by the counts of such kills in the same span, from a state watch post.

Acre, Amapa, and Amazonas now hold laws of their own on such classes. Past those three, the map is a patchwork. Amazonas runs the north's largest scheme, with the longest run. It also logged the north's lowest kill rate in 2025, down by a wide share since 2021. Steady, wide schemes track with the best trends, the team holds. But classes alone cannot end the harm; they are one shield in a wall that needs many.
openalex-w7213548089:
Valéria Fichman and co-authors study nutrition and pregnancy complications at a prenatal clinic in Rio de Janeiro. Their 2026 retrospective study covers forty pregnant patients, aged eighteen to thirty-nine, seen in 2019 at a national women's and children's health institute. Gestational diabetes and gestational hypertension are the outcomes of interest.

Records supplied social, body measurement, clinical, and diet data. Pre-pregnancy body mass index and a twenty-four-hour food recall were used to judge nutritional state and intake. Excess weight before pregnancy was common in the group, the authors report. Prevalence and adequacy measures were calculated for nutrients. The aim was to spot changeable risk factors early enough for prenatal nutrition care to act.
papus-tarot-des-bohemiens-1889:
Papus, born Gerard Encausse, built a full scheme of the tarot in Le Tarot des Bohemiens, out in French in 1889. The name means the tarot of the gypsies. Papus was a healer and chief of the occult in Paris. He links each card to myths of the Jews, stars, and signs of the East.

Keys, charts, and rules for spreads fill the book. French groups took it as their tarot creed at once. Its scheme still rules the French school of cards. Here is that school's source text in its own tongue. Papus led bands, wrote a shelf of books, and healed the poor. He was the face of the occult in Paris in his prime years.
patrick-heraclitus-fragments-1889:
Heraclitus of Ephesus, who lived around 500 BCE, wrote one book of dense, riddle-like sayings, and the book itself is lost. G. T. W. Patrick translated the surviving fragments into English in 1889, working from Bywater's Greek text. His edition was the first to give English readers Heraclitus on his own, apart from larger works.

Patrick opens with a long essay on the man, his age, and the schools that quoted him. The fragments follow, with fire as the core stuff of the world, all things in flux, and strife named as the father of all. Short as they are, these sayings shaped Greek thought for good.
plos-pbio-0020289:
Tammie Bishop, Kah Weng Lau, Andrew C. R. Epstein, and their team used the worm C. elegans to study a tumor suppressor in PLOS Biology in 2004. In humans, loss of the VHL gene causes kidney tumors and blood vessel growth run wild. The worm has its own version of the gene.

By breaking worm genes one by one, the team found which pathways the worm's VHL controls. Worms are far simpler than people, so each link stands out clearly. Several links matched the human picture, which validates the worm as a test system. Others were new leads. The study shows how a tiny animal can sort the wiring of a human cancer gene.
plos-pone-0000089:
Félix Gutierrez, Sergio Padilla, Mar Masiá, and a large team followed HIV patients over the long term in PLOS ONE in 2006. Modern antiretroviral therapy can hold the virus at undetectable levels for years. The team asked how patients who kept that control actually fared in health over time.

Sustained control turned into real gains: fewer AIDS events and better survival than in earlier eras of care. Long follow-up is what proves a therapy's worth beyond lab numbers. Their report captures the moment HIV care shifted from crisis control to chronic disease management. It also sets a standard: new regimens must match this durable success, not just short term viral drops.
plos-pone-0000189:
Aartjan J. W. te Velthuis, Tadamoto Isogai, Lieke Gerrits, and colleagues published this protein evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. The PDZ/LIM family is a set of proteins that organize signaling and the cell skeleton, found across animals. The authors trace the family's molecular evolution and identify a new conserved protein motif within it.

A motif kept across species usually marks a part a protein cannot do without. Finding a new one in a well-studied family opens fresh questions about what these proteins do. The paper gives the family a clearer family tree and a new feature for other researchers to test.
plos-pone-0000289:
Jill M. Ferdinands, David M. Mannino, Marta L. Gwinn, and colleagues published this respiratory study in PLOS ONE in 2007. It draws on the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study, a large US cohort. The authors examine the ADRB2 gene's Arg16Gly variant, in the beta-2 adrenergic receptor, alongside beta-agonist inhaler use, lung function, and mortality.

Earlier evidence hinted that one genotype might make asthma drugs harmful for some patients. The authors test that worry in a big population sample with long follow-up. Their results help doctors judge whether this common gene variant should change how inhalers are prescribed.
plos-pone-0000389:
Vincent Guiyedi and colleagues studied severe malaria in Gabonese children, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. Cerebral malaria, where the disease attacks the brain, is among its deadliest forms. The team looked at whether the children's immune reactions against alpha spectrin, a protein from their own non-red blood cells, tracked with this severe form.

Self-reactivity means the immune system attacks the body's own proteins, not just the parasite. Finding that such reactions correlate with cerebral malaria suggests the damage is partly self-inflicted by the immune response. That insight could guide efforts to predict which children are at risk of the worst outcomes and to treat the harmful response itself.
plos-pone-0000489:
Rangarajan Sampath and colleagues built a mass spectrometry system to watch flu viruses change worldwide, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their method performs global surveillance of emerging influenza virus genotypes. It identifies viral strains by the masses of their genetic pieces. That is far faster than slow full sequencing.

Speed is the point: knowing which flu strains are emerging, and where, guides vaccine selection each year. Mass spectrometry can process many samples quickly and flag unusual genotypes for closer study. The paper describes an early high-throughput surveillance platform, built in an era of heightened concern about a possible influenza pandemic.
plos-pone-0000589:
Ilja Mikenberg and colleagues tracked how a master inflammation switch reaches its workplace, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. NF-κB is a transcription factor that turns on immune and stress genes; it must travel from the cell body into the nucleus to work. In hippocampal neurons, the team showed it is transported via the cytoplasmic dynein/dynactin motor complex, the cell's cargo-hauling machinery.

Neurons are long, so how a signal travels from a distant synapse to the nucleus is a real logistics problem. Pinning NF-κB's ride on the dynein motor explains a puzzle. It shows how synaptic events can switch genes on hours later. That step matters in forming lasting memories and in brain inflammation alike.
plos-pone-0000689:
Masatoshi Suzuki, Jacalyn McHugh, Craig Tork and colleagues tested a cell therapy in a rat model of familial ALS for PLOS ONE in 2007. ALS is a fatal, progressive disease where large motor neurons in brain and spinal cord die. Patients lose muscle control and face eventual paralysis. Growth factors such as GDNF can support struggling neurons.

The team used human neural progenitor cells engineered to secrete GDNF. Their title reports a split outcome: the cells protected dying motor neurons, but not the neurons' projections to muscle. Saving the cell body without saving its connection limits the benefit. That distinction tells therapy designers what still needs fixing.
plos-pone-0000789:
Se-Jin Lee reported quadrupling muscle mass in mice by blocking growth-limiting signals, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Myostatin is a member of the TGF-beta family that normally acts to limit skeletal muscle growth. Mice engineered to lack myostatin activity carry about twice the muscle mass throughout the body. Similar effects appear in cattle, sheep, and dogs with natural myostatin mutations.

Doubling was not the ceiling. By targeting TGF-beta signaling pathways more broadly, Lee pushed muscle mass toward four times normal. The pathway matters for muscle-wasting diseases, livestock breeding, and basic questions about how body size is set. Bigger is not automatically healthier, which is why the mechanism matters.
plos-pone-0000889:
Johannes Muller and Linda Tsuji found signs of advanced hearing in early land reptiles, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. A working middle ear that matches sound pressure between air and the inner ear is a mark of sharp hearing in land vertebrates. When that system first appeared was an open question in the story of amniotes, the group that includes reptiles, birds and mammals.

The authors read the fossil evidence for an impedance matching ear in Paleozoic reptiles, from long before mammals existed. Their case pushes refined hearing far back in time. It suggests the first land vertebrates were sensing their world in more detail than often assumed.
plos-pone-0000989:
Catriona Paul, Joanne Povey, Nicola Lawrence and colleagues deleted sperm protecting genes in mice and measured the fallout, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Infertility touches about twenty percent of couples in Europe, and in half the cases the cause lies with the man. Damaged DNA in male germ cells is poorly understood, though it may raise miscarriage risk.

Mouse models let the team remove genes thought to guard germ cell DNA integrity. They then counted DNA breaks and germ cell loss. The deletions did not all act alike; effects differed by gene. That difference itself guides which guards matter most for fertility.
plos-pone-0001089:
Rossarin Suwanarusk and co-authors profiled chloroquine resistance in the other malaria parasite, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Plasmodium vivax causes the second major form of human malaria. Drug treatment failure for vivax had reached high levels in eastern Indonesia, yet its resistance had not been profiled in the lab or tied to gene markers.

Using a modified test of the parasite's blood stage, the team measured resistance directly and checked for links to gene variants. Vivax hides in the liver and relapses, so failing blood treatment compounds the problem. Defined markers would let health officials map resistance without slow culture work.
plos-pone-0001189:
Lymphatic filariasis, a disfiguring disease caused by the parasitic worm Brugia malayi, threatens more than 1.5 billion people. Sanjay Kumar and colleagues mined the worm's genome for drug targets in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The completed draft sequence of the parasite's genome made a genome-wide search possible.

The authors report the first genome-wide application of a rational drug target selection method to a metazoan pathogen. They focused on predicted essential genes, genes the worm likely cannot live without. A shortlist like this gives drug developers concrete starting points against a neglected disease.
plos-pone-0001289:
A high share of male infertility has no known cause. Sahar Houshdaran and colleagues looked for epigenetic defects in the sperm of such men, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Abnormal epigenetic programming of the germline, the chemical marks that organize DNA without changing its code, had been proposed as a mechanism compromising sperm production.

The authors report widespread epigenetic abnormalities in abnormal human sperm, suggesting a broad DNA methylation erasure defect. Erasure is the step that wipes old marks in the germline so new ones can be written. A failure there could underlie many unexplained cases at once.
plos-pone-0001389:
Manjula Pandey, Smita Patel, and Abram Gabriel published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on an enzyme from a yeast element that can copy itself. Enzymes that build DNA use a shared way to add each new unit. The enzyme here works in reverse, building DNA from an RNA guide. The team traced one step of that work in fine detail.

The authors map the path by which the enzyme can also run the build step in reverse. That reverse step can undo gains and shape how the element spreads. Fine maps like this help explain how jumping genes move and change genomes. They also add to the base facts on how all such enzymes work.
plos-pone-0001489:
Irina Tcherepanova and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE methods paper on a tailored HIV therapy. The therapy uses a patient's own immune guide cells loaded with their own virus. Past trials of that plan needed large amounts of live virus, which is hard to get. The team built a way to copy HIV genes in bulk instead.

Their method copies many HIV genes at once from a patient's virus. Those copies can load the guide cells without vast virus stocks. That makes the tailored plan more feasible for clinics. It is a step toward immune care built for each patient's own virus strain.
plos-pone-0001589:
Birger Scholz and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on the Parkinson's drug L-dopa in monkeys. The drug can cause wild, unwanted moves after long use. That harm grows with each dose, a process called sensitization. The team used the standard monkey model to read protein shifts in a key brain zone.

They found the protein pattern after the first dose much like that after long use. In other words, the first dose already sets the long term state. That shifts the search for the harm's roots to the very start of care. It may open a window to block the harm before it builds.
plos-pone-0001689:
Kaspar Delhey and Anne Peters measured how variable bird colors are in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. A key idea in evolution says ornaments used in sexual selection stay highly variable. Bright plumage is one example, and its quality depends on the bearer's condition. Only a bird in good shape can afford a top-grade signal, so condition-dependent models predict signaling traits should vary more than ordinary traits.

The authors quantified color variation across traits and species to test that prediction. The full text gives the color measurements, the comparison between signaling and non-signaling traits, and how strong the difference was. A careful test matters because the prediction is widely assumed in sexual selection theory but had rarely been measured across many birds at once.
plos-pone-0001789:
Tetsuro Tamaki, Akira Akatsuka, Yoshinori Okada, and their co-authors tested muscle-derived stem cells for heart repair in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Cellular cardiomyoplasty, transplanting cells to repair heart attack damage, had been tried with various cell types. None had shown complete differentiation into heart muscle cells, though functional benefits were reported.

The team used skeletal muscle-derived multi-myogenic stem cells, which can form several muscle types, and transplanted them into infarcted myocardium.
