Wei Li and colleagues film flat crystals melt through a twin wetting path in a 2026 study. Flat melting has fueled decades of debate, since one grand theory has bulk crystals melt in two smooth steps with a sixfold phase between. Their light-driven bead solids let each grain be tracked as heat rose.

A near-hexatic skin formed between the solid core and an outer near-liquid skin. Both skins thickened into the bulk with a power-law surge as melt neared. The hexatic skin pushed in first, which split melt into two surface-led steps. Free edges spat flaw pairs into the solid without pause, which drove the skins inward. The authors say surface-led melt rewrites the bulk-only tale for flat matter.
pmc-13444489:
Tausif Ahmed Siddiqui and colleagues report brain spread of an EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma after a stem cell transplant in a 2026 case paper. The patient was a 29-year-old man with chronic active EBV and past NK/T-cell lymphoma, treated with donor stem cells. A fresh seizure and a ring-shaped brain lump brought him back.

The lump mimicked cerebral toxoplasmosis on scans, a common trap in weak immunity, so germ drugs came first and the true call lagged. Growth forced a needle biopsy, which showed EBV-positive T-cell lymphoma with a STAT3 fault, p.Y640F, that switches the gene on. That hot profile likely fed the fast course. The authors urge early tissue checks when brain lumps in such patients shrug off germ care.
pmc-13445189:
Sarah D. Lichenstein and colleagues link the full mix of a young person's surroundings, called the exposome, to brain wiring and thinking skills, in a 2026 study. The data come from a large United States study of brain growth in children. The team asked whether brain links might form one path by which home and neighborhood shape the mind.

Using brain scans taken at rest and during three tasks, learning methods found wiring patterns tied to exposome scores in more than six thousand early teens. Those patterns held up across study sites. The shared wiring also tracked scores for general thinking, planning skills, and learning and memory, which supports a brain path between surroundings and school-age skills.
pmc-13445489:
Dibya Prabha and colleagues report a woman whose fading sight in both eyes proved to be the first sign of her leukemia turning aggressive, published in 2026. She had chronic lymphocytic leukemia in remission when painless blur set in. Eye scans showed pale patches under the retina in both eyes, a pattern that fits lymphoma inside the eye.

Drug shots into the eye cleared the patches at first, and sight returned. A year later one eye relapsed, and biopsy of eye tissue showed large B-cell lymphoma, the change known as Richter transformation. Body scans found swollen glands, yet gland biopsies showed no spread. The case urges fast biopsy and full staging when eye lymphoma appears in such patients.
pmc-13445789:
Ramirez and team asked how best to process dog urine for microbiome profiling. Urine's very low bacterial content makes the thickening method and sample volume key choices. Using pooled urine from 15 healthy dogs split into five batches, they weighed vacuum filtration against centrifugation pelleting. Volumes ran from 1 to 50 milliliters, in pairs.

Fifty aliquots were run, although three large-volume samples of 30 milliliters or more clogged their filters and could not be finished. Sequence depth, DNA yield, contaminant load, and diversity were broadly similar across volumes tested. Filtered samples carried a higher share of contaminant reads. Community composition also shifted slightly by method. But the batch itself dwarfed both effects, accounting for 65 percent of variation versus 3 percent for method. The authors advise pelleting and mid-range volumes of 1 to 10 milliliters.
pmc-13446189:
Paola Naal-Chan and colleagues report two Mexican teenagers with Sanfilippo syndrome, a rare storage disease that erodes the mind, in a 2026 case series. The disease stems from missing enzymes that break down a sugar chain, so waste piles up in cells. It is little diagnosed in Latin America, and no cases of these two subtypes had been confirmed in Mexico.

Both fifteen-year-olds were seen at a genetics center in Yucatán after steady loss of skills. Whole-exome gene reading found the cause in each: one boy carried two copies of a known faulty gene for type C, while the girl carried two apparently new faults for type A. Her history held regression from age four and hard seizures. The pair marks the first confirmed cases of their subtypes in the land.
pmc-13446289:
Stephen Kinsey-Trotman and colleagues trace twenty years of male breast cancer care in Australia and New Zealand through a surgical audit, in a 2026 registry study. Female care changed much in that span, yet male care, for a rare group, may have stood still. Records covered diagnoses from 2003 to 2022, split into two decades for contrast.

The audit held more than a quarter million patients, of whom 1,542 were men. Male care barely moved across the decades, save one change: sentinel node biopsy, a gentler armpit check, climbed from under half to two thirds of cases. Female care shifted in near every field in the same span. The authors read the gap as a call for male-specific guidance, so men gain from the same steady refinement.
pmc-13446889:
Julia G. Lebovitz and Sohee Park study how people with strong depersonalization, a felt split from self and world, register emotions in the body, in a 2026 survey study. The state often travels with trouble naming feelings, called alexithymia. The team set thirty-three adults with high scores beside sixty-six with low scores from the general population.

On a body map task, the high group marked where each feeling lives in the body. Their maps ran more diffuse and less pinpointed for high-arousal feelings, rather than simply blank. Higher depersonalization also went with higher alexithymia scores. The authors argue the pattern is not plain numbing: some strong states may land harder and wider in the body, a nuance for how the disorder is framed.
pmc-13447289:
Darong Lu and colleagues build a prediction model for pneumonia after bleeding stroke in a 2026 study. Lung infection is a serious and common complication that worsens recovery. Spotting high-risk patients on admission could shift care from reacting to preventing, if a stable and explainable model can be built from routine data.

Records for eight hundred twenty-two patients admitted between 2019 and 2024 supplied fifty-seven candidate measures, narrowed to fourteen by a shrinkage method. Five learning algorithms were trained and compared on held-out cases, with plain logistic regression performing best. Explanation scores ranked leg muscle strength, cholesterol measures, white cell count and alertness among the strongest signals. The authors offer the model as a quantitative aid for sorting patients and targeting prevention early.
pmc-13447789:
Lynn Addington argues that age subgroups matter in partner homicide against older women in a 2026 brief research note. Women past fifty form a fast-growing population group, yet studies often lump everyone over fifty into one bucket. That habit can hide sharp differences between women in their fifties and women in their eighties, including how killings unfold.

National violent death records were explored with simple descriptive statistics split by age band. Killings of women in their fifties and sixties more often involved prior partner violence. Killings past age seventy more often involved a partner who was also a caregiver, or ended as homicide followed by suicide. Firearms featured in most cases at every age, with their share rising as age rose. Age-aware risk research is the note's central plea.
pmc-13448489:
Zhang and colleagues present in 2026, as abstract BSLD-08, a hunt for what lets lung and breast cancer cells colonize the leptomeninges. The leptomeninges are the fluid-filled membranes around the brain and spinal cord. Tissue from this niche is scarce, so the team profiled cell-free RNA in spinal fluid instead.

Sequencing spinal fluid from fifteen lung and fifteen breast leptomeningeal patients against seven non-cancer controls found the protein MAL2 consistently and significantly raised in both cancer groups. Patients with high MAL2 survived a median of about two months against about eight and a half in the low group, though the difference was not statistically significant. Single-cell and spatial analyses pinned MAL2 to the tumor cells themselves, not surrounding tissue, and brain-tropic cell lines carried enriched levels. The authors propose MAL2 as both a prognostic marker and a possible drug target.
pmc-13449789:
Maren Hülsemann and a large Berlin team audit in 2026 how well the flood of COVID-19 studies using human organ models reported their methods. The pandemic pushed laboratories to repurpose organoids and other human models of varying complexity against the new virus, creating a natural experiment in research practice. The systematic review covered 558 studies, split into pandemic and post-pandemic periods, and judged how each investigated host factors, viral replication, and immune responses.

Reporting weaknesses ran deep: outcome measures varied so much that studies could barely be compared, model traits and procedures went undocumented, and quality fluctuated widely. Post-pandemic papers improved only partly. The authors link the gaps to harder bias assessment and shakier evidence synthesis, exactly when pooled answers mattered most. Their prescription is community-driven reporting standards and fuller methodological transparency before the next pandemic tests the same models.
pmc-13449989:
Serna and colleagues report a 2026 study of gut bacteria inside tumors and survival in bowel cancer that can be removed by surgery. Nine centers enrolled stage I to III patients, and a central lab tested tumors for Fusobacterium. The team tracked recurrence and survival for about four years.

About one in five of 740 patients had Fusobacterium-positive tumors, which were more often right-sided, high-grade, and invasive, with less immune cell entry. Positive patients relapsed sooner, with recurrence risk near double that of negative patients even after other factors were weighed. Added chemotherapy after surgery clearly helped bacteria-negative patients but showed no clear gain in positive ones.
pmc-13450189:
Xiaoyan Zhang and co-authors characterize in 2026 Campylobacter bacteria collected from chicken farms and shop-bought poultry across ten regions of Jiangsu Province, China. The genus is a leading cause of foodborne diarrheal disease, and chicken meat is its main route to people. The team typed 128 isolates genetically, tested them against ten antibiotics, cataloged their resistance and virulence genes, and checked how well some strains form biofilms.

Genetic types sprawled widely, including nine sequence types never recorded before. Nearly half the isolates, 46.6 percent, resisted multiple drugs, and the species split sharply: Campylobacter coli hit 75.4 percent multidrug resistance against only 17.5 percent in Campylobacter jejuni. The commonest resistance gene rode in a pump variant carried mainly by jejuni. Seven jejuni isolates carried wlaN, a gene linked to the paralyzing Guillain-Barré syndrome, a finding the authors flag for surveillance.
pmc-13451589:
Arko Dhar and co-authors link in 2026 a heart health score to vessel function in the Jackson Heart Study, a large Black adult cohort. The score, Life's Essential 8, grades habits and health factors from diet to blood pressure. Scores came from early study visits, while vessel tests ran years later in over 2,000 members.

Higher scores went with slower pulse waves in stiff main arteries, lower center pressure, and better flow surge in the arm after a squeeze test. Blood sugar and blood pressure grades drove most of the links. The authors read the pattern as proof that a healthy daily life leaves a mark on vessel walls, and they call for work on whether raising scores repairs vessels.
pmc-13451789:
Aarno Hatsala and co-authors release in 2026 a data set from lab tests on a layered timber floor built with glued wood trusses. The floor was built step by step, adding board skins, ceiling panels, a concrete cap, and light walls. Each stage was loaded and shaken so the effect of each layer could be read on its own.

Weight tanks drove bend tests, read by dial gauges, while heel drops set off shakes caught by motion sensors at many spots. Files hold raw and cleaned measures, sensor maps, and diagrams for free reuse. The team offers the data for checks of floor comfort rules, design guides, and new timber floor studies.
pmc-13452089:
Hannah Rowe and Frank Guenther review in 2026 a brain model of speech control called DIVA and what it says about speech disorders. The model maps how the brain turns word plans into mouth moves through three loops: a preset move plan, hearing feedback, and touch feedback. Each loop is tied to named brain zones and paths.

That map lets the team read disorders such as stuttering as faults in set loops, rather than as vague breakdowns. The review walks the model's build, its uses across speech ills, and how it could steer care and speech tech. Rival models are set beside it so readers can judge where DIVA fits in the field.
pmc-13452189:
Reshmi Talwar and a large team report in 2026 on a joint eye clinic set inside a cancer center for transplant patients at risk of an eye attack by donor cells. The eye form of graft-versus-host disease hits about half of stem cell transplant patients, yet watch rules are vague. The Maryland clinic opened in 2021, and the team set 76 later patients against 107 earlier ones.

Eye disease struck about a fifth of the earlier group and near an eighth of the later group within two years of transplant. Adjusted odds ran lower after the clinic opened, though the gap fell short of firm proof. First-visit eye treatments were also checked for links. The authors back built-in eye watch as part of transplant care.
pmc-13453489:
Kor and colleagues used gene editing in 2026 to change how rice builds starch in its grains. They disabled a gene called OsSBEIIb, which helps branch starch chains, in the widely grown IR64 variety.  The team then measured starch shape, cooking traits, protein, and small chemicals in the grain.

The edited rice had fewer short starch chains and more long chains, plus much more resistant starch, which resists digestion. Its predicted glycaemic index, a score for how fast food raises blood sugar, fell from 80 to 57 in the edited lines. Protein content rose by up to a tenth, with more of several essential amino acids. The trade-offs were chalkier grains and lighter seeds. The authors see these lines as a base for healthier rice, once grain quality improves.
pmc-13453589:
Ram and Damodaran review a class of small RNA molecules in cancer and argue that where and when they act matters as much as which ones are present. These molecules, called oncomiRNAs, tune gene activity after a gene is copied, and they can push tumors to grow or hold them back. The 2026 review stresses that most past work ground up whole tumor samples, which hides how these molecules vary across regions, spread sites, and stages of disease.

New tools such as spatial gene mapping, single cell profiling, and repeat blood tests now reveal that variation. The review links shifting oncomiRNA patterns to drug resistance, escape from the immune system, and mixed patient outcomes. The authors urge studies that sample many tumor regions over time, feed the data into shared models, and design trials that adapt treatment to each patient's changing pattern.
pmc-13453789:
Ge Li and Wenshi Wei test a nutrition score as a death risk signal in critically ill stroke patients and build a machine learning model around it. The score, called CONUT, blends albumin, cholesterol, and a white cell count to grade nourishment. Their 2026 study draws 1,103 patients from a large intensive care database and checks the result in 659 patients at a Chinese hospital.

Each one point rise in the score came with a 14.1 percent rise in 30 day death risk and a 15.9 percent rise over a year. Survival curves sank step by step as nourishment grades worsened. Of six learning methods, a model called CatBoost sorted risk best, holding up in the outside hospital check. The authors present the simple score plus model as an early warning pair for stroke units.
pmc-13454389:
Thibault Schutz, Nezha Badi, and Filip E. Du Prez introduce, in 2026, molecular tags that let makers trace plastic goods through production and recycling. The tags are short chains built from a four-letter chemical alphabet, mixed into plastic at less than 0.05 percent by weight. Each chain spells a code that marks the batch or product.

Light-based checks give a first read of the tag, and a scripted mass spectrometry routine confirms the full sequence. The team compared two backbone designs to find which survives heat better. Tags stayed intact inside both soft plastics and hard resins, enduring extrusion at up to 270 degrees and full curing steps. The authors present the system as a practical tool against fakes and for sorting plastics by origin.
pmc-13454589:
William Z. Zhang leads a large team studying, in 2026, an iron-storage protein that worsens severe lung failure. In acute respiratory distress syndrome, blood levels of ferritin, a protein that stores iron, track with worse outcomes. The team found both ferritin parts enriched in the blood and lung macrophages of patients, and matched the pattern in mice with oxygen-driven lung injury.

Deleting the heavy-chain part of ferritin only in immune cells softened the lung damage. Macrophages showed less ferroptosis, an iron-linked form of cell death, and the airways released less free iron. Lung wash fluid rich in the light-chain form protected other mice when transplanted into them. A drug that blocks ferroptosis before injury, by contrast, did nothing. The authors name macrophage ferritin handling as a lever for future lung therapies.
pmc-13454989:
Fu and colleagues tested in 2026 crocin I, a pigment from saffron, for its power to slow cell ageing in human lung fibroblasts. These WI-38 cells were aged two ways: by long culturing until they stopped dividing, and by a chemical that forces early ageing. The team measured growth, ageing stains, reactive oxygen, gene activity, and key proteins across treated and untreated cells.

Fu found crocin I boosted cell growth at moderate doses and cut the share of cells showing the classic ageing stain in both models. Harmful reactive oxygen levels also fell. Gene readouts pointed to energy and sugar pathways, and docking plus protein tests singled out PKM2, a sugar-burning enzyme, as a likely target. The compound raised the protective protein SIRT1 while trimming ageing drivers p53 and p21 and easing lactate build-up, a pattern the authors link to better cell energy balance.
pmc-13457389: Venous malformations of the knee in children — success and influencing factors of percutaneous sclerotherapy. Zhuang Liu, Xin Zhang, Liang Wang, and others sclerose the malformations. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is child blood vessel. It scleroses children's knee veins. success, studied. Knee, child.
pmc-13457589:
Özlem Sağıroğlu and Muzaffer Arıkan built a catalog of microbe made peptides that appear able to fight both bacteria and cancer cells. Some peptides, short protein chains that living things use as natural defenses, kill germs and also attack cancer cells. Microbial sources had been little explored for this dual talent. In their 2026 study, the pair ran five prediction programs over public collections of short microbial gene fragments. Three programs screened for cancer fighting activity and two for germ killing activity. They kept only peptides all tools agreed on and that looked safe.

The screen covered more than 124 million peptides from microbial catalogs. It surfaced 40,251 safe peptides predicted to carry both activities. The team organized them into a searchable public resource called the Dual Activity Microbial Peptides Catalog. Drug researchers gain a ready shortlist for lab testing against resistant infections and tumors.
pmc-13457789:
Kong and colleagues compared four commercial anti-adhesion products after open thyroid surgery in a 2026 prospective study at one hospital. Adhesions, internal scar bands, can cause neck tightness and swallowing trouble after this surgery. Two hundred patients received one of four barrier products, and 180 finished follow-up at two and twelve weeks.

Adhesion symptom scores rose at two weeks and improved by twelve weeks in every group. No significant differences appeared between products at either visit. Scar scale scores followed the same pattern, apart from a brief higher pigmentation score in one group at two weeks that did not last. Complication rates were low and alike across groups. The authors conclude the four products work about equally in the short term, with none clearly superior.
pmc-13458389:
Paasche and colleagues found in 2026 a second job for a gene switch protein: it grips the cell's split frame and times the cell's exit from the split's mid stage. The protein, ZNF512B, was known to hush genes in stem cells. Split frames are the cord sets that pull twin gene packs apart. The team tracked the protein in split cells, cut it out, and dosed it high. A mid span with stacked repeats proved to be its frame grip.

Too much of the protein froze cells mid split, a stall that killed them. Too little sped stem cell growth, a rush with a cost. The rushed cells lost their knack to turn into ripe kinds. Growth genes ran hot in the drained cells. The team casts the protein as a brake and gate for sound splits. Both dose ways break stem cell fate.
pmc-13458489: Drug-induced liver injury comes in six idiosyncratic flavors — and each has its own immune fingerprint. Rolf Teschke studies them alone. The 2026 Europe PMC paper is hepatology. Using RUCAM-ascertained cases with refined classification, it details the immunology and autoimmunity specifics of each type, clarifying how immune workings differ across them.
pmc-13459089:
Alexander Krawzow and co-authors ask which hormone measurement in the overnight oral metyrapone test best detects adrenal insufficiency. This test checks the pituitary-adrenal axis by blocking cortisol production and watching the response. Their 2026 study re-examines whether three other hormones can match the standard marker, 11-deoxycortisol.

Among 190 study participants who took the test, 67 had adrenal insufficiency and 123 did not. The standard marker performed best, with sensitivity of 83 percent and specificity above 90 percent at its chosen cutoff. The alternatives, 17-hydroxyprogesterone, androstenedione, and corticotropin, all performed worse, though their surges tracked the standard marker. Other pituitary problems also carried information: prolactin deficiency was highly specific for adrenal insufficiency. The authors keep 11-deoxycortisol as first choice while noting possible bias from earlier studies.
pmc-13459789:
Ethan Humm and co-authors report in 2026 the complete genomes of two subspecies of Syntrophomonas wolfei. These bacteria gain energy by breaking down fatty acids, but only when a partner microbe consumes the hydrogen they release. One subspecies came from a sewage digester and handles fatty acids up to eighteen carbons long. The other came from rice field mud and grows on shorter and branched fatty acids.

Both are rod-shaped, motile bacteria among the few known strains that thrive under such tight energy limits. Their genome inventories reveal the metabolic machinery behind this partnership lifestyle. For researchers of anaerobic digestion and microbial cooperation, complete sequences from both subspecies give a firm reference. That reference helps them compare how related strains divide labor with different partners.
pmc-13461489:
Alholimie and co-authors mapped a 2026 scoping review of oral health promotion in adults with type 2 diabetes, who face higher risks of gum disease, cavities, and dry mouth. Five databases were searched for English peer reviewed studies from 2015 to 2025. The review charted patient awareness, provider practice, and barriers to care.

Of 412 records, only nine studies met the criteria Alholimie set, showing how thin the evidence base remains. Three themes emerged: hygiene habits and blood sugar control, patient knowledge of the diabetes and mouth link, and provider awareness with teamwork between professions. Many patients did not know their mouths were at extra risk, and dental guidance was delivered inconsistently. Where guidance was given, hygiene behaviour and outcomes improved noticeably.
pmc-13462389:
Díaz-Guerra and colleagues built a 2026 model of executive function in Cuban university students, based on students' own ratings. Executive functions are the mental skills for planning, watching, and steering goal directed behaviour, and they support school success. Lab tasks rule older models, so self-report adds a real life view.

The sample held 1,233 students with a mean age of twenty years, who filled in a Cuban version of an executive function questionnaire. A decision tree picked out the key factors, and a second modelling step confirmed how the parts relate. Díaz-Guerra found four stacked levels, from metacognitive evaluation at the top through emotion control and behaviour control and attention, down to goal directed action. Fit scores for the final model were good by standard cut-offs.
pmc-13462889:
Warachya Arjhan and colleagues compare, in a 2026 case series, three support materials used in implant-based breast reconstruction after mastectomy at one Bangkok hospital. The options were a skin-derived matrix, no matrix, and a titanium-coated mesh called TiLOOP. Thirty-six patients treated by one surgeon between 2018 and 2022 were grouped by material, with follow-up averaging over two years. Complications such as implant loss, hardening scar shells, skin death, and infection were the outcomes.

 Infections and hardening each struck a fifth of the matrix group, with one case of skin death. The no-matrix group saw two implant removals, two hardenings, two local cancer returns, and one distant spread. The mesh group had two hardenings, both in irradiated patients, one reaching the severest grade. Groups were small and care was not random, so the authors present the series as a descriptive comparison, not crowning a winner.
pmc-13463889:
Huihui Li and eight co-authors map three phage defense systems packed together in a dangerous E. coli strain. The strain, a Shiga toxin producer called EDL933, shrugs off many bacteria-eating viruses known as phages. All three systems, Zorya II, Druantia III, and ARMADA II, sit on one island of its genome.

Deleting each system in turn showed Druantia III and ARMADA II doing most of the guard work across a wide phage range. Pairing those two gave stronger joint defense than either alone. Zorya II covered a narrower slice, adding cover against one virus order. The same trio appears in 426 related strains, so the findings matter for any future phage therapy against this germ.
pmc-13464989:
Ji and colleagues studied in 2026 a puzzling pattern after treatment for gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, a pregnancy-related tumor: the hormone hCG stays mildly raised during follow-up. This can mean the disease is returning, or it can settle on its own. At one centre, the team followed 46 such patients and tracked who later needed retreatment against who stayed treatment-free.

Ji found most patients did eventually relapse and receive more anti-tumor treatment, while some stayed free of it for months or years. Patients whose hCG held at or below a set low level during early watching had a higher chance of staying treatment-free over the next year. Those whose levels rose above that line fared worse. Every retreated patient later reached very low hCG again. The authors say the early hormone course helps sort who needs treatment from who can be watched.
pmc-13465189:
Elisabetta Lacolla and four co-authors review cyclodextrin-grafted polysaccharides, hybrid materials joining sugar rings onto natural polymer chains. Cyclodextrins are cup-shaped sugars that trap greasy molecules in their hollow core, lifting them into water. Grafting pins those cups onto sturdy, body-friendly backbones for longer duty.

Drug makers use the hybrids to carry hard-to-dissolve medicines, raising their uptake and steadiness. In water treatment the same traps soak up dyes, pesticides, and heavy metals with strong pull. Build methods range from chemical linking to gentler assembly routes, each with trade-offs in load and release. The review ties lab chemistry to clinic and field use, arguing the hybrids fit a greener materials future.
pmc-13465389:
Safiye Kübra Çetindağ Karatlı and four co-authors link the HALP score, a blood index joining hemoglobin, albumin, lymphocyte, and platelet counts, to sugar control in older home-care patients. The study covered 201 people aged sixty-five and up with type 2 diabetes, all screened to exclude malnutrition. Poor control meant a hemoglobin A1c at or above eight percent.

A quarter of patients crossed that poor-control line, at a median age of eighty-three. High HALP scores cut the odds of poor control by roughly seventy percent, even after other factors entered the model. Repeated checks with age, sex, function, and dementia held the link steady. Alone, though, the score sorted patients only weakly to modestly, so the authors advise reading it beside full clinical judgment.
pmc-13465489:
Zhang and colleagues in China built in 2026 a home made one step filter tube. It pulls three classes of farm taint from eggs in a single pass, for a fine mass tool to read. Hens pick up vet drugs, crop sprays, and mold toxins from feed, and all three can lodge in eggs. Old lab ways treat each class apart, at a slow grind. The team's tube blends trap stuff tuned by math, so sixty taints clear the egg's fat and protein in one go.

All sixty taints read true across their ranges, with find floors as low as a tenth of a part per billion in egg mass. Spiked eggs gave back seven to twelve tenths of each taint, with tight spread. For three in five taints, the egg base barely bent the read. The authors pitch the tube for fast food safety screens.
pmc-13465589:
Morisaki and Morisaki wrote a 2026 review on a newer kind of cancer vaccine. Their focus is neoantigens, proteins that appear only on tumor cells after mutations. Early vaccines aimed at killer T cells, the immune cells that attack tumors directly. The authors argue that helper T cells deserve equal billing in vaccine design.

The review shows how helper cells keep killer cells working over time. Helpers support immune memory and help stop killer cells from wearing out early. Vaccines built only for killer cells have shown weak results in patients so far. Adding helper targets may explain why some vaccines work better than others. The authors map recent trials and set out design rules for future personalized vaccines.
pmc-13465789:
Maksimovic and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how economic thinking explains decisions in dementia care and similar life-limiting illness. Such decisions are shared among patients, family carers, and professionals, and they drive much of the cost. The search spanned four databases plus targeted economics sources. From 9,854 studies, 62 were kept for close reading.

Six economic concepts organized the evidence. They are the principal-agent problem, uncertainty, and asymmetric information. The empathy gap and hyperbolic discounting follow, and the non-linear value of time completes the set. Together they help explain familiar patterns, like high spending at the end of life. They also explain why advance care planning works unevenly. Global dementia costs were estimated above 1.3 trillion dollars, half of it unpaid family care time. The authors call for dynamic three-way communication as the practical fix.
pmc-13465889:
Akın Özdemir, Mehmet Altay Sevimay, and Ercan Karakaş ran matching surveys of dental implant patients and their dentists to see where expectations line up and where they part, in a 2026 study. Two hundred fifty patients and two hundred dentists answered parallel sixteen-item questionnaires. Items covered hopes for the final result and worries about the surgery itself, each rated on a five-point scale.

The two groups differed clearly on thirteen of the sixteen items. Total scores, though, came out nearly equal because gaps in opposite directions cancelled each other. The surgical worry section held several of the sharpest mismatches. For clinics, the lesson is practical: asking about single topics beats trusting an overall score that hides real gaps in understanding.
pmc-13466289: Hector Guadalajara and colleagues issued a correction in 2026 to their rectal cancer study from the FOREST project. The notice is a correction only. It adds missing affiliation lines for three of the authors. The added lines name doctoral programs in Madrid, at the Autonomous University of Madrid in Spain. No data, methods, or findings change. The authors state that the study's conclusions stand as before. The journal's academic editor approved the fix, and the original article was updated to match.
pmc-13466689:
Eui-Jong Kwon, Bong-Woo Lee, and Ji Hyeon Ju map the cytokine networks that drive Sjögren's disease and differ between its many faces, in a 2026 narrative review. The autoimmune condition dries the eyes and mouth as immune cells invade glands, yet many patients also suffer effects far beyond the glands. Signaling proteins from both the innate and adaptive arms sustain that attack.

In glands, interferon signals and helper T cell cytokines keep inflammation alive and even build lymphoid clusters. Across the body, the BAFF and APRIL signals plus interferon signatures drive antibody production. Sorting patients by which network dominates could guide targeted therapy, the direction the authors favor.
pmc-13466789:
Hatice Duman and colleagues produce a gut bacterium's sugar-cutting enzyme and test how broadly it can strip complex sugars from proteins, in a 2026 study. Such sugars, called N-glycans, shape how proteins fold and behave, yet freeing them intact usually demands harsh pre-treatment. The enzyme, EndoBI-1, comes from a Bifidobacterium strain that lives in infant guts.

Two very different test proteins were used: bovine lactoferrin from milk and soy protein from plants. Precise mass analysis showed the released sugar sets differed by source, with complex and sialic-acid-bearing forms among them. A versatile, gentle release tool matters because sugar profiles are read as clues in food science and disease research alike.
pmc-13466889:
Wang and co-authors describe a cheap, sunlight-driven material for cleaning antibiotic-contaminated water in this 2026 study. Powdered catalysts that break down pollutants under light are often costly and hard to handle. So the team set bismuth tungstate, a light-active compound, into a geopolymer. That is a stone-like material made from inexpensive industrial ingredients. Their target was tetracycline hydrochloride, a common antibiotic found in wastewater.

With only four percent bismuth tungstate in the mix, the composite removed 82.7 percent of the antibiotic after 300 minutes under visible light. The test ran at a mildly alkaline pH of 8. pmc-13467689:

pmc-13467889:

pmc-13468289:

pmc-13468489:

pmc-13468689:

pmc-13468789:

pmc-13468889:
Mao and co-authors simulate transformer oil breaking down, hunting earlier warning gases. Their 2026 paper models mineral insulating oil with reactive molecular dynamics. The authors propose adding these intermediates to monitoring practice for earlier transformer fault detection.
pmc-13469189:
Bowen Tian and colleagues fuse infrared and visible images in 2026 with a method that asks how much each pixel region of each source can be trusted. pmc-13469589:
Zhang and colleagues propose a 2026 security scheme for groups of small internet-connected devices that must prove their identity to each other without heavy computation. pmc-13469989:
Martinez and colleagues in Canada asked in 2026 whether a stand in score can speed kidney cancer trials: time free of disease in place of time alive. A drug that cut the disease return risk by near a tenth or more could be read as a life gain. No slant showed in which trials saw print. The authors back the stand in score for new trials, with long checks still run.
pmc-13470189:
Aishwarya S Borkar, Yvanna Todorova, and Oonagh Markey pool trial evidence in 2026 on whether a component of milk fat can improve heart, metabolic, and brain markers in adults. A protein marker tied to cholesterol particles and the ratio of total to protective cholesterol also fell. The reviewers graded the certainty behind each key outcome, giving readers a cautious summary of what is known.
pmc-13471389:
Romano and colleagues built a drug carrier from red blood cell vesicles, tiny bubbles shed by red cells, to deliver two cancer drugs together against triple-negative breast cancer. pmc-13471489:

pmc-13471589:

pmc-13472889:

The exchange, they suggest, sharpens how the field should hunt the true sources of REM-triggering input.
pmc-13473289:
Changjiu Liang and colleagues build a tool in 2026 to flag early death risk in a fast-moving blood cancer. pmc-13474689:
Yi Liu and co-authors report a plant biochemistry study, published in 2026. It traces how moringa sprouts make glucomoringin. This sulphur-rich compound is valued as the source of moringin. Candidate genes were named for each step. Several enzyme genes were among them. Two further genes were flagged as likely converters. They would turn glucomoringin into moringin. Breeders and growers now have targets for raising levels of the compound.
pmc-13474889:
Yalcin and co-authors looked for warning signs that womb cancer has spread to the para-aortic lymph nodes, glands high in the abdomen whose involvement worsens the outlook. pmc-13476889:

pmc-13477389:

pmc-13479889:

pmc-13481489:

pmc-13482289:

pmc-13482589:

pmc-13482989:

pmc-13483389:

pmc-13483489:

pmc-13483689:

pmc-13484989:

pmc-13486489:

pmc-13487389:

pmc-13487989:

pmc-13490389:

pmc-13490589:

pmc-13493689:

pmc-13495389:

pmc-13498589:

pmc-13499689:

pmc-13502389:

pmc-13503489:

pmc-13503689:
Janne Van Hauwenhuyse leads a large team reporting a new cancer drug in a 2026 preclinical study. The drug blocks XPO1, a protein that ships cargo out of the cell core and helps tumors live. Drugs now in use bind this target for good and break the protein down, which limits their use.

The new drug, FR-027, binds the same spot through a distinct chemical step, yet its hold can reverse. Tests on the bound pair show a closed shape that shields the protein from breakdown. The drug killed many cancer cell types and slowed tumors in mice, with longer life as a result. Blood counts, a known weak point of older drugs, stayed near normal even with heavy dosing.
pmc-13503789:
Seyed Ali Asghar Hashemi and three colleagues map the gene makeup of a fungus that rots oak trees in Iran, in a 2026 study. The fungus causes charcoal canker in the Zagros forests, which hold most of the country's oak woods. Knowing how its strains differ can guide how the disease is fought.

The team gathered 159 samples from sick oaks in four provinces and read them with gene markers. Diversity was high, and most of it sat inside each local group rather than between groups. Still, strains grouped by place of origin, with some mixing that hints at gene flow. Tests showed all sampled types could cause canker. Western strains hit trees harder than southwestern ones, so control plans may need to vary by region.
pmc-13503989:
Abhinandan Singla leads a team comparing side-effect reports for two hormone-blocking drugs in women, in a 2026 study. Spironolactone is an older drug for heart and kidney disease that often causes hormonal side effects. Finerenone is a newer, more selective drug in the same family.

The team mined the U.S. drug safety database for reports from 2022 to early 2026, with far more reports for the older drug. Across hormone, skin, mood, and reproductive groups, the older drug drew far more reports per use than the newer one. High potassium, a shared risk, showed no gap between them. The authors warn that report data cannot prove cause, and the two patient groups differed in age.
pmc-13504289:
Jácome-López and colleagues classified the boundaries between genome domains by how accessible their chromatin is. they uncovered a protein module that insulates those boundaries, in a 2026 study of human leukemia cells. Domain boundaries keep genes and their switches in neighborhoods, and broken insulation causes misregulation. What makes some boundaries stronger than others was unclear beyond the CTCF protein and cohesin complex.

Jácome-López found the most accessible boundaries carry more proteins including CTCF, insulate contacts more strongly, and stay conserved across cell types. Mining proteins enriched at accessible boundaries revealed two partnerships: CTCF and cohesin together with a protein REST, and a pair, ZNF316 with EMSY. Deleting the pair's binding site at a CTCF-free boundary increased cross-domain contacts, proving the new module insulates. The authors conclude boundary strength depends on protein combinations and abundance, not CTCF alone.
pmc-13507089:
Roopali Singh and colleagues introduce, in 2026 work, RETROFIT, a computer method that unmixes cell types in spatial gene data without a reference atlas. Spatial methods read gene activity in intact tissue, yet each spot often mixes several cell types. Most unmixing tools need matched single-cell data or marker lists, which may be missing or flawed.

RETROFIT works from raw counts alone with a Bayesian model, a method that weighs likely explanations, and adds labels later if help exists. Tests on simulated and real tissues beat other reference-free tools and matched reference-based tools when references were imperfect. Fine detail held even at near single-cell resolution. Broad use across platforms looks feasible.
pmc-13507189:
Zhihui Wu, Yongxin Yu, Cong Zhao, Lingjun Zhang, and Yunlong Sun study, in 2026 tests, how sound signals reveal tensile failure in active waveguide rods used to watch rock slopes. Buried rods carry faint cracking sounds, called acoustic emissions, from deep rock to surface sensors. Lab pulls at varied loading rates tracked signal strength, energy, and pitch bands as rods stretched and cracked.

Signal spread grew from low to high strengths as load rose, with energy climbing steadily. Near peak stress, signals spiked and high-pitch events formed about a third of all events. Event counts also separated loading rates cleanly. Signal patterns can flag tensile stage and crack growth, which supports early warning for slope failure.
pmc-13507889:
Sahoo and colleagues reported in 2026 a rare molecule chaining five metal atoms: gallium, zinc, iron, zinc, and gallium. Molecules with direct bonds between different metals offer unusual bonding and reactions for chemists to study. The team made the chain by a salt-exchange reaction between a gallium-zinc starting compound and an iron carbonyl salt.

Reactions with a potassium reagent stripped the chain down to a smaller gallium-zinc product, also made directly by a second route. The team characterised all products by structure determination, spectroscopy, and computer modelling. Together these methods revealed how the metals share electrons along the chain. The authors present the work as a window into metal-metal bonding that could guide future catalyst and materials design.
pmc-13508289:
Fiorella Prada leads a fourteen-author team studying how ocean acidification changes the skeletons of a deep cold-water coral in the Mediterranean, in 2026 work. Cold-water corals build reef-like homes in deep seas, much as tropical corals do in warm shallows. The Mediterranean absorbs extra carbon dioxide, making it a preview of wider ocean change. The team collected the coral Desmophyllum dianthus from depths of 400 to 1,200 meters, where water chemistry varies in how much building mineral it can supply.

As the water's mineral supply fell, skeletons grew more porous at the large scale, changing their overall architecture. Fine and middle-scale features, though, stayed the same across the whole depth range. The coral seems to guard its basic building blocks tightly while letting the larger frame loosen. That split response matters for predicting whether deep reefs can keep their strength as oceans keep acidifying.
pmc-13511289:
W Timothy Garvey and colleagues report trial results, published in 2026. They cover TERN-601, an experimental once-daily pill. It activates the GLP-1 hormone receptor for weight loss. Phase 1 and 2 studies were randomised and placebo-controlled. Adults with obesity or overweight took rising doses. Safety, body levels of the drug, appetite, and weight change were tested. Follow-up ran up to twelve weeks.

The pill produced modest weight loss. The loss was dose-dependent. Appetite fell and stomach emptying slowed. This matches its drug class. Three Phase 2 participants developed a similar pattern of liver enzyme rises, though. Drug-induced liver injury was confirmed or not excludable. Development of TERN-601 was stopped. The authors discuss this as a warning for similar small-molecule designs.
pmc-13511689:
Siqi Gan, Qixuan Zhang, Chan Zhang, Li Yan, Yue Yin, Heng Ma, and Zihui Zhang review the two-way signaling between fat tissue and the heart in cardiovascular disease, in 2026 work. Fat is now seen as an active hormone and immune organ that talks to the heart through signal proteins, inflammatory messengers, metabolites, and tiny released packets. In health, that talk supports balance in metabolism and vessel function.

When fat tissue malfunctions, the same channels promote inflammation, scarring, vessel injury, and heart muscle reshaping. The review links fat depots and their secretions to artery hardening, heart failure, high blood pressure, diabetic heart muscle disease, and irregular heartbeat. It closes with candidate markers and treatment ideas aimed at the fat-heart axis, arguing that depot-specific signals could guide sharper diagnostic and drug choices for heart-metabolic disease.
pmc-13511789:
Mirasheh and colleagues review in 2026 the population evidence linking pesticide exposure to gynecological cancers of the ovary, endometrium, and cervix. Farm and household exposures are common, and several pesticide types can mimic hormones or damage DNA. The authors searched major sources for studies from between 2000 and 2025 and paired the population findings with the known mechanisms.

Organochlorine pesticides showed the strongest links, acting through estrogen mimicry, DNA damage, oxidative stress, raised inflammation signals, and altered cell signaling. In contrast, most studies found no clear link for triazines such as atrazine. One pesticide, carbendazim, showed a dual role, carcinogenic in exposure studies yet useful against cancer when given with nanotechnology. The authors conclude that such exposure is a real factor overall, but the evidence strength varies by pesticide class and more work is needed to prove cause and effect.
pmc-13512089:
Jin and colleagues published a 2026 study on teaching computers with mislabeled training photos. Wrong labels poison image models, and early mistakes tend to snowball. Their method, CANNE, first borrows a vision-language model's judgment to seed clean examples. It then refines the set during training using neighbor patterns in feature space.

On a standard photo set with 90 percent wrong labels, accuracy stayed above 96 percent. A harder hundred-class set also held up well under heavy noise. Real-world noisy sets from animals and the web confirmed the pattern. Repeated runs showed the seed set steadied training from the start. External priors, they argue, beat self-judgment for early cleaning. Open-set noise, from classes outside training, also tested the framework.
pmc-13515989:
Changde He leads a twelve-author team building an ultrasound kit that finds and sizes bubbles inside silicone sealing rings, in a 2026 study. Hidden bubbles weaken seals, yet the standard X-ray check is bulky, slow, and a radiation hazard. Their pocket system uses two tiny chip-based ultrasound arrays, each under nine millimetres square, with matched sending and receiving electronics.

Sound travel time gives the silicone thickness. How much the returning signal fades, checked against how similar it stays to a reference, reveals bubble size. Tests on factory-grade silicone, backed by computer simulation, reached a spatial resolution of half a millimetre and tracked bubble-driven signal loss well. He's team frames the kit as safer and more portable than X-ray inspection, suited to live checks on the factory floor and faster quality control in seal production.
pmc-13516489:
Kubra Cigdem Pekkoc-Uyanik and colleagues sequenced potassium channel genes in Turkish epilepsy patients to see if gene variants predict drug response. These channels control electrical signals in brain cells, and about a third of patients stay drug-resistant.

The team read six channel genes in 31 patients and found 181 variants, including six of uncertain meaning and two never reported before. One paired variant pattern in the KCNV2 gene showed up far more often in patients whose drugs failed than in responders. That pattern appeared in 18.5 percent of persistent cases against 0.8 percent of responsive ones, a clear gap in this small group. Pekkoc-Uyanik calls the link a lead for personalised prescribing, while stressing it needs proof in larger groups.
pmc-13517389:
Xu and colleagues fed polypropylene microplastics to mice in 2026 to test effects on immunity, fertility, and gut microbes. Polypropylene is one of the most common plastics in daily life, and its tiny worn fragments reach food and water. What those fragments do inside mammals is still poorly known.

Over five weeks, exposed mice showed no change in blood antibody levels or sex hormones, and the weight of testes and ovaries stayed normal. One immune response did drop, and only in females. Gene activity in the testes shifted, with collagen genes standing out among the changes. Gut microbe mixes also shifted, with fewer helpful Lactobacillus microbes in exposed mice. The authors suggest that altered gut microbes may link the plastic exposure to the testis gene changes, and call for more work on that chain.
pmc-13518889:
Rabia Tehseen and five colleagues present Electric_Fed in 2026, a decentralized system letting homes in a residential block forecast and trade electricity among themselves. Developing countries face chronic power shortages, and sharing local surplus could cut grid dependence. Privacy rules out simply pooling household data.

Their model trains a shared forecasting system through federated learning, where devices learn locally and share only model updates. A central server spots surplus and shortage homes, then blockchain smart contracts settle peer-to-peer trades transparently. Using a year of production and consumption data, the system met 89.2 percent of the region's electricity need in tests. Two example clients reached full self-sufficiency through trades.
pmc-13520389:
Oluwatosin A Ayeni and colleagues review in 2026 care and survival for 642 women with cervical cancer in Johannesburg, South Africa. All women were referred for radiation care at a public tertiary hospital. Records span January 2021 to December 2022. Women counted even if care never started in the end.

Over half the women were under 50 years old. About six in ten lived with HIV. Half held stage III disease at referral. Median wait to start care was about four months. Two-year survival was just over 57 percent in total. Survival fell hard at the most advanced stage. Model checks then weigh which traits tracked with survival.
pmc-13521589:
Diana Maria Ibarra Tostado and colleagues describe in 2026 a 70-year-old man with a rare skin cancer above his right eyebrow. The cancer is called microcystic adnexal carcinoma. Growth is slow but deep. Return after poor removal is common.

The spot looked like a firm yellow plaque with fuzzy edges. A small tissue sample showed nests and cords of odd cells that invade nearby skin. Layer-by-layer Mohs surgery cleared the growth while sparing healthy tissue. A flap then closed the wound. Healing went smoothly. No return showed at six months. The team restates Mohs surgery as the best care path here.
pmc-13521889:
Yunus Bayram Koçyiğit, Belgin Karaoğlan and Aslı Kuruoğlu examine in 2026 whether beliefs about one's own thinking track with fibromyalgia burden in Turkish women. Metacognition covers confidence in memory, perceived need to control thoughts and beliefs about worry danger.

Questionnaires covered 56 women with fibromyalgia and 69 matched healthy women. Patients scored higher on every thinking-belief subscale and on all impact measures. Within patients, higher thinking-belief totals tracked with higher impact totals at a moderate strength. Depression and anxiety scores were also collected. The link suggests thinking style may amplify lived burden beyond pain alone, meriting attention in psychological care.
pmc-13522489:
R Vimal Prakash and R Rengaraj model electricity market behavior with an evolutionary algorithm in a 2026 study of flexible power demand. Households, prosumers who also generate power, aggregators, and utilities adjust their use in response to prices and grid limits. The proposed method lets simulated agents evolve shifting strategies over repeated rounds, guided by cost, peak load, and stability goals.

Compared with four established optimization methods, the new approach converged faster and reached the best overall fitness score after five hundred rounds. Reported gains included lower energy costs, a lower peak load, much higher renewable use, and fewer curtailments. The authors present the model as a tool for demand management systems, tariff design, and energy policy in decentralized grids.
pmc-13522589:
Yamane and co-authors reported a 2026 immunology study on why a weak protein handshake inside T cells matters. When a T cell receptor spots its target, adapter proteins gather the enzyme PLC-gamma1 into a four part complex. The link between two parts, SLP-76 and that enzyme, is naturally weak and conserved across vertebrates.

Yamane engineered mice whose T cells carried a mutation making that link stronger, which raised enzyme activity and signal strength. The stronger signal distorted development of several T cell types in the thymus and gut. After viral infection the mice made fewer central memory CD8 T cells, the long lived cells that guard against repeat infection. Their antibody responses through germinal centres also suffered, showing the weak link fine tunes defence.
pmc-13522689:
Susan D Leonard and Albert K Bui present a 2026 case report linking a common acid-blocking drug to restless legs syndrome. A forty-one-year-old man developed restless legs and major sleep disturbance soon after starting pantoprazole for a bleeding duodenal ulcer caused by painkillers. Iron deficiency from blood loss was another possible cause, so iron supplements were given first.

Symptoms persisted through the full eight-week drug course despite iron treatment. Within days of stopping the acid-blocking drug, the restless legs resolved. The close timing, lack of response to iron, and rapid recovery after stopping lead the authors to judge the drug a probable cause. The case reminds clinicians to consider these medicines when restless legs or sleep problems begin after treatment starts.
pmc-13522789:
Teodor G Calina leads a large team using DNA methylation to classify a rare ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. Mucinous ovarian carcinoma is often confused with mucinous cancers that spread to the ovary from elsewhere, because the two look alike. Genome-wide profiles of those marks were collected from tumors held at six centers, covering cancers, metastases, and borderline tumors.

Methylation split the borderline tumors into two groups, one resembling normal ovary and one resembling cancer. The cancers themselves formed two subtypes with possible prognostic value. A three-step machine learning tool built from these and outside profiles separated true ovarian cancers from spread tumors with high success in both internal and external testing. The authors offer the tool as a robust aid for a difficult diagnostic call.
pmc-13523389:
Hüseyin Karakaya, Mahmut Gümüş, and Gökhan Doğukan Akarsu present a giant ovarian cyst case in a 2026 report. A forty-five-year-old woman arrived with breathlessness and progressive abdominal swelling. Imaging revealed a cystic mass roughly forty-five by twenty centimeters occupying almost the whole abdominal cavity and compressing neighboring organs.

Surgery removed the uterus, both fallopian tubes, and the affected ovary, extracting a forty-two centimeter mucinous cyst without complications. Tissue examination confirmed a benign mucinous cystadenoma, a fluid-filled tumor that can grow very large when diagnosis is delayed. The authors stress thorough imaging and timely, multidisciplinary surgical planning, since such giant cysts can mimic acute abdominal emergencies and threaten serious complications if they rupture or twist.
pmc-13524089:
Helusová and co-authors study how plants switch off auxin, a hormone that drives growth. Their 2026 paper examines GH3 enzymes, which deactivate the main auxin, called IAA, by attaching amino acids to it. Different GH3 family subgroups respond to auxin in opposite ways, and the team asked whether they also attach different amino acids.

Working with tobacco cell lines that could be switched on or knocked out, the authors profiled auxin breakdown products. One enzyme, NtGH3.1a, mainly attached aspartate, while NtGH3.6e attached glutamine and produced two less-studied compounds. Matching enzymes in Arabidopsis showed the same split in preference. Both tobacco enzymes sat in the nucleus and the cytoplasm whether auxin was present or not, supporting a conserved division of labour.
pmc-13524589:
Natarajan and colleagues published a 2026 study on how a tilted heart valve stirs clot risk. Replacement aortic valves delivered by catheter can land slightly canted. Leaflet clots have emerged as a worry after such implants in patients. The team tested three tilt angles in a patient-shaped aortic root model.

Canting reshaped swirl and washout in the valve's pockets unevenly. The tightest pocket held the stalest blood in every tilted setup. One tilt direction left 92 percent of one pocket nearly still. Clots in blood-loop tests formed exactly on those poorly washed leaflets. Overall valve function looked alike, hiding the local clot risk well. Deployment angle deserves the same care as valve size choice. Blood-loop tests used real whole blood flowing past the valve leaflets.
pmc-13524689:
James J. Rutowski and others survey, in a 2026 national study, how nephrology fellowship programs use night float systems, where trainees cover patients only at night in rotating blocks. Residency programs use night float widely for wellness and duty-hour limits, yet its spread in kidney training programs was uncharacterized.

Directors of all accredited adult nephrology fellowship programs were invited, and 77 programs responded, of which 28 used night float. Programs with night float had more fellows and covered more hospitals overnight. Most suspended continuity clinic and lecture attendance during night rotations. Directors most often praised improved trainee wellness and satisfaction, while lost clinic continuity and missed teaching were the commonest drawbacks. The authors call for balancing rest with educational continuity.
pmc-13524889:
Xingnan Yi and colleagues use a 2026 cross-sectional survey of 40,600 Hong Kong households to examine who provides family care for people with disabilities and what drives caregiver stress. In East Asian societies, filial expectations and limited formal services place much care on families. Data came from the 2019-2020 Hong Kong General Household Survey.

Among weighted respondents in households including a person with disability, 14.5 percent were family caregivers. Women and unmarried respondents were more likely to provide care. Helping with daily living activities more than doubled the odds of longer weekly hours, and women also reported more hours. Severe mental stress was tied to being female, helping with daily activities, and caring for a relative with mental health disability. The authors urge targeted support that addresses gendered expectations.
pmc-13525189:
Adnan Imran and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, evidence linking vitamin D deficiency with heart, metabolic, and kidney outcomes in autoimmune rheumatic diseases. These chronic immune diseases carry extra cardiovascular and renal burden, and vitamin D deficiency is common within them. Searches covered five databases through March 2026 without language limits.

Eighteen observational studies qualified, with four independent cohorts feeding at least one pooled analysis. Deficiency was associated with roughly double the all-cause mortality hazard. The cardiovascular event estimate was large but imprecise, and the link between vitamin D level and protein in the urine in children with lupus was inconclusive. Other metabolic and vascular studies pointed adverse but could not be pooled because measures differed. The authors flag confounding and varied definitions.
pmc-13525289:
Surender Himral and colleagues examine, in a 2026 retrospective study, how often a completely blocked culprit artery hides inside heart attacks that lack the classic electrocardiogram pattern. Such occlusive infarctions can be missed when patients are sorted by tracing alone. The cohort came from an Indian tertiary cardiac center.

The study included 340 patients arriving within a day of chest pain who underwent angiography. A blocked or near-blocked culprit artery defined occlusion, found in 112 patients, about one third. Heart pumping fraction was lower in the occlusive group at presentation and stayed lower at three months despite improvement in both groups. Baseline features were otherwise similar, and death rates by nine to twelve months did not differ significantly. Lower pumping fraction was the strongest correlate of occlusion.
pmc-13525689:
Abdulrahman Arabi leads a large team in a 2026 nationwide analysis of trends in emergency angioplasty for major heart attacks in Qatar over nine years. This procedure, primary percutaneous coronary intervention, is the standard for ST-elevation heart attacks, yet long-term Middle Eastern trend data were scarce.

The registry held 7,959 patients treated at Qatar Heart Hospital between 2015 and 2023. Annual volume rose by over half, average age was forty-nine, and most patients were male and non-Qatari. Risk factors climbed over time, while ambulance use, radial access, and vessel imaging all increased, and door-to-balloon time fell from sixty to forty-five minutes. In-hospital mortality dropped from four point four percent in 2016 to one point five percent in 2023. Shock, cardiac arrest, older age, and delay predicted death.
pmc-13528089:
Haiou Yang and eight colleagues uncover how low oxygen helps bowel cancer resist a key drug in a 2026 study. Tumors often sit short of oxygen, which rewires their chemistry. The team screened RNA strands active in low-oxygen cancer cells. One long non-coding RNA stood out. They named it lnc-IRP.

The strand carries a hook shaped like an iron-control signal. With it, the strand grabs IRP2, a master switch for cell iron. The metal then stayed locked in storage form instead of the loose pool cells use. That shift blocked two death routes, apoptosis and iron-driven ferroptosis. Cancer cells survived the drug oxaliplatin more easily. The authors propose lnc-IRP as a drug target. Freeing the iron switch could restore sensitivity, they argue.
pmc-13528389:
Si and co-authors diagnose why clinical prediction tools powered by artificial intelligence so rarely reach patients, despite thousands of published models. Their 2026 narrative review argues the failure is planned in from the start: researchers build models first and wonder about deployment later. The authors propose reversing the direction, a bedside-to-bench discipline. It begins by defining the clinical question, the intended user, and the exact point in the care pathway where a score would change a decision.

Around that core they arrange the neglected homework: early and continuing engagement with clinicians and patients, and a programme theory linking model outputs to changed outcomes. Regulatory routes, funding models that keep software alive, equity checks, and the engineering of implementation and monitoring complete the list. Methodological hygiene still matters, they note, since reviews keep finding sloppy methods and incomplete reporting, but rigour alone cannot cross the translational gap.
pmc-13529189:
He and colleagues mined the Food and Drug Administration's adverse event database for safety signals of acyclovir, in a 2026 analysis. Acyclovir is the first-line drug for herpes simplex infection in newborns. Safety evidence in babies under one month old is thin despite wide use at high doses. The team screened reports from 2004 through late 2024 with acyclovir as the suspect.

He found 130 neonatal reports covering 409 adverse events and applied four statistical signal methods at once, keeping only signals positive on all four. Four organ groups stood out: skin and tissue under it, general and injection-site problems, liver and bile disorders, and kidney and urinary disorders. The strongest signals involved tissue death or swelling at the infusion site and skin peeling or death. Three reported events, including Kawasaki disease and gut inflammation, do not appear in product labeling, which the authors say warrants confirmation and monitoring.
pmc-13530189:
Yi Zhang and co-authors build a 2026 low-cost method for generating traditional decorative patterns with artificial intelligence, using ancient Egyptian designs as the test case. Training image models normally demands heavy computing and large pattern collections, both scarce for heritage material. Their route adapts a big image model through small trainable add-on layers only.

Pattern sorting by content and form cleaned the training set before fine-tuning. Judging covered shape, color, beauty, novelty, and use value, backed by numeric image scores. Trainable parts shrank by over 99 percent, and memory needs fell sharply. Trials on Chinese patterns held steady.
pmc-13530589:
Pianka and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 149, ten-year results after hip arthroscopy for femoroacetabular impingement, split by where the pain sits. The condition is a painful hip shape conflict. Classic pain is in the front groin; lateral or posterior pain is called atypical and sometimes prompts doubts about operating.

The retrospective cohort covered primary arthroscopies from 2010 to 2013 with at least ten years of follow-up, matched three-to-one into 81 typical and 27 atypical pain patients. Both groups improved greatly on two standard hip scores, and the improvements, near forty points on each scale, did not differ between them. Revision surgery and conversion to a hip replacement each occurred in about six percent of the typical group and four percent of the atypical group. Success thresholds were met at similar rates.
pmc-13531789:
John Y Rhee and co-authors untangle in 2026 an ethics puzzle around limited feeding at the end of life. Minimal comfort feeding gives food or fluids only when a dying patient shows hunger or thirst. The same practice can mean comfort care during active dying or a deliberate step to hasten death.

Two clinical cases show how intention and timing change the moral reading under a virtue ethics framework and the doctrine of double effect. The authors propose split names: proportionate comfort feeding when death is foreseen yet unintended, versus minimal feeding to hasten death when speed is the goal.
pmc-13532289:
Dingxiang Zhu and colleagues report in 2026 how the silkworm virus protein GP64 reaches the cell surface. GP64 helps the virus infect cells, and in silkworm cells it keeps a small tag called a signal peptide. The team asked whether GP64 needs the normal route through the Golgi, a part of the cell that sorts proteins.

Blocking that route had no clear effect in silkworm cells, yet it cut GP64 surface levels in cells from another moth. A control protein that needs the Golgi route was blocked in both settings. Readers learn how a virus protein can bypass a main cell route in its true host.
pmc-13532889:
Peyton M Day and colleagues track in 2026 heart forces inside the left ventricle in mice with reversible pressure overload. The forces come from ultrasound measures of heart motion and blood flow, and they can flag poor pumping earlier than standard scores. Eight male mice had scans before narrowing, after narrowing, and after release.

Forces along the long axis during systole shifted clearly with overload and with recovery. One new ratio of early to late systolic force linked most strongly to both states. Sideways force during the impulse phase also hinted at who would recover well after release.
pmc-13534889:
Ciara Rhodes and colleagues compare in 2026 two ways to prepare historic human bone for DNA identification work. Grinding bone to powder is standard, yet it can harm fragile genetic profiles in aged remains. Paired bones from the 19th century were either ground or softened and sliced without powder.

Slices gave far more human DNA on average than ground samples from the same bones. No ground sample produced a standard profile, while slices gave partial profiles and much higher marker recovery in targeted sequencing. Labs gain a workflow built from common reagents that lifts success on hard cases.
pmc-13538389:
Rasheed Omobolaji Alabi and colleagues build a learning model for early death in head and neck cancer in a 2026 population study. Death within six months stays common despite better care for early to mid-stage tumors. Registry data for 4,802 patients supplied model building, with checks in near two thousand German registry cases and a small Finnish hospital group. Risk factors were ranked for death at six months, two years, and five years.

The model predicted early death fairly in the main registry and moderately in outside checks, weaker in the smallest group. Older age, prior other cancers, unmarried status, larger tumor stage, and throat or voice box sites led early death factors. Rankings shifted modestly at later time points. The authors propose the model to flag high-risk patients for faster, tailored decisions.
pmc-13538689:
Su-Jung Ji and colleagues sequence the first complete mitochondrial genomes of underground aquatic crustaceans in a 2026 phylogeny study. The tiny eyeless order lives only in subterranean waters, yet none of its roughly 340 species had a full mitochondrial genome before. Four species from two families were sequenced and placed within a broad crustacean family tree.

The genomes showed extensive gene shuffling, strong composition biases, and fast evolution. Tree analyses firmly supported the group as one lineage, though very long branches hint that underground simplification blurs deep relationships. The two orders once grouped as close kin landed far apart, suggesting their shared traits evolved independently. The authors offer the genomes as resources for rethinking crustacean classification.
pmc-13542589:
Chang and co-authors upgrade sorghum for meat ducks by fermenting it with microbes and an enzyme. Their 2026 paper prepares the feed with Bacillus subtilis, Candida utilis, and phytase, an enzyme that unlocks phosphorus bound in phytic acid. Two experiments followed: a digestibility trial in 128 young ducks and a 21-day growth trial in 240 ducks where the treated sorghum replaced most of the corn.

Fermentation raised the sorghum's protein and ash while cutting phytic acid and fibre. Ducks digested its protein, fat, zinc, phosphorus, and energy better, and absorbed several amino acids more completely. In the growth trial the fermented diet beat plain sorghum on final weight and daily gain with a leaner feed conversion ratio. Gut enzyme activities rose, caecal fermentation acids increased, and gut microbe diversity improved with a shift toward Firmicutes. The authors endorse the co-fermentation strategy.
pmc-13543489:
Xiaoyan Wang and colleagues published a 2026 cohort study asking what happens when frailty and metabolic syndrome occur together, tracking fatty liver disease, diabetes, and death in the UK Biobank. More than 165,000 participants were grouped by having neither condition, one, or both. A multi-state model followed them from health into metabolic fatty liver disease, onward to diabetes, or to death across nearly thirteen years of follow-up.

People with both frailty and metabolic syndrome faced almost triple the risk of developing fatty liver disease compared with those who had neither. Their risk of progressing from fatty liver to diabetes was higher still, at over four times. Survival curves confirmed the ordering of the groups. Frailty alone is easy to overlook beside laboratory measures, yet pairing the two assessments, the authors argue, sharpens early identification of people on the road to liver and metabolic disease.
pmc-13543589:
Xinming Hu's team published a 2026 study of why kidney cancers stop responding to sunitinib, a standard targeted drug, using tumour organoids grown from patient tissue. Gene profiling of treated organoids flagged ALDH1L2, a metabolic enzyme, which also ran high in real tumours and marked worse survival. The team raised and lowered the enzyme in organoids and in tumours grown in mice to watch drug response change.

Extra ALDH1L2 blunted the drug's effect by damping ferroptosis, the iron-driven death the drug partly relies on, keeping oxidative damage low. Removing it had the opposite effect, restoring sensitivity. A ferroptosis-triggering drug cancelled the protection. Screening then found a plant-derived compound, hederacolchiside A1, that binds and reduces the enzyme and strengthened sunitinib's attack in the models. Shield proteins like this one may explain, and eventually reverse, drug resistance.
pmc-13544089:
Run Wang and colleagues published a 2026 perspective proposing an equity-centred version of PEDALs, a staged model for getting proven health practices into routine use. The know-do gap, the lag between evidence and practice, persists worldwide, and implementation work that ignores equity can widen the very disparities it hopes to close. Their adaptation threads fairness through every stage, from problem definition to long-term scale-up.

At the problem stage, root causes of inequity come first. A later stage admits practice-based knowledge and even the removal of harmful practices. Determinants are analysed with marginalised voices in the room, actions are co-designed for context, and long-term outcomes are measured through an equity lens. The authors commend hybrid designs and rapid, participatory methods, under a philosophy of radical incrementalism: steady, equity-driven steps rather than revolutions, especially for lower-income health systems.
pmc-13545689:
Aljahdali and colleagues systematically reviewed in 2026 the use of a patient's own fat-derived products in nose surgery and nasal reconstruction, where thin or scarred skin makes outcomes fragile. The authors judge the products well tolerated and promising as surgical adjuncts, and call for standardized, objective outcome tracking.
pmc-13547289:
Sara Darabi, Gholamreza Heidari, and Payman Salami compared in 2026 poultry manure with chemical fertilizer across three cereal crops at a university farm in Iran over two growing seasons. Pearl millet, sorghum, and maize each received no fertilizer, manure alone, full chemical fertilizer, or blends of manure with urea and phosphate. Soil chemistry and enzyme activity, a sign of living, working soil, were measured.

Manure alone gave the richest soil carbon in every crop and the strongest activity of both phosphatase enzymes, which free up phosphorus for plants. The full chemical treatment led on potassium but lagged on biology. Manure also raised soil salinity somewhat, so the authors advise controlled rates with regular monitoring rather than abandoning a practice that clearly feeds the soil.
pmc-13547389:
Massimo Apicella and colleagues studied in 2026 whether poor control of emotions adds risk for suicide attempts in teenagers beyond depression itself. Their clinic sample held 182 adolescents, average age near sixteen, of whom 41 had recently attempted suicide. The full model explained about a third of the differences between groups. The authors argue suicide risk checks should cover emotion control, not mood alone.
pmc-13547889:
Afsar Murat and Çelik Çetin followed in 2026 an invasive red-eared slider turtle population in a wetland in western Turkey. They asked how the animals handle heat in a habitat that suits them poorly. The species ranks among the world's worst invaders. From March to October 2024 the team measured turtle body temperatures alongside air, water, sunlight, and wind, and separately measured the temperatures turtles choose in the laboratory.

Habitat quality was suboptimal during the turtles' active hours, yet the animals held their bodies close to their preferred range with high precision, scoring strongly on effectiveness measures. Body temperature tracked water and air temperature closely. The authors read this skillful behavioral regulation as a built-in advantage that helps the invader thrive and may expand with warming.
pmc-13548489:
Usame Rakip and colleagues validated in 2026 three CT scoring systems used to grade head injury severity. They tested them head-to-head in 657 adults treated between 2022 and 2024 at a Turkish neurosurgical center. The authors recommend the scores for early sorting and clear communication rather than as stand-alone prognostic tools.
pmc-13548589:
Asli Bahar Ucar and colleagues study how visible agitation shapes emergency care for adults in substance-related crises, in a 2026 chart review from a Turkish referral hospital. Many such visits now involve unsteady behavior rather than a clear poisoning picture. The team analyzed ninety visits where patients got calming drugs.
