Most patients arrived severely agitated. About a quarter needed a second calming drug, and seven in ten were admitted to psychiatry, with both outcomes rising step by step across agitation levels. Severe agitation independently predicted admission with nearly eightfold odds, while older age lowered the odds. The authors suggest a set agitation score at the door could help teams plan sedation and placement earlier.
pmc-13548689:
Dagyeong Kwon and colleagues hunt for apple genes that resist anthracnose, a fungal disease complex rotting fruit and spotting leaves, in a 2026 genetic association study. Breeders need resistance that holds up in real orchards. The team scored 440 apple genotypes, mostly offspring of six crosses, across several years of natural orchard exposure. They then challenged fruit and leaves with the fungus under controlled conditions, using wounded and unwounded tissue.

Disease severity swung strongly with the year's weather, underlining how environment steers infection. Association mapping on the 2019 field scores found a significant region on chromosome fifteen linked to milder disease. The region sits far from a previously known resistance region on the same chromosome, so it is likely new. Controlled inoculation scores produced no such signal. The authors stress that field testing across seasons is what reveals resistance worth breeding for.
pmc-13548789:
McKay and colleagues reviewed bone health in advanced prostate cancer and how to protect it within care, in a 2026 narrative review. Hormone therapy that lowers testosterone accelerates bone loss from the moment it starts, and once cancer spreads to bone. happens in the great majority of resistant cases, patients face fractures, spinal cord compression, and other skeletal events that erode quality of life.

Several cancer drugs, including abiraterone, enzalutamide, and radium-223, help bone. The authors supply a test-and-treat algorithm and argue management, though underused, should be standard practice.
pmc-13550489:
M. Siva Ramkumar and colleagues coordinate electric vehicle charging with a hybrid control system meant to keep a renewable-fed smart grid steady, in a 2026 engineering paper. Their stack pairs a single-switch high step-up converter, which lifts voltage efficiently, with two algorithms. One optimizer, inspired by leaves riding wind, tunes the controller settings. The other, a spiking deep residual network, forecasts the best operating parameters as conditions change.

Simulations in MATLAB compared the stack against four rival learning and optimization pairings. The proposed system posted converter efficiency of ninety-nine point seven percent, energy use efficiency near ninety-nine percent, and the lowest system error at one and a half percent. The authors claim the coordination smooths charging while solar and wind inputs fluctuate, though all results come from simulation rather than hardware.
pmc-13551689:
Jiahui Liang, leading five colleagues, published a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of vascular crisis after surgery for mouth and face cancers. Such a crisis, where blood flow through repaired vessels fails, is among the most serious complications, and its risk factors lacked consensus. The team searched nine Chinese and English databases to August 2025, screening studies with two independent reviewers.

Twenty-seven studies reported 44 candidate factors, and pooled incidence of vascular crisis came to about 14 percent in the figures given. Twelve factors held up, including diabetes, hypertension, mouth infection, prior radiotherapy, smoking, and alcohol history, plus several blood measures. The authors advise tailored prevention and closer monitoring for patients carrying these risks.
pmc-13551989:
Abolfazl Rezaei, Maryam Jahanbakhsh, and Hamid Reza Dehghan published a 2026 review on electronic medical records in developing countries. Paper records still rule in many such settings. They limit the accuracy and speed of care. The team searched five databases for studies on record system design and rollout. Eligible papers went through qualitative coding. Eighty studies yielded 204 refined codes. The codes formed a three-layer frame: foundation, core cycle, and optimization. Seven categories sat inside, from strategy and design to ethics and new tech. The team argues for a flexible path. Core needs come first, and refinements can follow as local resources allow. That order fits poor settings better than a rigid, linear plan.
pmc-13554189:
Binbin Xu leads a seven-author team surveying what nurses in Guizhou, China, know about caring for long-term vein catheters in a 2026 study. These catheters, threaded from an arm vein toward the heart, serve patients needing weeks of infusions. The web survey drew 3,528 nurses from eighteen hospitals in nine cities. Average knowledge scores sat below half of the top mark, and only about one nurse in six passed.

Higher scores followed senior titles, more schooling, hands-on catheter work, and past training. Workplace guidelines and felt training needs mattered in big hospitals, less so in smaller ones. Big-hospital employment itself lifted scores. The authors call for training tailored to hospital level, since the drivers of knowledge clearly differ between settings.
pmc-13555889:
Hoon Kim leads a five-author team measuring the energy cost of bounce squats versus standard squats in a 2026 study. Nine trained adults squatted under five loads, from none to full body weight, while cameras, force plates, and muscle sensors recorded them. Computer models of the body then estimated energy use for the whole body and for single muscles, split by movement phase.

Bounce squats cut total energy cost by about a tenth overall. The saving concentrated in the lowering phase, where cost fell by about a quarter. Thigh muscles called the vasti drove the saving during descent across all loads. The rising phase gained nothing from bouncing. Tendon recoil at the quick reversal likely explains the cheaper lowering.
pmc-13558389:
Junko Mukohyama and thirteen colleagues surveyed newly certified surgeons in Japan in 2026 about when, and why, they chose the specialty. Knowing the decision moment could sharpen recruitment, especially for women, who remain a minority in surgery. A nationwide questionnaire drew 758 responses, and the team split trainees into those who decided before junior residency and those who decided during or after it.

Men more often reported choosing surgery before medical school, while women clustered their decisions in the second postgraduate year. Later deciders included more women and more urban residents, and they leaned less on family influence or a glamorous image of surgeons. Among women who decided late, direct recruitment by working surgeons carried real weight. The authors advise departments to court trainees during residency, not only at the school gate.
pmc-13558489:
Leonardo Spagnol Abraham and eight colleagues surveyed in 2026 the real-world burden of alopecia areata among adults in Brazil. The autoimmune disease strips hair in patches or entirely and carries heavy psychological weight, yet Brazilian data were sparse. Dermatologists in a structured programme completed record forms for 341 adult patients during 2024, covering hair loss extent, symptoms, treatments, and whether care came through public or private services.

Patients with at least half their scalp hair lost showed more chronic disease and stronger symptoms than those with less loss. They were managed with whole-body rather than local treatments. The newest advanced drugs were still rarely used for them. Doctors most often named reducing hair loss itself as their goal. Public sector patients faced steeper barriers to newer therapies. The survey gives Brazilian planners a baseline picture of unmet need by severity and by care route.
pmc-13558589:
Seong Duk Do, Yeonhui Lee, and Jae-Sung Rhee sequenced in 2026 the first complete mitochondrial genome of the sea cucumber Ocnus glacialis and compared it across its order. This group of sea cucumbers is species rich, yet scarce mitochondrial data leave its family history fuzzy. The circular genome held the standard 37 genes, and the authors analysed base composition, selection pressure, gene order, and divergence timing against relatives.

The species showed the highest share of A and T bases in the group and the most scrambled gene order, built through repeated duplication and loss events. Several genes carried signs of relaxed or positive selection, and evolution ran faster on this branch. The authors tie the pattern to a move into Arctic cold and deep water combined with small population sizes. Their timeline gives the order a firmer evolutionary framework.
pmc-13558889:
Najirman Najirman and two colleagues measured in 2026 how blood markers of the bone-remodelling command chain relate to a marker of bone breakdown in people with rheumatoid arthritis. The disease speeds bone loss through a signalling trio that governs the cells dissolving bone, and the breakdown marker CTX-1 shows how fast skeleton is being eaten away. The two activating members of the trio correlated almost perfectly with the breakdown marker. The trio's brake protein also correlated strongly. A brake rising alongside breakdown is notable, since it suggests the system is straining to compensate. Average patient age was about forty. The authors conclude that circulating levels of the whole pathway track skeletal turnover in this disease, a possible handle for spotting patients whose bones need protection.
pmc-13559589:
Mengxiang Huang and colleagues trace a small regulatory RNA that reins in exosome release and movement in pancreatic cancer. Restoring the microRNA in cancer cells lowered RAB27A, cut exosome output, and slowed migration in dish and animal tests, without changing growth. Putting RAB27A back undid those effects, proving the chain of control. The authors present the pair as a regulatory axis behind exosome-driven spread. They suggest it as a foothold for future anti-metastasis strategies in a cancer that badly needs them.
pmc-13560389:
Shuai Zhang and colleagues report a multi-omics study, published in 2026. It maps how mouth microbes and body chemistry change as upper digestive tract cancers develop. A screening programme supplied the participants. The team enrolled 420 people in four equal groups. They ranged from healthy through two precancerous stages to cancer. Saliva microbes were profiled. Saliva and blood metabolites were profiled too.

Each stage carried a distinct signature. Saliva microbes remodelled strongly early. This was at the low-grade precancer stage. Whole-body metabolic shifts marked the move to high-grade lesions. pmc-13562689:
Nimra Iman and five colleagues train a neural network to outline narrowed heart arteries in X-ray angiograms, a task that eats expert time and invites human error. Training data came from the ARCADE set, angiograms from 1,500 patients split into training, validation, and test groups, enlarged by augmentation.

The authors present the system as an assistant to flag narrowed regions for a cardiologist's final judgement.
pmc-13563789:
Sina Meisamy and six colleagues listen to tumour temperature as an early whisper of whether cancer treatment is working. Melanoma received a vaccine-style immunotherapy, breast cancer a standard chemotherapy pairing, and colon cancer an anti-PD-1 immune drug.

pmc-13563889:
Li-bing Liang and five colleagues set out the protocol for a trial pairing an exercise with brain training for older adults whose memory is slipping. The team hopes the brain data explain any synergy, guiding non-drug care.
pmc-13571389:

A standard reverse tracking method then completed the opening. The authors note the connecting channel may first need gentle widening to deliver devices.
pmc-13573489:

pmc-13575189:

pmc-13575389:

pmc-13576389:

pmc-13578489:

pmc-13579089:

pmc-13579889:

pmc-13579989:

pmc-13584289:

pmc-13584389:

Game-based students scored a touch higher on every test and rated their method a bit better, with the clearest gain among students whose past grades were lower. None of those gaps, though, reached the level statisticians call solid. The authors conclude that either method works well in a virtual flipped class.
pmc-13584489:

Fifty-one of them shifted clearly with drought, near genes for wood-like wall building, a dry-stress hormone, and ion storage. pmc-13587389:

pmc-13589389:

pmc-13591889:

pmc-13592689:

Losing recA or uvrD shook the network widest, and each gene's core mechanical job proved required. pmc-13593689:

Computer simulations of the event-driven networks back up the analysis.
pmc-13594389:

pmc-13596889:

pmc-13597989:

pmc-13599289:
Xiaoyan Fei and three colleagues introduce BCP-YOLO in 2026, a computer vision system built to spot colorectal polyps during colonoscopy in real time. Polyps are small growths that can turn into bowel cancer. They are easy to miss, since their edges blur into the gut wall and light reflections confuse the image. A system that flags them live could help doctors catch more of them during screening.

Built on the YOLOv8 network, the design adds a module that focuses attention on likely polyp areas and a sharper way to rebuild fine detail. A lighter convolution step cuts computing cost. On the Kvasir-SEG test set it reached a mean average precision of 88.5 percent, beating the base model by 3.4 points. It runs at 104.1 frames per second with 11.7 million parameters, fast enough for live use. Repeated cross-checks on two datasets supported its reliability.
pmc-13599689:
Eva-Maria Kurz, Sven Bölte, and Terje Falck-Ytter follow sleep in very young children who later receive diagnoses of autism, ADHD, or both. Their 2026 study grew out of an infant sibling project that tracked 209 children from babyhood. Parents rated sleep at 10, 14, 24, and 36 months, and diagnoses were settled at 36 months. Comparing groups over time let the team see when sleep troubles actually begin.

At 10 and 14 months, sleep looked much the same across all groups, diagnosed or not. By 24 and 36 months, children with autism, ADHD, or both took longer to fall asleep, slept too little more often, and showed more disturbed sleep overall. In autism alone, resistance at bedtime eased between 24 and 36 months. Because the same pattern crossed diagnostic lines, the authors suggest early sleep problems in these conditions reflect shared processes rather than separate ones for each diagnosis. They call for studies adding measured sleep data to parent reports.
pmc-13602089:
Valentin Cavoy leads a seven-author team showing in 2026 that spring temperatures decide how many young perch a lake produces. Year-to-year swings in Eurasian perch numbers have long puzzled ecologists. In two large French peri-alpine lakes, the team analyzed twelve years of late-summer acoustic surveys counting young-of-the-year fish. They tested thermal measures built from 36 years of spawning records, including daily temperature swings, not just monthly averages.

Embryonic-phase conditions alone explained 44 to 88 percent of the variation in young perch density. Warmer embryonic periods helped survival, while strong day-to-day temperature swings hurt it. Food supply and adult stock size showed no consistent effect. The result confirms the central place of spring thermal conditions in perch recruitment, the authors say. For climate research, daily temperature behavior may matter as much as seasonal averages.
pmc-13614889:
Lynn Cockburn leads a team writing in 2026 about the digital divide inside international development research teams, drawing on their PIRL Project, whose members worked mainly in North America and Sub-Saharan Africa. Good global research needs every member able to join fully, yet gaps in devices, connections, and skills can quietly shut some researchers out. The team mixed community members with academic researchers. Some members had disabilities, and some had low incomes.

The group used a shared, participatory study of their own habits to map where technology helped or blocked inclusion. Fixes included joint planning for tech use, reliance on smartphones, free apps, and training for all. Their account shows that fairness in research starts with the tools on the desk, and that planning for the least-connected member lifts the whole team's work.
pmc-13615489:
Hernaiz-Llorens and colleagues published a 2026 study on an easier way to trace nerve fibers. The corticospinal tract carries movement signals from brain to spinal cord. After injury, its fibers may sprout new branches, a sign of repair attempts. Standard dyes for tracing them need extra surgery and heavy processing.

Their method uses a harmless virus to load nerve cells with a red glow protein. The glow shows fine fibers and fresh sprouts with no extra staining steps. A standard workflow kept labeling steady across animals in their tests. The virus can ride along with other viruses for paired gene tweaks. The team aims to lower the bar for axon repair studies. A cut pyramid tract served as the injury model in the work.
pmc-13618389:
Dominic Rafie and two colleagues report radiotherapy with a bolus for a twenty-three-year-old woman with a malignant phyllodes tumor of the breast. It is a rare fibroepithelial cancer that seldom strikes young adults and often recurs locally. After a lumpectomy left residual tumor, she underwent skin- and nipple-sparing mastectomy of the right breast. No consensus exists on radiation after surgery for this disease. The team reasoned from her high-risk features.

She received five thousand centigray to the chest wall over twenty-five fractions, then a boost. For six fractions a half-centimeter bolus was laid on the skin to defeat the skin-sparing effect near a close margin where her tissue expander flattened the target. Treatment was well tolerated, with soreness, itchiness, skin inflammation, darkening, dry peeling, and fatigue. The authors believe this is the first bolus report in an adult with this tumor.
pmc-13618789:
Adesina Adesuyi and four colleagues turn hard lessons from real artificial intelligence deployments in one English hospital trust into a readiness checklist for NHS providers. Governance guides give high-level guidance, but go-live surprises keep appearing after deployment. The team distilled safety gaps from two go-lives, an AI fracture detection system and an AI-supported prostate MRI pathway, plus a study of clinician-AI disagreements and improvement cycles.

The resulting SID and ADE checklist spans eight domains, from use-case scope and clinical safety through local validation, workforce readiness, information governance, buying risk, and monitoring with stop rules. Retrospective use on the originating deployments showed uneven results. Recurrent gaps sat in workforce readiness, validation, and monitoring. The authors present the tool as a practical prompt for structured debate before go-live, while noting its proof so far rests on the originating context alone.
pmc-13618889:
Amanda J. Gupta and nine colleagues map how researchers study depression in people with tuberculosis, a pairing that worsens diagnosis, adherence, and outcomes. Their scoping review searched nine databases without date limits and organized findings with an implementation framework covering reach, effectiveness, adoption, and maintenance. One hundred eighty-four studies qualified.

The field leans heavily on snapshots: about two thirds of studies were cross-sectional, and only eight were randomized trials, mostly of psychological interventions showing modest gains. Depression was almost always screened rather than diagnosed; just fifteen percent of studies used a formal interview or clinical criteria, and none ever checked how accurate any tool is. Over a third of the work came from India or China alone. Workforce shortages and stigma blocked integrated care, while task-shifting and embedding screening into routine visits helped, and no study examined long-term sustainability at all.
pmc-13618989:
Alessandro R. Marcon and three colleagues audit stem cell supplements sold on Amazon's Canadian storefront, checking whether they carry the natural product number license Health Canada requires for legal sale. Using a web scraper, they assembled one hundred stem cell supplements and, for comparison, one hundred vitamin D and one hundred longevity supplements. They then verified licenses against the regulator's database and analyzed the marketing.

They found a compliance gap: stem cell supplements were licensed far less consistently than comparison products, and their marketing pushed against regulatory limits. The study lands amid Health Canada's 2025 reforms, which cut red tape. The authors warn that easier licensing can lend an unearned stamp of legitimacy to products with weak evidence, turning a license into a marketing asset. For shoppers who treat a license as a quality signal, the gap between what a license means and what marketing implies is the practical takeaway.
pmc-13619089:
Stefania Nobili and six colleagues wrote a 2026 review on pairing two drug families for long-lasting pain. Gabapentinoids calm overactive nerve signaling, while duloxetine, an antidepressant, strengthens the brain's own pain-damping pathways. The authors argue that using both together follows logically from how chronic pain works, since such pain mixes nerve damage, tissue signals, and altered central processing.

Evidence summarized here covers diabetic nerve pain, pain after shingles, and fibromyalgia, where each drug alone already helps some patients. Pregabalin gets special note for fast dose adjustment and for easing anxiety-linked sleep problems. Early studies suggest the pairing may help people whose pain remains after one drug alone. The trials so far are small and short, so the authors frame the combination as a proof of concept needing fuller testing.
pmc-13621389:
Amir S Bernat, Lea Bromberg, David Sinefeld, and Boaz Arad built a framework for comparing the world's many skin tone scales against reality. Skin tone measurement matters for dermatology, device design, and fairness in artificial intelligence, yet the field leans on a patchwork of word-based and card-based scales. Their scale of scales rests on an archive of more than fifteen thousand spectral reflectance readings from a globally diverse group.

Laying the major scales over that ground truth showed wide gaps. The best-known clinical and design scales chopped a smooth, many-sided trait into boxes that miss real variation. A popular printed skin tone guide even shifted its apparent color under different lighting, a failure called metamerism. The authors conclude that subjective categories cannot carry rigorous science and urge a shared framework built directly on measured light spectra.
pmc-13622989:
Sean Burkitt and colleagues test a label-free way to track inhaled gold nanoparticles inside lung tissue. Gold particles this small are used in medicine and industry, yet their long stay in the body raises safety questions. Standard tracking attaches glowing labels that can fall off and give false signals, so the team used light the gold itself gives off under a special microscope.

Mice breathed in the particles through the nose at three dose levels, and organs were checked after one week and one month. Chemical analysis found the gold stayed in the lungs, with no sign of spread to liver, spleen, brain, or kidneys. The imaging method showed dose-linked deposits and clumping, and it still found the particles a month later deep in the tissue. The authors say the approach beat ordinary microscopy and could support both safety testing and inhaled drug design.
pmc-13623389:
Alan Messala de Aguiar Britto and colleagues report their experience with nurse-led care for pregnant and postpartum women riding ambulances in Rio de Janeiro's Cegonha Carioca programme. The report reads the service through the Three Delays Model, which blames maternal deaths on slow decisions to seek care, slow arrival at a facility, and slow treatment on arrival. Their account spans 2012 to 2024.

Against the first delay, public awareness of the free ambulance service and humane onboard care encouraged women to call early. Against the second, free access, well-placed ambulances, and a named referral maternity hospital cut the search for a bed. Against the third, clear communication, triage by urgency, and alert systems sped up proper care. The authors present the nurse-led transport model as a workable way to shave minutes off obstetric emergencies and lower maternal deaths.
pmc-13624389:
Xiaoyuan Pan and colleagues survey why older adults in two Chinese cities underuse dental care, testing a combined behaviour model that merges belief-based and intention-based theories of health action. China's older population carries untreated dental disease, and visits tend to happen late, when pain forces the issue. The team questioned 356 older adults in Foshan and Guangzhou in mid-2023.

Only a third actively sought dental knowledge, two-thirds skipped regular check-ups, and barely half had received treatment. A quarter of respondents delayed care when tooth pain disrupted daily life. Path analysis showed the strongest driver of using services was intention backed by a sense of control, followed by believing treatment helps. Social expectations mattered only by feeding intention. Education, income, and city versus countryside residence shifted several factors. The authors recommend campaigns that build confidence and correct rosy misjudgements about oral health, backed by social support.
pmc-13625289:
Mahmoud F Mubarak and co-authors build a better desalination membrane by seeding three nanomaterials into its thin active skin. Reverse osmosis membranes usually trade flow against salt blocking, so the team added graphene oxide flakes, a porous crystal called ZIF-8, and treated carbon nanotubes during the skin-forming reaction. Microscope and surface tests confirmed the additives landed, leaving the surface smoother, wetter, and more negatively charged.

Under standard test pressure, the membrane let water through far faster than a plain one while still rejecting nearly all salt. A statistical design hunted the best running settings, flow models fit the data closely, and the membrane recovered almost fully after protein fouling, then held steady for thirty days. The blend, the authors say, narrows the flow-versus-blocking gap.
pmc-13627189:
Radmila Matijevic and colleagues test whether weak muscle and thin bone truly hunt together in older adults, or merely share birthdays. Their community study measured 649 people aged sixty-five and over, mostly women, with body scans, grip tests, and a short physical battery. Osteoporosis followed world criteria, while sarcopenia was scored three different ways, since rival definitions of low muscle mass disagree widely.

The definition changed everything. Low muscle mass ran from under four percent to nearly sixteen percent of the group. Confirmed sarcopenia ran from about one to four percent. Osteoporosis, by contrast, sat at about eighteen percent. Yet under no definition did the two conditions overlap more than chance predicts. The pairing named osteosarcopenia, the authors conclude, may be less a single syndrome than shared aging, and clinics should measure both on their own terms.
pmc-13637089:
Mary Kate LoPiccolo and eleven colleagues published this 2026 screening study of disordered eating in people whose inherited metabolic diseases demand strict lifelong eating rules. Diets that ban protein, sugar, or fat are the main treatment for these rare conditions. Clinicians suspected the constant food vigilance breeds eating problems, yet nobody had measured it. The team recruited patients aged sixteen and over on prescription diets at a New York metabolic center and gave them two screening forms.

Fifty-one patients completed both tools. The quick screen flagged a likely eating disorder in about a third of them, roughly triple the general population rate. The longer inventory showed more binge eating, restriction, excessive exercise, and hostility toward obesity than population norms. Most participants managed low-protein diets for phenylketonuria, the commonest condition here. The authors urge metabolic clinics to screen routinely, since eating disorders can wreck both diet control and mental health.
pmc-13637389:
Yasemin Gümüş Şekerci and two colleagues published this 2026 study of delayed health care among survivors of the 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake in Türkiye. Nearly two years on, many survivors still lived in temporary accommodation centers. The team surveyed five hundred ninety-six adults in Hatay centers during mid 2025. A validated scale measured how much people put off needed care, and a classic behavioral model sorted the influences into predisposing, enabling, and need-based factors.

Almost half the survivors showed delay behavior. All three factor families fed the pattern in the model, which explained about a quarter of the differences between people. The authors read the persistence as structural, not personal: displaced people face broken continuity, cost, and access hurdles long after the emergency phase ends. They call for accessible, continuous, trauma-aware services in recovery settings, arguing delay this widespread widens health gaps between displaced and housed populations.
pmc-13639589:
Kojima and colleagues assessed in 2026 a blood-test screening plan for venous thromboembolism, dangerous clots in veins or lungs, after total hip replacement. D-dimer testing is common after surgery, but the best cutoff is disputed. Their hospital measured D-dimer one week after surgery in 1,651 hip replacements from 2007 to 2023 and sent patients at or above a set level for contrast CT scans.

About one in five hips crossed the threshold. 31 of those patients proved to have clots: most were isolated deep vein thrombosis, a few lung clots, and two had both. Every diagnosed patient received anticoagulation, and no fatal or severe clot event occurred in the cohort. Female sex, older age, treated diabetes, and greater blood loss each tracked with higher D-dimer levels. The authors call the strategy feasible while asking for work to fix the ideal cutoff.
pmc-13643189:
Petersen and colleagues published a 2026 ecology study on why young grey wolves leave the pack where they were born. Grey wolves live in family groups and breed cooperatively, meaning only some adults raise pups while others help. The team worked in Idaho and asked how food, crowding, hunting deaths, and sex shaped that first move away from home.

Working from DNA in samples taken from harvested wolves, Petersen rebuilt family trees for 182 sibling groups and judged the status of 224 animals. Eighty-six had left home and 138 had stayed, and leavers travelled about 82 kilometres on average. Leaving was more likely where prey was plentiful and wolf density was low. Deaths caused by people showed no clear effect, and males and females behaved alike.
pmc-13645589:
Taparia Saloni, Nagaraju Chaithra, and Shivaswamy Umamaheshwari review lab and animal evidence on using probiotics, helpful live microbes, against Candida yeast infections. Candida can cause surface infections and dangerous deep infections, above all in people with weak immune defenses. Drug resistance and stubborn biofilms are making treatment harder. Their review searched three databases for studies from 2015 to early January 2026.

Eighteen studies qualified, most testing Lactobacillus types in lab dishes rather than in living hosts. Probiotics slowed yeast growth, blocked sticking to surfaces, and reduced the shift into the invasive thread-like form. They also made antimicrobial substances and helped restore a healthy microbe balance. Results from live models stayed thin, and study methods varied too much for pooled numbers. The authors see promise here, while calling for stronger trials.
pmc-13645889:
Jan-Lucca Hennes and eight colleagues test gentler scanning setups for imaging the aorta, the body's main artery, with a newer photon-counting CT scanner in 2026. Lower radiation and less contrast dye both protect patients, yet image quality must stay high. Records covered fifty-seven patients scanned over about eight months, split among low-dye, low-dose, and combined low settings. Four radiologists rated the images, and matched standard-scanner groups served as comparisons.

The low-dose setup cut radiation by roughly two fifths compared with a standard scanner while still giving sharper contrast measures. Low-dye scans were rated better in quality than the standard comparison, and the combined low setting matched it. The authors conclude that both dose and dye can be cut substantially on this scanner type without losing diagnostic quality. That matters for patients who need repeated aorta checks or whose kidneys limit dye use.
pmc-13646089:
Xinyun Li and Lin Wu examine how gentle ultrasound pulses help bone-forming cells grow inside porous titanium scaffolds meant for large bone defects. The metal scaffolds are strong, yet their surface does little to invite bone growth on its own. Mouse bone precursor cells were seeded into the scaffolds and given low-intensity pulsed ultrasound. The pair tracked cell shape, survival, bone-related gene activity, and the cells' small-molecule chemistry.

Cells receiving ultrasound looked healthier, died less, and switched on more bone-building genes than untreated scaffold cells. Chemical profiling found eighty-six changed metabolites, spread across vitamin, fat, and amino acid pathways. The shifts sketch how a physical signal may rewire cell chemistry toward bone formation. The authors present the results as a mechanism lead for pairing ultrasound with metal implants in repair of big bone gaps.
pmc-13646289:
Wujie Wang and five colleagues uncover a hidden noise source that limits fiber-optic sensing over single cables carrying light both ways, in a 2026 paper. Such two-way links let existing communication cables double as sensors, yet leftover noise has forced engineers to abandon the design at large scale. The team splits the mystery noise, which they call ghost noise, into two parts tied to light polarization and to calculation cross-talk. They then build a countermeasure that sweeps polarization while scrambling the signal phase.

The hybrid method added no noise at all across a seven-kilometer test link. Over ten kilometers it cut background noise by nearly ninety-five percent. The team says the usable low-noise distance grows about sixfold. Their result could let sensing networks ride on the world's installed communication fibers instead of needing dedicated lines, a shift with wide reach for monitoring infrastructure and environments.
pmc-13646389:
Janet A. Deatrick argues, in a 2026 paper, that family ethics deserves a higher place on nursing's agenda. Family nursing, she writes, is morally bound to the well-being of families and of society, and ethics should match that reach. Her vision rests on relational ethics, which judges choices inside the web of family ties. She lays out consequences for practice, research, and teaching.

In practice, she calls for team care protocols that build in structured family ethics conversations, informed by how family systems work. Research should widen, asking how the values families and cultures hold can feed moral distress and steer care. Teaching should bring real cases, study of culture, and training in emotional intelligence into classrooms and skills labs. Together, she argues, these steps would prepare nurses who are both ethically grounded and responsive to the diverse families they serve.
pmc-13647089:
Matthias Pierce writes a 2026 commentary on an editorial warning that rising mental-health awareness could carry hidden costs. The editorial used a systems model to predict that surges in help-seeking might dilute diagnostic accuracy and treatment benefit, harming patients on balance. Pierce finds the framework timely and valuable. His piece then takes its assumptions apart one by one.

The predictions rest on new help-seekers being milder cases, on diagnostic thresholds drifting downward, and on treatment helping less as volume grows. Evidence for each assumption, Pierce notes, is still thin. Where the mechanisms do operate, he suggests counters such as targeted campaigns aimed at those most in need and triage systems that sort urgency well. His commentary turns an alarming model into a research agenda: test the assumptions before fearing the awareness itself.
pmc-13647389:
Sebastian Holm and Reza Tabrisi present a surgical case in which a jaw was rebuilt with a bone flap from the lower leg of a patient who had varicose veins. This free fibula flap method is the gold standard after oral cancer removal, yet almost nothing is written about whether ropey leg veins endanger the flap. The report details how venous congestion was handled during the operation and how the patient fared afterward. A scoping review searched for any related publications.

The review found only two relevant papers in the entire literature. With evidence that thin, the authors refuse any causal claim linking surface varicose veins with flap trouble. They frame the case as hypothesis-generating and name the gap plainly. Their call is for research on whether targeted vein checks before surgery would help selected patients, rather than assuming the finding is harmless or dangerous.
pmc-13649389:
Xidong Wu and four colleagues tracked body heat in stroke patients after a clot was pulled from a brain artery. Most past work used one reading or a fever cut-off, which hides how heat changes over time. The team used care unit records for 237 patients and grouped their heat curves over three days.

Four groups emerged, from stable normal heat to heat that stayed high. The group with lasting high heat had far more deaths at 90 days than the stable group. Yet the gap shrank in checks that took early fever care and new infections into account. The authors call the heat groups a research lead, not a proven tool for care.
pmc-13650689:
Takeshi Kashiwagi and six colleagues, publishing in 2026, test a shortcut for palliative radiotherapy in a Japanese community hospital. Instead of bringing patients back for a dedicated planning scan, the team planned treatment directly on recent diagnostic scans. The aim was to cut the days that people with painful spinal metastases wait for relief.

Five patients with six spinal sites were enrolled in June 2024, each receiving a single radiation dose with mandatory image-guided positioning checks. Every patient completed treatment, and the average total time in the center was under an hour. Pain eased partly or fully for a quarter of patients at four weeks, and the complete response share rose by twelve weeks, with no acute side effects appearing. The authors judge the workflow feasible and safe under careful patient selection, while the tiny enrollment marks the study as a first feasibility step.
pmc-13651489:
Gabrielle M Beaudry and four colleagues use linked Welsh health records to measure how much an emergency department visit for self-harm raises a young person's risk of dying, and from what. Self-harm in youth is common and tied to suicide, yet deaths from accidents and other causes after presentation are less often quantified.

Records from 2008 to 2023 covered over six hundred thousand young people aged five to eighteen, of whom about fourteen thousand had presented with self-harm. Deaths were more than three times as common in that group after adjustment. Suicide risk spiked in the first year after presentation and stayed elevated afterward, and accidental death showed a strikingly similar pattern, very high early and still raised later. No clear link appeared for other causes. The authors argue that prevention after a self-harm visit must reach beyond suicide to accidental death, especially in the first fragile year.
pmc-13654389:
Taisuke Nakade and thirteen colleagues use a large Japanese heart failure registry to ask whether frailty raises the risk of bleeding. Frail patients are widely assumed to bleed more easily, especially on blood-thinning drugs, yet direct evidence in heart failure care was thin. The analysis draws on the JROADHF-NEXT registry of patients hospitalized with acute decompensated heart failure across Japan.

The team measured how often bleeding events occurred, whether risk climbed with frailty severity, and whether a bleed predicted later death among patients receiving antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy. Answers to those three questions shape everyday prescribing, where doctors balance clot prevention against bleeding danger in patients least able to tolerate either. Registry analyses like this one give that balancing act actual numbers instead of habit and worry.
pmc-1563489:
Raj, Peskin, Tranchina, and co-authors study why identical cells make uneven amounts of messenger RNA. Even in a uniform group, single cells have been found to hold different counts of a given protein. The team asked where that variation begins in mammalian cells.

They counted single mRNA molecules made from a test gene, one cell at a time. Their counts show that production comes in bursts rather than a steady flow, which explains much of the spread. Burst-like production is now a basic idea in how scientists think about noise and chance inside cells.
pmc-4086089:
Biasini, Bienert, Waterhouse, and their colleagues described SWISS-MODEL in 2014. The server builds three-dimensional models of proteins from their sequences. Such homology modelling, which copies the shape of a known related protein, had become routine when no measured structure exists.

SWISS-MODEL is fully automated and works through a friendly web interface. Users get a reliable model without needing complex local software or deep expertise. The method uses evolutionary information, since related proteins tend to keep the same fold. These models help researchers plan experiments, explain mutations, and search for drug binding sites on new proteins.
pmc-4246889:
Wang, Liang, and Zen reviewed in 2014 the molecular mechanisms that set the balance between macrophage types. Macrophages are a core part of innate immunity and can either slow or drive cell growth and tissue repair. Variety and flexibility are their hallmarks, the authors stress.

The review contrasts classical M1 activation, which fights germs and inflames, with alternative M2 activation, which heals. It maps the signals and gene switches that push cells toward either pole. That balance goes wrong in infection, cancer, and chronic wounds. Knowing the controls points to ways drugs might nudge macrophages toward the state a patient needs.
pmc-5073889:
Becht, Giraldo, Lacroix, and their co-authors introduced MCP-counter in 2016. The method estimates how many tissue-infiltrating immune and stromal cells are present in a tissue sample, using gene expression data. Tissues are heterogeneous, mixing many cell types, which hides who is actually there.

MCP-counter gives a robust count of how abundant each of eight immune cell types and two stromal types is. The authors validated it with in vitro mixtures of messenger RNA of known makeup. Knowing a tumor's immune makeup helps predict its course and its response to immunotherapy. A method that works on standard expression data makes such estimates widely available.
pmc-6891889:
Maigeng Zhou, Haidong Wang, Xinying Zeng, and coauthors analyzed health in China and its provinces in 2019. China holds about a fifth of the world's people, and its government treats public health as a priority. Province-level evidence is what policy actually needs.

Using Global Burden of Disease data, the study tracks deaths, disease, and risk factors province by province. Stroke and heart disease lead, while smoking and diet risks loom large. Richer coastal provinces look very different from inland ones. The results guide where China should aim its prevention spending first.
pmc-7245089:
Xu and co-authors reported in 2020 on treating patients with severe COVID-19 using tocilizumab, a drug that blocks the receptor for interleukin-6. Their reasoning starts from the biology of severe disease, where large numbers of immune cells switch on and release signaling proteins. That flood of signals can drive a dangerous whole body inflammatory reaction often called a cytokine storm.

The authors describe giving the drug to severely ill patients and watching how their condition changed afterward. Their report argued that blocking this one immune signal could calm the harmful response. Coming early in the pandemic, when few proven treatments existed, the work drew wide attention to immune calming drugs as a path worth testing in larger, stricter trials.
pmc-7385689:
Valentina Puntmann and colleagues asked in 2020 what COVID-19 leaves behind in the heart after patients seem to have recovered. They studied one hundred patients recently recovered from the infection, found through a testing center rather than through heart complaints. Each person received detailed heart imaging with cardiac magnetic resonance, a scan that can reveal swelling, scarring, and weakened pumping.

The scans showed signs of heart involvement in a striking share of these recovered patients, including in some who had not been severely ill. That finding shifted attention from the lungs alone to the need for follow up care after infection. It also raised open questions, still debated, about how lasting such heart changes are and what they mean for long term health.
racine-phaedra-boswell-1889:
Robert Bruce Boswell translated Racine's Phaedra into English for this edition. A note up front recalls that Racine was born at Ferte-Milon on December 21, 1639. He won fame with Andromaque and wrote his masterworks between 1669 and 1677.

Phaedra closed that great run in 1677 and crowns French classical tragedy. Phaedra, wife of Theseus, burns with forbidden love for her stepson Hippolytus. Her confession sets off a chain of lies, curses, and deaths that no one can halt. Racine kept the strict form set by Corneille and filled it with fierce feeling, so passion is staged with rare force.
schiller-ghost-seer-1789:
The Ghost-Seer, Schiller's unfinished novel of 1789, reached English in the Bohn Standard Library translation. A German prince visiting Venice falls in with a mysterious Armenian who seems to command spirits. Secret societies, staged apparitions, and a Sicilian inquisition thicken the plot around him.

Schiller never finished the tale, and it breaks off amid its mysteries. Even so, its mix of conspiracy, fraud, and the occult proved potent. The book helped found the German tradition of the eerie romance. Later writers borrowed its secret-society machinery for decades of thrillers. Read as a fragment, it still casts a spell: reason keeps failing, and the dark keeps its secrets.
scientific-american-supplement-no-711-au: How to raise turkeys opens the agriculture contents of Supplement No. 711, dated New York, August 17, 1889, in Volume XXVIII. That piece collects hints and suggestions on raising the delicate fowls, so often the cause of trouble to farmers. Pear Duchesse d'Angouleme follows, the history of the famous pear tree with hints on culture and general treatment.
scientific-american-supplement-no-717-se: The Girard hydraulic railway leads the civil engineering contents of Supplement No. 717, dated New York, September 28, 1889, in Volume XXVIII. Called one of the great curiosities of the Paris exposition, the almost frictionless railway is shown with sectional illustrations of its structure in eight illustrations. Electricity gives early electric lighting, electric lighting in Salem in 1859 as a curious piece of early history. An electric motor for alternating currents follows, on an entirely new principle, with results obtained and the economic outlook of the invention.
solovyov-russie-eglise-universelle-1889:
Vladimir Solovyov, Russia's great religious thinker, wrote his masterwork in French in 1889. La Russie et l'Église universelle argues that Russia bears a special call in the life of the Church. The text here is his own French, the tongue he chose for the West.

Solovyov holds that the split between Rome and the East must heal, and that Russia can help heal it. He reads Russian history as a stage in a wider drama of faith and rule. The book blends deep thought, history, and a poet's fire. It remains the core text of his hope for one Church.
spalding-s-baseball-guide-and-official-l: Spalding's Base Ball Guide and Official League Book for 1889 opens with trade matter rather than play. A page on the Spalding trade mark warns that base ball and athletic goods draw copyists, as all lines of trade do. Such folk, the firm says, steal its first designs, styles, and names, and use like pictures and wording to fool buyers into taking poor goods for Spalding's own make.
spallanzani-dissertations-natural-histor:
Lazzaro Spallanzani, an Italian priest and fine trial maker, gave his great work on living things to English readers in 1789. The two parts deal with how beasts and plants breed and grow. His chief foes were Needham and Buffon, who held that life can spring from rot.

Spallanzani sealed broth in glass, boiled it long, and kept it clean of all germs. No life grew in it, though air and heat had their full play in his tests. His work first made the old claim of life from rot hard to hold with a straight face.
spr-proceedings-vol5-1888-1889:
Parts twelve, thirteen, and fourteen fill volume five of the SPR Proceedings, dated 1888 to 1889. Three parts in one binding show the society's pace of work. Experiments on thought transference grow more exact, with random targets and sealed records. The census of hallucinations gathers pace in the background.

Witnesses describe seeing figures of the dying at the moment of death. Investigators print failures beside successes, a habit that set their work apart. Mediumship sittings, including trance cases, receive full transcripts. The debate over evidence runs through British learned life in these pages. Volume five is a thick slice of that debate. It rewards readers who like primary sources.
stevenson-master-ballantrae-1889:
Robert Louis Stevenson published The Master of Ballantrae in 1889, a novel of two brothers torn apart. The Durie family must choose sides in the Jacobite rising of 1745. By a coin toss, the elder brother James joins the rebels while Henry stays home. James is reported dead but returns, bitter and demanding.

The brothers' hatred grows over years and follows them to America. James, the Master, is charming and cruel in equal measure. Henry suffers in silence as his life is ruined. The feud ends in the wilds of New York. Stevenson called up a dark, brooding tale of envy and fate.
strindberg-pariah-1889:
August Strindberg wrote Pariah in 1889, a one-act battle of wills, here in Edith and Warner Oland's translation. The scene sets two men with criminal pasts against each other in Darwinian naturalism at its most concentrated. Strindberg wrote it for his experimental Scandinavian theatre in Copenhagen that same winter of bold new drama.

Mr. X, an archaeologist, hosts Mr. Y, a traveler who slowly reveals he knows X's buried crime. Each man has killed, in fact or in law, and each tries to master the other's conscience. Talk of guilt, heredity, and suggestion turns the visit into a duel fought with words and silences. X wins, if winning it is, by the colder nerve and the stronger will to live unashamed. The Olands' version keeps the talk taut in English, a small masterclass in psychological fencing.
strindberg-the-stronger-1889:
August Strindberg wrote The Stronger in 1889, a ten-minute scene, here in Edith and Warner Oland's translation. The one-woman duel of two actresses is often called the most perfect miniature in modern drama today. Only one of the two women speaks, yet the silent one may be the stronger of them.

Mrs. X meets Miss Y, her husband's former lover, in a café on Christmas Eve in town. She talks, probes, boasts, and accuses while Miss Y sips, sews, and never says a word aloud. Doubt grows whether the silent woman lost the man or in fact kept his heart all along. Strindberg leaves the verdict open, and actresses relish the paired roles of speech and silence in performance. The Olands' version made the tiny play a staple of English studio theatres.
tavernier-travels-india-ball-vol1-1889:
Jean-Baptiste Tavernier, a French gem merchant, made six voyages to Persia and India in the seventeenth century. Volume One of his Travels in India, in Valentine Ball's 1889 translation, opens the record. Tavernier knew diamonds the way sailors know winds.

He describes the Mughal court, the great diamond mines of Golconda, and the roads and dangers of Asian trade. The Koh-i-Nur and other famous stones pass through his hands and his pages. Ball, a geologist, adds notes that test Tavernier's claims. Merchants, kings, and jewel thieves all move through this firsthand source on the gem trade.
tavernier-travels-india-ball-vol2-1889:
Volume Two of Tavernier's Travels in India, in Ball's translation, completes the gem merchant's six voyages. Tavernier had traded from Paris to the courts of Persia and India for forty years. His eye for stones and prices never dulls.

This volume details the diamond mines, the weighing and pricing of gems, and the customs of Indian merchants. Tavernier also reports on coins, weights, and the routes caravans took between ports and mines. Ball's notes correct and confirm the text from later knowledge. The result is a working manual of the seventeenth-century jewel trade, told by its most famous dealer.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-01-: A portrait of Mr. Daniel Hand fronts the January 1889 number, which starts volume 43. Editors greet the new year, note large gifts from the wealthy, size up the Southern situation, and mark the death of Mrs. George A. Woodard. The Reverend C. J. Ryder writes on spending in a planned way. Scraps from letters fill the Chinese pages, Mrs. A. A. Myers reports on mountain white work, and Mrs. G. W. Moore states the needs of colored women and girls.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-02-: February 1889 names its helpers good Samaritans and prints a plain warning next to the perks of life membership. Editors contrast their own work among the freedmen with Roman Catholic efforts, then list every field worker. A meeting of colored Roman Catholics is reported, as is time among the Tennessee mountains. The Chinese section marks an anniversary of missions and peeks at a shady side. Mountain girls anchor the women's pages.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-03-: Pastors and churches get a call to enlist in the March 1889 number. Editors face white race rule in the South head-on and report training colored students for Episcopal ministry. Southern items tell of revival at Le Moyne Institute, crowded school-rooms, and daily life, with an obituary for Mrs. Hattie B. Sherman. A plea from Loo Quong fills the Chinese pages, and a monthly concert plan is laid out for supporters.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-04-: April 1889 asks a sharp question about a remedy: who is to furnish it? Curious facts, school echoes, and a doctrinal sermon fill the opening pages, with book notices at the end. The Ballard Building is dedicated in the South, one worker marks ten years at the front, and Thomasville, Georgia, gets a new organ. Indian news comes by way of a visit to Park Street Church station, and a San Diego Chinese mission reports in.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-05-: Money and a centennial frame May 1889, with Georgia Congregationalism, bright spots in the South, and the government's hand in Indian affairs up front. Georgia churches meet as an association, field laborers preach and teach at Thomasville, and the death of Mrs. Bennett is noted. Perils of missionary life and first fruits come from the Indian field. Los Angeles reports on its Chinese mission, Alabama women organize, and young readers learn how the pennies grew.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-06-: June 1889 prints voices from the field, a line drawn between two centuries, and a notice of Frederick Douglass. A church goes up in a single day in the South, Tougaloo University and Hampton both report, and Whitley County sends items. One piece works to build love of country among colored people, and a Black girl's prose poem is printed. Indian pages ask what one day's missionary work looks like, while Chinese Sunday-school method is spelled out step by step.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-07-: Atlanta University and Georgia Congregationalism lead July 1889, with editors also praising the skill and hard work of Black labor and deploring caste inside churches. Southern stops include mountain work in Tennessee, Williamsburg Academy in Kentucky, Marshallville and Albany in Georgia, Wilmington in North Carolina, and the senior class at Le Moyne Institute. A trip runs among Indian out-stations. The Reverend Dr. Dana reports on Chinese work, and women's state groups meet and report from Meridian and Macon.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-08-: August 1889 mixes figures that keep improving with letters on civil rights in court. Its Southern centerpiece describes a trip through the Cumberland Mountains, pictured with cuts of cabins, a native mountain church, and the academy at Williamsburg, Kentucky. Anniversary exercises follow at Fisk, Talladega, Straight, Le Moyne, and Avery Institute, plus a new church and school at Alco, Alabama. Miss Collins writes from the Indian field, the Ramona Indian School appears, and Chinese work is noted at Oroville, Marysville, and Petaluma.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-09-: Five questions and a short catechism on the Association's work open September 1889, with editors also taking up cars, church, and courts, and Rome's bid for Black loyalty. Southern pages cover the Hand Fund, Howard University, and Tillotson Institute, plus a call from Aunt Mary. A letter comes from the school at Oahe in the Indian field. Petaluma reports outreach work among the Chinese, and women's state groups send in paragraphs.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-10-: October 1889 closes the money year and prints letters from givers. Editors discuss voting members, compromises, the Congregational churches of Georgia, and Indian contract schools, with a minister's testimony added. District notes run under the motto about giving freely. Southern items gather field news, a vacation at Tougaloo, a teacher's voice from the Tennessee mountains, and signs of progress, ending with an obituary and a student's letter.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-11-: Free Once More heads the November 1889 number, which also reports the National Council, colored delegates, and the Mohonk Conference, and notes the deaths of Superintendent Hall and Dr. Lane. A broad survey then walks the whole field: Southern schooling, church work, mountain work, Indians, Chinese, new building, women's work, and money. The Chinese field gets its own review of the year, and North Carolina women's work is singled out.
the-american-missionary-volume-43-no-12-: December 1889 gives its pages to the annual meeting: full proceedings, the treasurer's report in brief, and the Daniel Hand Fund. Secretary Strieby sets out the Association's place and work, while Secretary Beard gives a missionary view of the Southern situation. Committee reports draw replies from ten named speakers, among them Wright, Woodbury, Taylor, Hiatt, and Fisk. The Reverend Dr. Taylor gives the closing address, and press notices on the meeting are gathered in.
the-constitution-of-the-empire-of-japan-:
The 1889 constitution of the Empire of Japan opens with the emperor's oath, sworn in the sanctuary of the imperial palace. He swears to the founder of his house and to his other forebears that he will keep the old form of government from decline. He follows a policy as wide as heaven and earth.

He explains that, as human affairs move forward, he has set the house law and the constitution down in clear written rules. They are to guide his heirs, widen his subjects' scope to support him, and keep the laws honored for ages. A rescript follows, in which he issues the basic law by the supreme power passed down from his forebears, for his subjects and their children.
the-mirror-of-literature-amusement-and-i:
The Mirror's number for Saturday, September 6, 1828, No. 330, asks why the English are not a musical people. The editors concede the charge from newspaper critics: England has no national music like the Welsh, Irish, or Scotch. English music, like English language, is a patchwork stolen from every nation in Europe. Yet the king plays the violoncello delightfully, and an Academy of Music exists.

Counter-evidence piles up wryly. An Italian theatre ruined Mr. Ebers, who lost 47,000 pounds by being married to sweet sounds. An English Opera House performs scarcely any but foreign music, successfully. Pepys's Diary shows Italian singers arrived under Charles II, brought by Killigrew from Venice about 1688, though they sang only detached scenes. Readers get a national failing argued from opera-house ledgers and a diarist's evenings.
the-works-of-the-highly-experienced-and-: The Works of the highly experienced and famous chymist John Rudolph Glauber, 1689. The chemist's works. This book preserves that alchemy. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
theocritus-bion-moschus-lang-1889:
Andrew Lang rendered Theocritus, Bion, and Moschus into English prose in 1889. Theocritus, a Sicilian Greek of the third century BCE, invented pastoral poetry with his Idylls. Bion and Moschus followed him a century later, and their few poems travel with his in this volume.

Singing shepherds trade verses for a carved cup, a lovesick goatherd pines for a city girl, and a sorceress works a spell at night. City pieces and court poems break the country calm. Bion's Lament for Adonis and the Lament for Bion close the set in grief. Lang's clear prose keeps the songs close for readers without Greek.
tob-10789:
Franz Hartmann, a Theosophist and physician, argued in Occult Science in Medicine that healing involves forces beyond the scalpel. Drawing on Paracelsus and the mesmerists, he pointed to magnetism, suggestion, and the spirit's power over the body. Mainstream doctors of his day mostly dismissed such claims.

Hartmann sketches a healing of the whole person, in which the patient's inner state matters alongside drugs and surgery. Whatever modern readers make of his occult framework, the book preserves a lively period debate about mind, body, and cure. It stands as a period piece from the borderland where nineteenth-century science and occultism still overlapped.
tob-13789:
Annie Besant and C. W. Leadbeater turned their claimed clairvoyant mind-sight on the atom itself in Occult Chemistry, first published from their investigations in 1908. Using what they called a magnifying power of consciousness, they pictured the inner structure of elements as neat geometric shapes and counted subatomic units decades before such images were common.

Hydrogen, oxygen, and heavier elements are described and drawn as clusters of ultimate physical atoms. Supporters later claimed striking matches with real subatomic knowledge; skeptics see pattern-hunting and error. V1 evidence frames it fairly: either amazing or absurd, depending on what you believe. As a historical curiosity of Theosophy meeting science, it has no rival.
tob-4089:
Volume thirty-nine of the Sacred Books of the East holds James Legge's Texts of Taoism, part one. Legge, the Scottish scholar of China, translated the Tao Te Ching and writings of Chuang Tzu with full introductions and commentary. Victorian readers gained their first complete Taoist canon in English here.

Lao Tzu's short book of the Way praises softness, silence, and rule by non-action. Chuang Tzu answers with parables, jokes, and dreams of butterflies. Legge, a missionary by training, treats both with respect and care. Verified from the 1919 edition, part one opens the Taoist shelf of Muller's great series.
tob-4189:
Sanskrit fables of statecraft fill the Hitopadesha, the Book of Good Counsel, drawn from the older Panchatantra tradition. Edwin Arnold's translation of 1861 introduced the tales to England. A king's dull sons must learn rule, so a sage teaches them through the doings of beasts.

Jackal ministers plot, lion kings blunder, and geese and owls go to war in stories within stories. Each tale lands a maxim on alliance, caution, or the reading of character. Arnold's verse and prose keep the bite of the originals. The evidence notes no public-domain text has yet been located for this entry. The offspring rivaled its parent in fame.
tob-9389:
Ptolemy of Alexandria summed up ancient astronomy in the Almagest, the work that ruled the science of the heavens for fourteen hundred years. Earth stands still at the center; sun, moon, planets, and stars wheel around it in circles upon circles. His star catalogue lists over a thousand stars with their places.

Halma's name attaches to the famed translation noted in the record. The evidence adds that no public-domain text has yet been found for this entry. The Almagest's system was wrong about the center and right about the motions, accurate enough to steer calendars and charts until Copernicus rebuilt the whole scheme.
tolstoy-kreutzer-sonata-1889: Leo Tolstoy's Kreutzer Sonata and Other Stories, translated by Benjamin R. Tucker, is laid out in a contents list. A translator's preface precedes the title story's twenty-eight chapters. A lesson of the Kreutzer Sonata follows as a separate piece. Ivan the Fool comes next, its own chapters listed, and further stories continue beyond what is shown. The volume's cover and contents are what is present here, so Tolstoy's stories themselves do not appear.
un-ga-res-1889:
Southern Rhodesia drew the General Assembly back in Resolution 1889, adopted on 6 November 1963. The colony's case had filled vote after vote: the 1960 call to end colonial rule, and texts of 1962 and October 1963. A fresh report from the decolonization team lay before the Assembly. It stressed one point: the vast African majority were still denied their basic rights to vote and to take part in rule.

Reports of the Secretary-General from late 1962 and mid-1963 were weighed as well. So were pleas heard in person by the Fourth Committee. The text also takes note of stands taken at Addis Ababa in May 1963. There, heads of free African states had met. They called for swift freedom across the continent.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
General Assembly Resolution 1889 (XVIII), adopted on 6 November 1963, pressed Britain once more on Southern Rhodesia. The Assembly approved its Special Committee's report. It restated the people's right to self-rule and freedom. It voiced deep regret that Britain had not acted on the chain of earlier resolutions about the territory.

The minority government in the colony had asked Britain for independence under the 1961 constitution. The Assembly told Britain to refuse until majority rule based on a vote for every adult was in place. It told Britain to call a conference of all parties at once. The conference was to plan independence on that footing.
un-sc-res-1189: The formal record of the Security Council includes the text numbered 1189, catalogued for 1998. The Charter gives the Council power to bind member states, which is why its resolutions are kept with such care. Here the primary source stands on its own, with the formal phrasing that lawyers and historians rely on. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-1289: In the sequence of Security Council decisions, Resolution 1289 is the entry catalogued for 2000 in this library. Council texts of this kind carry weight under the UN Charter, since the Council holds the main duty for peace and security. The entry gives the decision in full, as transcribed on English Wikisource from the records of the United Nations.
un-sc-res-1389:
Sierra Leone's coming elections were written into UNAMSIL's tasks on 16 January 2002. Disarmament had officially ended, and the peace process was advancing. The electoral commission had asked the United Nations for support. Free, fair, and open elections were judged key to the country's long-term stability. The Secretary-General's report of 13 December 2001 set out the needs.

The Council decided that UNAMSIL would help the smooth holding of the elections. Its Chapter VII powers under resolution 1270 (1999) were restated. The mission's civilian police element would grow as the Secretary-General had proposed. An interim electoral section inside UNAMSIL was welcomed, with offices planned in each electoral district. The mission's public information work for the electoral commission drew praise. The Council underlined that Sierra Leone's government and commission bore the prime duty for free and fair polls, and it urged help for voters and parties alike.
un-sc-res-1489:
The looting of Congo's mineral wealth kept an expert panel in place under a Council decision of 13 August 2003. The panel's chairman had told the Council in July that the plunder went on, above all in the east of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. A transitional government had just taken office in Kinshasa.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to extend the Expert Panel's mandate. It repeated its demand that all states act at once to stop the illegal taking of Congo's resources. The panel would share its information with the governments concerned. Parties that settled their cases could be struck from its annexes. The Council stressed the link between resource theft and the small arms trade that kept the eastern war alive. This hosted file carries the same text as resolution 1499, adopted at the same meeting.
un-sc-res-1589:
UNAMA was renewed after Afghanistan's first presidential vote on 24 March 2005. The presidential election of 9 October 2004 had been held with success. Parliamentary and local elections now had to be prepared. Narcotics, weak security in some regions, terror threats, and illegal armed groups all pressed at once. The Secretary-General's report of 18 March guided the renewal.

The Council extended UNAMA's mandate for twelve more months. It praised the United Nations' work beside the Afghan government and people. A framework for the mission's work with Kabul had to be set urgently, the Council stressed. Security for credible parliamentary, provincial, and district elections was named vital. The Council welcomed the world's help in setting up the new Afghan parliament. Substantial progress in disarming the militia forces was greeted. Kabul's fight against the drug trade won backing, with a call for stronger action by all states.
un-sc-res-1689:
Liberia's forests and gem fields meet in Resolution 1689, adopted in June 2006. Timber money had helped fund Charles Taylor's war effort, and sanctions had blocked the trade. With a new elected government in place, the Council lifted the timber ban while keeping diamond controls.

The split decision is the point of the text: reward reform in the timber sector, where new laws met Council terms, but hold diamonds until Liberia joined the Kimberley certification system. It shows sanctions being used as a lever that can move both ways. Few texts show that bargaining as clearly as this one.
un-sc-res-1789:
In a vote on 14 December 2007, the Council passed Resolution 1789 on Cyprus. The island remained divided, and the peace process had yet to restart in full. The United Nations Peacekeeping Force in Cyprus, called UNFICYP, had patrolled the buffer zone since 1964.

The text extends the mandate of UNFICYP until 15 June 2008. It keeps faith with the goal of a bicommunal, bizonal federation with political equality. Both sides are urged to move from groundwork into full negotiations without more delay. The Council repeats its call to restore the past military position at Strovilia, as in earlier votes on Cyprus.
un-sc-res-1889:
Women's part in peace and security was pushed forward on 5 October 2009. The Council restated its line of texts from resolution 1325 (2000) through 1888 (2009). It had the Secretary-General's report of 16 September 2009 before it. It praised states that had drawn up national action plans under resolution 1325 and urged more of the same.

The Council urged member states and regional bodies to raise women's roles at every stage of peace work. It restated its call for all parties in armed conflict to respect the law that protects women and girls, and it condemned every breach of that law. The Secretary-General was asked to build a strategy to raise the number of women in decision posts on peace and security. His country reports had to carry data on women in armed conflict.
un-sc-res-189:
Cambodia charged South Vietnam with raids across its border in 1964. Saigon's troops had crossed into Cambodian land. People had died in the raids. Saigon's government said it was sorry for them. On 4 June 1964 the Council deplored the raids. It took note of the regrets. Both states, it noted, wanted their ties back to normal.

Fair payment had to be made to Cambodia for the harm done. Those at fault had to act to stop more raids. All states had to respect Cambodia's neutral stance and its borders. The vote passed with no one against. Raids tied to the Vietnam War kept troubling Cambodia for years.
un-sc-res-2389:
The Great Lakes region was the matter before the Council in Resolution 2389, adopted on 8 December 2017. Displacement had passed ten million people across the region. Armed groups in eastern Congo still drew money from stolen minerals and wildlife. The 2013 peace framework for the region had won fresh pledges that October in Brazzaville.

The Council demands that all armed groups stop fighting at once. The FDLR, the ADF, and the LRA must disband, disarm, and free every child in their ranks. Ex-M23 and disarmed FDLR fighters should be sent home without conditions. States must not shelter war criminals or back armed groups in any form. Congo should press on with army reform and rebuild state authority in the east.
un-sc-res-289: At number 289 in its series, the Security Council decision is catalogued here as a 1970 record. A resolution may address a conflict, a court vacancy, a new member, or the running of the United Nations itself. Anyone studying UN practice can read the decision itself here, in the Wikisource transcription of the official record. The catalog places it in the DECLASSIFIED group of official public records.
un-sc-res-389:
East Timor's occupation was challenged again on 22 April 1976. The Council recalled resolution 384 (1975) and had the Secretary-General's report of 12 March 1976. East Timorese spokesmen had addressed it. Indonesia's forces, which had entered the territory the previous December, remained in place. The question also sat before the General Assembly.

The Council called on all states to respect East Timor's territorial integrity. It restated the people's right to self-determination under the 1960 declaration on self-rule. Indonesia was called to withdraw all its forces from East Timor without further delay. The Secretary-General's special representative was to continue the task set under resolution 384 and keep consulting the parties. He also had to report on the text's progress as soon as possible. All states were asked to help the United Nations win a peaceful solution and finish freeing the territory.
un-sc-res-489: Bearing number 489, this resolution of the Security Council is dated 1981 in the catalog. Formal decisions of this sort guide UN staff, peacekeeping forces, and governments in the years that follow. What is preserved is the exact formal wording, transcribed on English Wikisource from the official record of the Council. Its place here reflects the library's aim of keeping primary records readable.
un-sc-res-89:
Palestine's armistice deals needed guards, and Security Council Resolution 89, passed on 17 November 1950, deals with their watch. The text recalls the vote of August 1949 that hailed the armistice deals struck between the sides in the Palestine fight. Those deals, made by talks under the UN mediator, bound each side to shun all fresh acts of force. Their terms were to be watched by joint teams of the sides themselves.

Each such team is chaired by the chief of staff of the UN Truce Supervision Organization in Palestine, or by his named deputy. The Council had leaned on the sides to keep the deals in full. The text weighs how that watch should run, and how claims of breach should be heard. The armistice lines of 1949 held, in form, till the war of 1967.
un-sc-res-989: Listed under 1995, Resolution 989 preserves formal action taken by the United Nations Security Council. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades. No summary replaces it; the record itself is the content of the entry.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Security Council resolution 1189, adopted in 1998, responds to the terrorist bomb attacks of 7 August 1998 in Nairobi, Kenya, and Dar es Salaam, Tanzania. The Council strongly condemns the attacks, which killed hundreds of people, injured thousands and caused massive destruction, and expresses its deep sorrow and condolences to the victims' families.

The Council calls on all states and international institutions to support the investigations under way in Kenya, Tanzania and the United States. That support is so the perpetrators are caught and brought swiftly to justice. It thanks those who answered Kenyan and Tanzanian requests for help. It urges further assistance with reconstruction and disaster preparedness. It calls on every state, as a priority, to adopt practical measures against terrorism. Those measures are for the prosecution and punishment of those responsible.

Security Council resolution 1289, adopted on 7 February 2000, expands UNAMSIL, the United Nations Mission in Sierra Leone, as the West African force ECOMOG prepares to withdraw. The Council notes that UNAMSIL's deployment under resolution 1270 (1999) is nearly complete. It thanks ECOMOG for restoring security. It worries that disarmament is sporadic, abductees and child soldiers remain unreleased, and aid workers are still being attacked.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council raises UNAMSIL's military component to a maximum of 11,100 personnel. It adds tasks: guarding key sites in Freetown and Lungi airport, keeping supply routes open, and securing disarmament sites. The tasks include guarding collected weapons and protecting civilians under imminent threat of violence. The revised mandate runs six months. Reports come from the Secretary-General every 45 days. Troop levels can then be reviewed against conditions on the ground.

On 16 January 2002, by a full vote, the Council passed Resolution 1389. It backs Sierra Leone's shift from war to the ballot box. The peace had moved well by then. The laying down of arms had just been declared done. The Council called for stray guns to be picked up from townsfolk and ex-fighters. It asked for sound funds for the scheme that brings ex-fighters back to civil life.
